Native package scripts discovered through a builder are also labeled inferred; this distinguishes discovery from an Oyzu TOML definition, not script authorship. Cyan headings separate groups, inferred sources are muted and authored sources are purple. ui.color, NO_COLOR and terminal detection control color; Explicit ui.color=always/never wins; in auto mode NO_COLOR disables color and CLICOLOR_FORCE=1 enables it when NO_COLOR is absent. Long rows use lossless labeled records on narrow terminals. Unavailable tasks retain their reason. Commands quote arguments descriptively; they are not a portable shell script. Dependencies and hooks may add execution beyond that row. Credential-like command previews are withheld and terminal controls escaped. Do not embed credentials in task command arguments; use the supported environment or secret mechanisms instead. Listing reads discovery and resolved configuration but executes no tasks or native tools. JSON retains the task map and adds each task's origin object: kind (inferred or user-defined), source (full configuration source or null) and override (boolean). Existing argv and redacted environment fields retain their contracts. No configuration or lock files are changed by listing.
CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/configuration.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them.

publish.default selects a named OCI destination or publication set when oyzu publish has no --destination. publish.destinations is a typed map of names to registry, repository, and optional paired usernameEnv/passwordEnv credential references. publish.sets maps names to nonempty destination lists. Destination and set names must be distinct. Every selected destination is required. publish.requirements contains provenance (bundlePath, accepted Ed25519 publicKey, builderId) and signing (keyEnv, publicKey). Public keys are base64 raw 32-byte keys; keyEnv references a separately provisioned base64 32-byte signing seed. Never store secret values in project configuration. Evidence paths resolve relative to the source declaring effective requirements. These settings use the ordinary cascade, selected profiles and mandatory constraints. Each destinations map, sets map, and requirements object is atomic: a later source replaces the whole value instead of merging nested entries. The settings govern standalone safeguards; they cannot grant managed publication authority. See publishing for the complete example, evidence profile, digest-only coordinates and current limits. The configuration engine implements the public OEP-0002 draft in Rust. Its CLI and wire formats remain experimental; implementation authorization does not change the proposal's maintainer-review status. See the acceptance contract and measured implementation status. oyzu config show presents resolved status and profile first, followed by setting tables grouped by namespace and the computation digest. Keys retain their exact spelling; booleans use true/false and empty lists use []. Environment values and task bodies remain redacted under configuration inspection's contract; use oyzu env for environment inspection. --json retains the structured result. See the CLI style guide.

Oyzu captures caller environment hints once when opening the configuration session, before build workers set their own CI=true. Detection is offline and independent of terminals, hostnames, network access and operating system. This is unverified execution context, never runner authentication, authorization or release eligibility. The following nonempty markers identify providers. Empty values and the trimmed, case-insensitive values false, 0, no, and off disable that individual marker. Provider Marker GitHub Actions / Gitea Actions GITHUB_ACTIONS / GITEA_ACTIONS GitLab / Azure Pipelines GITLAB_CI / TF_BUILD Jenkins / TeamCity / Bamboo JENKINS_URL / TEAMCITY_VERSION / bamboo_planKey Buildkite / CircleCI / Travis / AppVeyor BUILDKITE / CIRCLECI / TRAVIS / APPVEYOR Bitbucket Pipelines / Bitrise BITBUCKET_BUILD_NUMBER / BITRISE_IO Google Cloud Build BUILDER_OUTPUT AWS CodeBuild / Harness CODEBUILD_BUILD_ARN / HARNESS_BUILD_ID Codefresh / GoCD / Prow CF_BUILD_ID / GO_PIPELINE_LABEL / PROW_JOB_ID Drone / Cirrus / Semaphore DRONE / CIRRUS_CI / SEMAPHORE Netlify / Vercel / Xcode Cloud NETLIFY / VERCEL / CI_XCODE_PROJECT TaskCluster requires both TASK_ID and RUN_ID to be nonempty (RUN_ID=0 is valid). Additionally, exact CI=woodpecker, CI_NAME=sourcehut, and CI_NAME=codeship identify those providers. Any enabled CI value selects CI behavior even when the provider is unknown. Multiple provider matches are retained in sorted order; CI=false disables only the generic hint, not an enabled vendor marker. With no matching signal the context is local. Unknown platforms without a recognized marker must supply the conventional CI=true; no detector can identify every future or privately hosted system without a signal. Generic variables such as BUILD_ID alone are deliberately insufficient. config explain exposes executionContext with ci, sorted providers, and matched variable names in signals. Values and private runner URLs are not recorded. Build plans retain the same context in oyzu.dev/execution-context. The detector follows the environment-marker approach used by ci-info; its implementation is first-party and adds no dependency or copied vendor dataset. Plain oyzu build defaults to artifact building and packaging locally, plus any check at level required. In the pr, ci and release contexts it also runs every builder check (test, lint, format-check) that is not off; see check levels. oyzu build --full runs every check that is not off regardless of context; it does not change context detection or profile selection. config explain includes the resolved fullBuild request (default false); build plans record fullRequested. oyzu --profile ci build also runs every check that is not off (oyzu's built-in ci profile sets checks.run = "all"). CI needs no extra flags. A different profile or --no-profile does not turn off the checks of a detected CI context; a project turns a check off, or narrows a context to required checks, in oyzu.toml. See build context behavior.

Status: implemented for detection, pinning, display, recording and explain (build intent slice 1, BIN-01, BIN-25 and the context part of BIN-22). The context selects per-context values, including oyzu's own check level defaults; nothing yet evaluates policy constraints against the context (slice 7). Every build resolves one context: local, pr, ci or release. Detection is the default and needs no flags. With no signal the context is local; any CI marker is at least ci; a documented pull/merge request or tag signal of a matched provider raises it to pr or release. When signals conflict the more demanding wins (release over pr over ci). Detection never fails a build. Provider pr signal release signal Documentation GitHub Actions GITHUB_BASE_REF set (pull request events only) GITHUB_REF_TYPE=tag GitHub variables GitLab CI_MERGE_REQUEST_ID CI_COMMIT_TAG predefined variables Azure Pipelines BUILD_REASON=PullRequest BUILD_SOURCEBRANCH begins refs/tags/ build variables, environment naming CircleCI CIRCLE_PULL_REQUEST CIRCLE_TAG variables Buildkite BUILDKITE_PULL_REQUEST is not false BUILDKITE_TAG environment variables Travis CI TRAVIS_PULL_REQUEST is not false TRAVIS_TAG environment variables Bitbucket Pipelines BITBUCKET_PR_ID BITBUCKET_TAG variables Drone DRONE_BUILD_EVENT=pull_request DRONE_BUILD_EVENT=tag DRONE_BUILD_EVENT AppVeyor none verified APPVEYOR_REPO_TAG=true environment variables Jenkins CHANGE_ID none verified multibranch Every other provider, and a bare CI, resolve to ci; Gitea Actions is left at ci until its documentation is checked. Signals are read only from the matched provider, and only fixed literals (=tag) are ever recorded, never values. Overrides. oyzu build --context <name> or OYZU_CONTEXT=<name> pins the context (the flag wins). An unknown name is the only context error (CONTEXT_INVALID); because every command that opens a configuration session resolves the context, an invalid OYZU_CONTEXT fails install, exec and config get as well as build. The rule is one-directional: under a vendor CI marker a pin may raise the context but not lower it (the request is ignored and a CONTEXT_OVERRIDE_IGNORED warning names why); with only the generic CI hint, or no signal, a pin may also lower it. Use OYZU_CONTEXT=release once in a manually triggered release workflow, which carries no tag signal. Resolved fact. extensions["oyzu.dev/execution-context"].context carries detected and detectedSource, requested (value, source), effective and its source, policy (the stricter of detected and requested, which policy constraints will evaluate against) and note. The one-line title shows only the value (context pr, context local); the Build context fact in Prepare gives the full detected via … or requested by … source text; build plans (--plan, --plan --json) and manifests record the same object in extensions["oyzu.dev/execution-context"]. oyzu config explain context reports the value, source and deciding signal. Facts are unverified hints: they never grant publication, credentials or cache authority.

Status: implemented (build intent slice 2, BIN-02 and the settings-resolution part of BIN-20). Policy constraints that select contexts (slice 7) and when/unless selectors are not implemented; this section covers ordinary values only. Check levels (slice 3) use it for their context defaults. Any registered setting can take a value that applies only when a given context is the build's effective context, in the same oyzu.toml that holds its base value: [checks] coverageMinimum = 50 [context.release.checks] coverageMinimum = 90 [context.pr] checks.coverageMinimum = 70 The table name is [context.<name>] with <name> exactly local, pr, ci or release; below it, tables and dotted keys are written as they are for the base value. The tables are valid in every scope that holds the setting (user, project root, component folder, oyzu.local.toml) and follow its scope rules: a project file still cannot set cache.remote or trust.enabled under a context. Precedence. Within one file the order, lowest first, is: the base value; the ci profile when CI inference (not the user) selected it; the effective context's value; a profile the user chose (--profile, OYZU_PROFILE, a task's inherited profile or profile.default). So an inferred [profiles.ci] table loses to the same file's [context.ci.*] table, while --profile ci beats it. This is the maintainer's decision of 2026-10-18 (decisions). Between files, the nearer scope wins, as for every other setting: built-in defaults, then user, then the project root oyzu.toml, then each component folder's oyzu.toml (nearest last), then oyzu.local.toml, then invocation inputs. So a component folder's base value beats the root's [context.release] value; to vary a component by context, write a [context.release] table in that component's file. A context table never applies when its context is not the effective one, whatever the other tables say. Administrative constraints always win. They are evaluated after every ordinary value, including context values and chosen profiles, exactly as for a base value: a required member is added to the set a context chose, and a value outside a lock, allowed set or bound cannot take effect (the build is refused with CONFIG_OVERRIDE_DENIED). Context and path selectors for constraints and the visible "policy overrode this value" display are slice 7 and not implemented. Per target or once per build. The registry declares how each setting resolves. A per-target setting (the default: checks, task and environment settings and most others) resolves from each target's folder chain exactly as tool pins do (build tool scope): a root value applies to every target, a value in docs-site/oyzu.toml to the targets under docs-site/, and targets sharing a folder share settings. There are no target-keyed sections and nothing in build.yaml. A once-per-build setting is one the build treats as a property of the whole run: the scheduling, presentation and selector settings (build.jobs, build.isolation, ui.color, profile.default, config.*) and the cache.* family. Its [context.<name>] values are accepted in the user file, the project root oyzu.toml and oyzu.local.toml, and a component folder's [context.<name>] table for it is a configuration error. Of that list, profile.default and the administrative config.* settings cannot vary by context at all, and cache.remote, cache.ciRemote and cache.dir are accepted only from user scope; the rest (build.jobs, build.isolation, ui.color and the other cache.* settings) can. scan.jobs is a per-target setting. A component folder's base value for a once-per-build setting is still read for its targets, and the build combines them: build.jobs is the minimum over the build root and every selected target. Explain therefore reports that minimum for build.jobs, with the folders that have their own value listed under targetValues and the rule under combine. Errors. An unknown context name ([context.relese]), a table that is not a table, an invalid value, a selector or trust setting that cannot vary by profile or context, compatibility/overrides inside a context, a once-per-build setting in a component folder, and tool pins ([context.<name>.tools], which are not supported yet) are configuration errors reported as CONFIG_CONTEXT_UNKNOWN or CONFIG_CONTEXT_INVALID with file:line:column and the table. A setting that a project or local file may never set (such as cache.remote or trust.enabled) keeps its typed CONFIG_SCOPE refusal, which now names the full key (context.release.cache.remote) and file:line:column. An unknown setting under a context table is, as in the base, an inert warning with its line. Explain. oyzu config explain <setting> [--context <name>] [--target <name>] resolves as that build context (default: the detected or pinned one) for the named build.yaml target (default: the current folder) and prints the value, every scope that set it with the table's context (origins[].context), the contextValues considered for the setting (applied says the table's context matched, effective says that value is the one that took effect, so a matching value that a nearer scope overrode is applied but not effective; the human view labels these applied, overridden and not this context), resolution (perTarget or perBuild) and the target. A once-per-build setting is read at the project root whatever --target names (target.resolvedAt is build root), combined with component values as described above. When a pin was ignored because a CI provider marker is present (--context local under GitHub Actions), the human view prints that note and explains as the context actually in effect. --context and --target cannot be combined with --global, --project or --local, which read one file without resolving. An unknown target fails with CONFIG_TARGET_UNKNOWN listing the declared targets. Recorded. oyzu build --plan --json (per target as contextValues) and the plan and manifest targets of a build bundle (extensions["oyzu.dev/context-values"]) list the settings whose effective value was written in a context table, with the setting, value, context, source file and scope, so a build can be reproduced under --context. The configuration digest already covers the resolved values. Settings that the base value or a nearer scope decided are not listed. Known gap: isolated docker/image container plan targets (built through build/containers.rs) do not record oyzu.dev/context-values yet. Not covered here: per-context tool pins (follow-up) and when/unless selectors on context tables (slice 7/8).

Status: implemented (build intent slice 3, BIN-04, BIN-05 and BIN-06). Ordered levels in policy constraints (a minimum such as "tests at least enforce in pr") and the visible "policy overrode this value" display are slice 7 and not implemented. Each check a builder offers has one level. The registered checks are tests, coverage, lint and format; they replace the former checks.required set, which is no longer a setting (an old checks.required line is an unknown-setting warning and has no effect). [checks] format = "off" lint = "advisory" coverage = "required" [context.release.checks] tests = "required" Level Runs in A failure off never: the stage is not planned and its tools are not prepared (coverage: validation-only while tests run) — advisory builds that run every check a CHECK_ADVISORY warning; the build still succeeds enforce (default) builds that run every check fails the build required every build, including a fast local build fails the build Which builds run every check is the setting checks.run: required runs only required checks, all runs every check that is not off. Its oyzu defaults are per-context values at the lowest scope, shown by oyzu config explain checks.run with the source built-in: Context checks.run Checks that run local required (base default) required only (fast build) pr, ci, release all (built-in context values) every check that is not off any, with --full — every check that is not off A project can change them like any other value, per context and per folder, for example [context.ci.checks] run = "required" for pushes to a main branch, or [checks] run = "all" to run every check locally. --full and --profile ci (whose built-in value is checks.run = "all") run every check that is not off. No flag skips a check the project chose: turning a check off is a committed change in oyzu.toml. Each builder stage serves checks: the test stage serves tests and coverage (coverage is collected by the tests, so tests = "off" also turns coverage off), lint serves lint and format-check serves format. A stage runs when any check it serves runs; it is off when every check it serves is off. A test stage is advisory when tests is advisory. Each report is judged by its own check: a failing test report of an advisory test stage is a warning, while its coverage report follows checks.coverage, so required or enforced coverage (including a shortfall below checks.coverageMinimum) still fails the build; an advisory coverage shortfall is a warning. Coverage off is validation-only. Coverage is collected by each builder's test command (for example cargo llvm-cov with nextest for Rust, c8 for Node), and that command does not yet change with the coverage level: with checks.coverage = "off" and tests running, coverage is still collected and its tools are still prepared, but it is never judged (no minimum, its report is not required, a missing or invalid coverage report is a warning). Plan and --plan --json say Collected with test; not judged (checks.coverage = off). Running tests without coverage collection is a recorded follow-up. Levels resolve per target from the folder chain, like every per-target setting: the nearest folder wins, and a context value beats the base value in the same file. An administrative constraint still wins: a lock, or an allowed set such as ["enforce", "required"], refuses a project value outside it with CONFIG_OVERRIDE_DENIED. Errors. A level other than the four is CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE. A positive checks.coverageMinimum with checks.coverage = "off" (or checks.tests = "off") is CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE naming both sources. A required check, or a positive coverage minimum, that the selected builder cannot run fails in Plan with CONFIG_OVERRIDE_DENIED: <target> cannot satisfy required <check> check. An authored task that depends on the stage of an off check is CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE naming the action and where the check was turned off. A required test or coverage check also makes its report mandatory (report-missing when absent), as checks.required did. Shown and recorded. Plan shows an off cell with its source (format · disabled in oyzu.toml, test · disabled in oyzu.toml [context.pr]), a skip cell with its reason (fast local build, or only required checks run in ci (checks.run)), and an advisory note for advisory stages that run (build view). --plan --json reports stage status off with the same reason. Plan and manifest targets record extensions["oyzu.dev/build-checks"] with mode (fast or full), levels (each check's level) and off (each off stage and its source); each check action records extensions["oyzu.dev/check-levels"], and an advisory one has required: false (as do the report intents of advisory or off checks), so its failure is recorded with status failed, one CHECK_ADVISORY warning carries the native cause, the target's artifacts are still collected, the manifest status stays succeeded, the exit code is 0 and oyzu inspect dist accepts the bundle. This holds on the native host path and the isolated path alike. The plan policy's requiredChecks lists the checks at required. Tools follow checks. Builder tool requirements are derived from the stages that run, so a builder's own requirement for an off or skipped check is not prepared: with format = "off" the Rust builder no longer adds rustfmt. A component the project declares itself, such as components = ["rustfmt"] in rust-toolchain.toml, stays a declared requirement of the toolchain.

Slice 5 of the build intent draft (BIN-08 to BIN-11). Each target is built with the development profile (a fast edit-build loop) or the optimized profile. Optimization follows where the output goes: a target is optimized when this build sends its artifacts off the machine, and development otherwise. The build Optimized because is a slice (oyzu build --slice, with or without --handoff) artifacts are handed off (--slice) is configured to write results to a shared remote cache (a cache.remote or, in CI, cache.ciRemote with cache.write = true; not with --no-cache), for a target whose results can be cached remotely (not an external builder, a host image worker or a target with secret environment values) configured to write results to a shared remote cache (a remote that turns out unusable at open still counts) selects a target that packages this one: a materialize input with usage runtime or data, or the target's own container image artifacts are packaged by image runs in the release context (a tag, --context release, OYZU_CONTEXT=release) release builds are published does none of these development: local dist only build.optimized (boolean, unset by default) decides instead whenever it is set. It is an ordinary per-target setting: a folder's oyzu.toml sets it for the targets under that folder, optionally per context ([context.release.build] optimized = false), and policy can set or lock it. oyzu build --optimized and --no-optimized set it for one invocation, above every file; giving both is a usage error (CLI_USAGE, exit 2). Policy constraints still win: a locked build.optimized that a flag or file contradicts is CONFIG_OVERRIDE_DENIED, as for any constrained setting. A build.optimized in user configuration is ignored in CI, like every non-presentation user setting. # cli/oyzu.toml: the self-installed CLI is always fast [build] optimized = true # oyzu.toml: never optimize release builds of this folder [context.release.build] optimized = false What optimized means per builder. Each builder declares it: Builder Optimized Development rust/app (native and isolated) cargo build --release cargo build dotnet (isolated) --configuration Release for build, test and pack --configuration Debug go/app no difference: the Go compiler always optimizes and every build uses -trimpath Node, Python, Java (Gradle, Maven, Ant), Helm, Docker, external plugins no difference: no separate optimized build A builder with no difference applies development whatever was requested, so its artifacts are labeled development and its cache entries are shared. Test stages keep each builder's test mode (Cargo's test profile) in both profiles. The profile is resolved once per target before builder planning and recorded on the plan and manifest target as extensions["oyzu.dev/optimization"] (requested, applied, reason, builder); --plan prints it as Profile: optimized · --optimized (cargo build --release) and --plan --json reports it as each target's optimization with a summary. Each artifact's profile is optimized only when the builder's own optimizing commands produced it, so an authored replacement of the build stays development (build bundles). Optimized is not publishable. The profile never implies reproducible output or publication eligibility; native host output still confers none.

plugins.development maps a built-in builder id such as go/app to an absolute plugin executable path. It is accepted only from user, machine or administrative configuration and replaces that builder's native host operations for the invocation. See local development plugin bindings. plugins.packages maps such an id to { archive, sha256 } or { oci, identity?, trustedRoot? }: a verified, installed package whose selection oyzu.lock pins. Same scopes. See plugin packages. plugins.preview (boolean, default false) makes preview plugin releases from the catalog eligible. Same scopes, and never from a profile: a project file, oyzu.local.toml or profile that sets it fails with CONFIG_SCOPE. See plugin catalog.

Project trust controls are trust.enabled (boolean, default true) and trust.parents (absolute folder paths, default []). They and platform.url, platform.account, cache.remote, cache.ciRemote are rejected in project/local scope, including profile overlays. Set them in user/global, machine or administrative configuration. Supported invocation environment sources are OYZU_PROJECT_TRUST, OYZU_PLATFORM_URL, OYZU_PLATFORM_ACCOUNT, OYZU_CACHE_REMOTE and OYZU_CACHE_CI_REMOTE; each overrides ordinary files while remaining subject to administrative constraints. OYZU_PROJECT_TRUST accepts true/false, on/off, yes/no or 1/0. See folder trust for the environment application boundary and native user-state records.

build.yaml now accepts a builds mapping with uses, path, platforms, depends_on, materialize, bindings and with per entry. depends_on is an ordering-only list of producer build names; it does not transfer artifacts. bindings remains discovery-only and fails captured-build admission. Configuration owns normalization and freezes all declared platforms; builders own validation of with. See the Rust build options for the implemented options and execution limits. This is a partial implementation of the proposed build model, not support for every future example. Tool requirements remain in TOML and lock identities remain in oyzu.lock. The previous flat inventory is retained for compatibility; do not mix it with a builds envelope.

Configuration commands default to human-readable output. Pass global --json for structured results and errors; see CLI output. Use an Oyzu CLI built from this branch; these commands are not a promise about older releases. Standalone configuration inspection and editing require no platform account, Docker, native ecosystem toolchain or network service. The client has Windows, macOS and Linux implementations; platform qualification and measured checks are tracked in implementation status. Running tasks or builds additionally requires their explicitly provisioned native tools. In an otherwise empty directory named config-demo, save this as oyzu.toml: [build] jobs = 2 [profile] default = "dev" [profiles.dev.build] jobs = 3 [ui] color = "never" Run these commands from its parent directory. Expected values assume standalone operation with no administrative constraints, local overrides or OYZU_PROFILE selection: oyzu --root config-demo config get build.jobs oyzu --root config-demo --no-profile config get build.jobs oyzu --root config-demo config validate --strict --all-profiles oyzu --root config-demo --profile dev config set build.jobs 4 --project oyzu --root config-demo config get build.jobs oyzu --root config-demo --profile dev config unset build.jobs --project oyzu --root config-demo config get build.jobs The successive get results are 3, 2, 4, and 2. Validation reports success; with --json it returns valid: true. Removing the profile assignment exposes the base value; it does not restore the old value of 3. Set/unset return the destination path and updated key. No project task runs in this walkthrough.

oyzu --root path/to/project config show --json oyzu --root path/to/project config explain build.jobs --json oyzu --root path/to/project config profiles oyzu --root path/to/project config validate --strict --all-profiles oyzu --root path/to/project --profile integration run test oyzu --root path/to/project --no-profile run test --root explicitly fixes both build and configuration roots. Otherwise the nearest ancestor build.yaml within the current Git worktree selects the build; configuration still inherits from the Git worktree root. Outside Git, the outermost ancestor with Oyzu configuration or a build declaration bounds inheritance, falling back to the invocation directory. With no build declaration, that boundary remains the conventional-discovery root. -C / --directory selects the invocation directory; --root alone also selects that directory. Git boundaries require recognizable repository metadata: HEAD plus the common objects and refs directories. A .git file must contain a gitdir: <path> pointer to that metadata; linked worktrees use its commondir pointer for the common directories. Relative pointers are resolved from their declaring directory. An unborn repository and packed refs remain valid boundaries; no commit or loose branch ref is required. Empty .git directories, malformed pointers and missing metadata do not define a workspace. They are left intact. Recognition reads bounded local metadata without running Git, executing configuration or establishing repository integrity. Conservative nested repository/submodule exclusions during target traversal remain in effect. Entering an independent nested example and running oyzu build --plan therefore selects the example without --root. Its oyzu.lock and build outputs belong to that selected root. Parent inventories are not merged, and automatic discovery skips nested build roots. An explicit parent target path remains authoritative. Configuration retains normal project/local precedence, relative paths retain their declaring-file origin, and machine/enterprise constraints remain enforced. A selected build root may declare its default profile; ordinary target subdirectories cannot. Explicit composition and shared-workspace lock ownership are not implemented. Relative task cwd values are now relative to the TOML file that declares them. For a root-file override of api:test, use cwd = "api/checks" to select that directory. Multiple targets cannot own the same native build unit; use distinct project paths or distinct builders where appropriate. Sources resolve in this order: built-ins, verified corporate defaults, protected local administrative defaults, machine configuration, user configuration, root-to-target oyzu.toml, eligible root-to-target oyzu.local.toml, and invocation compatibility inputs. Each source applies its base followed by the selected profile. Siblings receive separate snapshots. Arrays replace, tasks replace atomically, and [overrides].remove removes explicit environment/task entries. Environment removals also unset inherited variables during development task execution. A task environment can replace a global variable with the same spelling, but case aliases such as TOKEN and token are rejected across the combined environment on every host. Known tool aliases share that same precedence. For example, project node = "22" overrides global "oyzu:node" = "latest"; a selected profile can override its base through either spelling. Inspection retains the spellings with their effective value and winning provenance. Lock ownership follows the winning source. Declaring multiple aliases for one tool in the same overlay remains ambiguous. Administrative constraints bind the selected value regardless of its spelling. Profile selection uses explicit --profile or --no-profile, inherited task selection, OYZU_PROFILE, the eligible root/default selector, inferred CI's empty ci profile, then no profile. Names grant no authority. Inferred CI excludes user computation settings and local files; --local-overrides requests local files, subject to administrative restrictions. Excluded local files are not parsed. config show, get, explain, profiles, and validate do not execute project tasks. If resolution is blocked, show and explain return an explicit unresolved status without effective values; validate remains the failing validation command. The credential-origin and trust-control scope ban is an exception: platform.url, platform.account, cache.remote, cache.ciRemote, trust.enabled and trust.parents in project/local sources are hard errors even for show and explain, in human and JSON output and in CI when that source is included. The error names the key, source and user/global or administrative remedy. Configuration inspection displays ordinary environment settings and path arrays; credential-like environment names and recognizable sensitive values remain redacted, as do task bodies. Discovery/task listing also redacts environment values. Explain includes source histories, byte spans, exclusions, constraint source IDs and the effective computation digest. Warnings carry severity, source byte spans when available, target scope, and a remedy without including the configured value. Unknown optional settings warn and stay inert; known invalid values, unsupported required capabilities, duplicate keys and unsupported schema majors fail. --strict rejects optional warnings. --all-profiles validates inactive capability requirements and profile outcomes.

oyzu --root path/to/project config set build.jobs 8 --project oyzu --root path/to/project config set checks.tests required --local oyzu --root path/to/project --profile dev config set ui.color never --global oyzu --root path/to/project config unset build.jobs --project Exactly one of --global (the user configuration file), --project, or --local is required. --directory can select a contained nested project scope. unset removes an assignment in that file and exposes inherited values; it does not create a removal tombstone. Ordinary edits remain available to repair invalid values even when resolution is blocked; they do not activate values or alter protected records. Edits preserve unrelated comments and unknown syntax, validate known types/scopes, and compare the original bytes before atomic replacement. Concurrent changes produce CONFIG_EDIT_CONFLICT. A small .oyzu-config-edit.lock coordinates Oyzu writers and is excluded from source snapshots. Only an explicit --profile NAME directs an edit into that profile. An inferred/default profile does not change the write destination: an edit without --profile writes the base section. Scalar booleans and numbers are parsed by type; strings are literal. Use --json-value for arrays or objects. The array example above uses shell quoting supported by PowerShell and POSIX shells. Edits cannot repair malformed TOML syntax; correct that syntax in an editor first. They cannot modify administrative or enrollment records.

All config commands default to human-readable output. Add global --json for structured results and errors. The JSON schema is experimental. Command Result and important behavior show Effective values, selected profile, digest, diagnostics and resolution status get KEY One effective value (a JSON value with --json); fails if the key has no effective value explain [KEY] Resolution evidence, optionally narrowed to a key; includes origins and constraints profiles Available profiles, selected profile and selection reason validate [--strict] [--all-profiles] valid: true on success; nonzero exit on validation failure status Standalone/enrolled state and managed cache health; does not refresh over the network refresh Explicit online policy acquisition; returns revision and offline deadline; requires protected enrollment set / unset Changes one ordinary file and reports its destination; does not establish that the edited value is effective show, get and explain accept mutually exclusive --global, --project and --local flags. These inspect only the selected file: the user configuration, oyzu.toml in the selected directory, or oyzu.local.toml there, respectively. For example, oyzu config get build.jobs --global reads the user declaration; oyzu -C packages/api config show --project shows that directory's declarations. Without a scope flag, the merged effective configuration remains the default. Scoped reads do not inject defaults, inspect other sources, contact policy services or execute tasks. They preserve the normal inspection redaction. An explicit --profile NAME overlays only that profile from the selected file; automatic/default profile selection does not apply to file inspection. show/explain report the source, scope and whether the file exists, with empty values when absent; get fails when the key is not declared there. These are declarations, not a claim that execution policy allows the requested values. TOML syntax failures identify file:line:column (one-based Unicode character coordinates) and the parser's reason, including during set/unset. Source snippets are omitted to keep configuration values out of diagnostics. Correct malformed syntax in an editor before retrying. Strict validation retains every warning's key, source, available line/column and byte span, message and remedy; human errors list them and JSON errors include a diagnostics array. Strict validation still fails instead of silently accepting the warnings. Human explain groups exact setting keys with effective values and their last source. Multiple origins appear as an ordered resolution history; the last source does not imply it supplied every element of a merged value. Only nonempty policy restrictions, exclusions and diagnostics are expanded. With no restrictions it prints one policy summary rather than an empty entry for every setting. Source paths omit Windows extended-path prefixes for display. Ordinary environment paths and compiler settings remain visible. Sensitive values stay redacted. explain <key> narrows the view; --json retains the complete metadata, including byte spans, constraint source IDs, context signals and digest. show and explain can exit successfully with status: "unresolved" and no effective values. status can likewise return an unhealthy managed state successfully. Automation must inspect these fields or use validate as its configuration gate. Execution errors are reported on stderr with a nonzero exit status. Inspection does not run tasks, but resolving an enrolled configuration can contact the policy endpoint and update its cache. Thus inspection is not necessarily network-free or free of persistent state changes.

Ordinary settings below can appear in machine, user, project or local configuration and in profiles, subject to eligibility and administrative constraints. An absent default means no value is contributed by the registry. Recognition of a setting does not imply that its downstream integration is available. Key Type and built-in default Current behavior scan.jobs Integer 1–65535; default 2 Bounds independent scan checks, including remote analysis waits; 1 serializes checks analysis.rules Table of rule id to off, advisory or enforce; no value (every rule advisory) Experimental (OEP-0020 S5). Unknown rule ids and levels are configuration errors that name the valid ids. The nearest scope that sets it replaces lower scopes as a whole; a managed constraint can pin the whole value. Consumed by oyzu build --check and oyzu build per target; never grants authority analysis.suppress Array of {rule, path?, reason} tables; none Experimental. reason is mandatory and non-empty, path is an optional project-relative glob over the finding's file. Suppressed findings do not fail and stay in --json; unmatched suppressions are reported as stale notes. Replaced as a whole by the nearest scope build.jobs Integer 1–65535; available logical parallelism, fallback 1 Bounds independent preparation and ready build actions; the smallest root/target ceiling and worker-memory admission apply. oyzu build --jobs N (-j N), then the OYZU_BUILD_JOBS environment variable, override every file for one invocation; see worker ceiling. Scheduling only: not part of the configuration digest, so a serial and a parallel build share cached results build.isolation auto, docker, crun; auto Which sandbox runs the isolated steps of Node targets on Linux: auto uses Docker when an engine answers and the daemonless sandbox (crun) otherwise; docker always uses Docker; crun uses crun even with Docker present. --no-docker and OYZU_NO_DOCKER=1 select crun. Scheduling only: not part of the configuration digest, so both backends share cached results build.optimized Boolean; no value Per target, per context allowed. Unset: optimization follows where the output goes; true/false selects the optimized or development profile. oyzu build --optimized/--no-optimized set it for one invocation; policy constraints win. Not part of the configuration digest: the profile a builder applies enters action keys instead, so builders that optimization does not change keep one entry version.strategy auto, native, tags, conventional; auto Selects artifact version inference; computation setting consumed by each builder; never grants release authority checks.tests, checks.coverage, checks.lint, checks.format off, advisory, enforce, required; enforce Check levels: off never runs, advisory failures are warnings, enforce runs in builds that run every check, required runs in every build and makes its report mandatory checks.run required, all; required, with built-in context values all for pr, ci and release Whether a build runs every check that is not off (all) or only required ones; --full runs every check checks.coverageMinimum Integer 0–100; 0 Positive minimum requires coverage evidence when coverage runs; missing or zero-denominator coverage fails (a warning when checks.coverage is advisory); with coverage off it is a configuration error ui.color auto, always, never; auto Human task labels/status only; JSON stays unstyled profile.default Profile name; absent Default selector; cannot be declared inside a profile or nested project selector scope cache.remote OCI URL; absent Destination of the experimental remote OCI action cache (oci://host[:port]/repository/prefix; plain HTTP only for loopback hosts). Credentials, query and fragment are forbidden. A registry that asks for sign-in gets a token through its token endpoint; the credential is never a setting: it comes from OYZU_CACHE_TOKEN, or in a CI job from its ID tokens (OYZU_ID_TOKEN_URL) toolIndex.url HTTPS URL (HTTP only for a loopback host), or false; https://github.com/oyzuai/tool-index/releases/latest/download/ Base URL of the signed public tool index; by default the newest release of the public index. false: no index, so registry packages resolve from the pinned registry. No credentials, query or fragment toolIndex.trustedRoot Absolute path; absent (Sigstore's production trusted root: compiled in, or newer from oyzu tools trust refresh) A Sigstore trusted_root.json (Fulcio CA certificates, Rekor log keys and timestamp authorities) to verify the index's signature bundle against, for a private Sigstore deployment. User or machine scope only (CONFIG_SCOPE in a project file) toolIndex.identity https: URI; https://github.com/oyzuai/tool-index/.github/workflows/release.yml@refs/heads/main The signing certificate identity (SAN URI) the index must be signed by, for a customer-signed index. The OIDC issuer (https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com) and runner environment (github-hosted) are fixed. User or machine scope only (CONFIG_SCOPE in a project file) toolCatalog.url HTTPS URL (HTTP only for a loopback host); absent Delivery edge of the organization tool catalog. Set: registry packages, all Oyzu archive providers and indexed Rust install only versions the organization approved, through the edge, with the token from OYZU_TOOL_CATALOG_TOKEN. Lock it in admin-settings.json to make it mandatory toolCatalog.keys Array of one to eight ed25519:<base64> public keys; absent The keys the edge's signed organization catalog must verify under. Required with toolCatalog.url; pin two while the edge rotates. User or machine scope only (CONFIG_SCOPE in a project file); lockable in admin-settings.json toolCatalog.maxOfflineAge 0, <n>h or <n>d (at most 366d); 7d How long after the edge built it the last good organization catalog may be used when the edge cannot be reached (network error or HTTP 5xx). 0 never uses it. User or machine scope only (CONFIG_SCOPE in a project file); lockable in admin-settings.json platform.url HTTPS URL (HTTP only for a loopback host); absent Platform for remote runs and secrets; no credentials, query or fragment. The access token is never a setting: it comes from OYZU_PLATFORM_TOKEN platform.account Platform account identifier (lowercase letters, digits, hyphens); absent Account that remote runs are created in and whose secrets oyzu secrets manages npm.sessionEndpoint Numeric-loopback HTTP URL; absent Opt-in experimental npm session; no credentials, query or fragment; requires a separately running laboratory agent nuget.sessionEndpoint Numeric-loopback HTTP URL; absent NuGet session prototype; user/admin authority only, no profile selection or implicit login python.sessionEndpoint Numeric-loopback HTTP URL; absent Python session prototype; user/admin authority only, no profile selection or implicit login cargo.sessionEndpoint Numeric-loopback HTTP URL; absent Cargo session prototype; user/admin authority only, one named sparse registry gradle.sessionEndpoint Numeric-loopback HTTP URL; absent Gradle session prototype; user/admin authority only, no profile selection or implicit login maven.sessionEndpoint Numeric-loopback HTTP URL; absent Maven session prototype; user/admin authority only, no profile selection or implicit login oci.sessionEndpoint Numeric-loopback HTTP URL; absent Isolated OCI session prototype; user/admin authority only, no implicit login or production agent cache.local Boolean; true Enables the local action cache (reuse of unchanged targets on the captured and native host paths). false runs every action, like oyzu build --no-cache, which bypasses it for one invocation cache.dir Absolute path; absent Replaces the default per-user action-cache store (Linux $XDG_CACHE_HOME/oyzu/actions, macOS ~/Library/Caches/Oyzu/actions, Windows %LocalAppData%\Oyzu\cache\actions). User or system scope only: a project oyzu.toml or oyzu.local.toml that sets it is rejected with CONFIG_SCOPE; not eligible for profiles; ignored with other user-scope settings in CI. Never part of an action key cache.ciRemote OCI URL; absent The CI repository: a CI build reads and writes only it; other builds read it first and never write it. Its trust comes from the registry refusing writes without the CI credential (OYZU_CACHE_TOKEN or the job's ID tokens from OYZU_ID_TOKEN_URL, environment variables, never a setting). Same URL rules as cache.remote cache.immutableTags Boolean; false Declares that every configured cache repository refuses to replace a tag, so pushes skip the racing-writer read and a refused tag write is a conflict. Never set it for a registry that replaces tags cache.read, cache.write Booleans; true, false Whether the remote OCI cache is consulted after a local miss and whether locally stored action results are pushed to it. No effect without cache.remote or with the local cache disabled. Transport preferences: not part of the configuration digest, so they never change an action key cache.nativeMaxMiB Integer 1–1048576; 8192 (8 GiB) Aggregate retained budget for the selected native Rust compiler caches; see retention. Independent of remote cache preferences. cache.dockerMaxMiB Integer 1–1048576; 20480 (20 GiB) Aggregate budget for Docker images Oyzu pulled; least recently used are evicted after isolated builds. See Docker storage budget. Not part of any action key tools.<name> Nonempty string; absent Explicit requests fail execution until a verified installation binding exists; no tool installation is performed env.<name> Literal string or { secret = "reference" }; absent Literal environment overlay; secret references require a future authorized consumer tasks.<name> Task record; absent Atomic task replacement; see syntax below docker.apparmorProfile Profile name; host-derived oyzu-buildkit when the detected Linux user-namespace restriction requires it, otherwise unconfined docker.frontends List of image references pinned by digest; empty # syntax= frontends a Dockerfile may request. A request matches an entry with the same repository and the same digest, or the same tag when the request has no digest. Oyzu's BuildKit frontend runs the approved frontend; any other request fails with FRONTEND_NOT_APPROVED naming the requested and approved references. See Docker frontends Environment names use ASCII letters, digits and underscores, beginning with a letter or underscore; the OYZU_ prefix is reserved case-insensitively. Values are not expressions or interpolation programs. Inspection redaction does not make literal environment values a secret store: literals can participate in build inputs/evidence. Do not use a literal as a substitute for the deferred secret consumer. Task records select either run (a shell command) or argv (an argument array), and accept shell, cwd, env, depends_on, inputs, outputs, cache, interactive and reports. cache = true with outputs makes an authored task cacheable by oyzu build (its inputs may only add paths inside its target); outputs on a hook lets the cache follow it; see authored tasks. Local oyzu run inherits stdin. Text-mode tasks recording a bundle tee stdout/stderr live and retain them in dist/logs; interactive = true instead preserves real output terminal descriptors, with no captured stdout/stderr logs. Tasks without a bundle inherit output directly. For PowerShell run scripts, interactive = true also omits -NonInteractive; it does not make captured builds interactive. JSON mode captures output while retaining stdin; see task streams and limits. Task env contains strings. Task execution also requires a discoverable native project. For example, with Node explicitly provisioned and a package.json containing {"name":"config-demo","version":"1.0.0"}, add this to oyzu.toml: [tasks.hello] argv = ["node", "-e", "console.log('hello')"] oyzu --root path/to/project run hello executes that command. A higher-priority task record replaces the entire record rather than merging its fields. To remove inherited environment/task entries, use dotted key strings in a removal list: Additional arguments after -- are appended to an argv task, including an argv that already contains -c or -Command (for example a Python expression). Tasks authored with run reject additional arguments; choose argv when a task needs parameters. This distinction follows the declared task form, not the spelling of arguments passed to the native executable. [overrides] remove = ["env.DEMO_MODE", "tasks.hello"] The following keys are administrative-only and cannot appear in ordinary files or profiles: Key Type and default Meaning config.localOverridesInCi Boolean; false Whether the local override request is eligible in CI config.allowedProfiles Set of names, including @none; absent Restricts selection when supplied tools.allowed Set of canonical tool IDs; absent Restricts tool eligibility tools.ignore Set of tool names; absent Folder-scoped: silences best-effort tool detection of the named tools (managed tools, host programs, fetching packages) for targets in that folder and below. Never removes a primary toolchain; an explicit [tools] pin still provides the tool. Ignored detections show in -v and --json as ignored by tools.ignore in <path> tools.catalogs Ordered string array; ["public"] Catalog preference; unavailable protected bindings block execution registries.routes Route array; [] Each entry has protocol, scope, connectorId; protocols are npm, pypi, maven, cargo, go, oci, tools; standalone Node/Go installation supports explicit host tool bindings; real Node proxy acceptance passed, Go proxy acceptance remains pending; other connector execution remains deferred npm.sources Set of HTTPS URL prefixes ending in /; [] Extra locations an isolated npm build may download locked packages from, in addition to https://registry.npmjs.org/. For example, https://codeload.github.com/<owner>/<repo>/tar.gz/ admits a package that pins a public GitHub commit as a tarball. Declare it in package.json as that same HTTPS tarball URL and record the URL and its sha512 in the lockfile; a git+https or github: spec in package.json is refused, because native npm would refetch it as a git dependency instead of using the captured tarball. Each package still needs the lockfile's sha512 integrity, which is verified. Credentials, queries and fragments are refused. Applies to the npm builder only; git+https lock entries remain unsupported fetches.sources Set of HTTPS URL prefixes ending in /; absent Administrative allowlist for declared fetches. Absent, any HTTPS URL is admitted. Set, each fetch URL and every redirect must fall under a listed prefix, or the build fails with SOURCE_DENIED or REDIRECT_DENIED; an empty list admits none. Project configuration cannot set it. Credentials, queries and fragments are refused maven.snapshotRepositories Set of HTTPS repository base URLs ending in /; [] (off) Snapshot repositories that captured Maven acquisition may use for snapshot version paths only, each through its own broker source; every other path keeps the Maven Central or session-approved route. Credentials, queries, fragments and plain HTTP are refused. Snapshot inputs are inventoried in the dependency snapshot, and a build whose version intent is not a development snapshot fails rather than use one. See Maven snapshot repositories

Host Machine directory User configuration User state directory Windows ProgramData known folder + Oyzu RoamingAppData known folder + Oyzu/config.toml LocalAppData known folder + Oyzu/state macOS /Library/Application Support/Oyzu ~/Library/Application Support/Oyzu/config.toml ~/Library/Application Support/Oyzu/state Linux /etc/oyzu $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/oyzu/config.toml, fallback ~/.config/oyzu/config.toml $XDG_STATE_HOME/oyzu, fallback ~/.local/state/oyzu Windows paths come from native known-folder APIs. Relative XDG paths warn and use the home fallback. The machine directory contains ordinary config.toml, protected admin-settings.json, and protected enrollment management.json. Project/local files are named oyzu.toml and oyzu.local.toml; keep personal local overrides out of version control. Oyzu does not auto-enroll the machine. For persistent user data, including the tool store, an absolute Windows HOME that differs from the native profile selects <HOME>/AppData/Local/Oyzu. This lets disposable homes isolate tool caches and rollback records. With HOME unset or naming the normal profile, native LocalAppData redirection is preserved. A relative HOME fails with CONFIG_SCOPE; use an absolute path or unset it. This data override does not redirect the configuration and managed policy state locations in the table, or the separate action/image cache locations. Existing data is not moved or deleted when selecting another home. OYZU_USER_CONFIG optionally selects an absolute user configuration file, useful for disposable environments and testing user defaults without modifying a real profile. Relative paths are rejected. The file retains user-level precedence and authority; this setting cannot redirect machine policy, enrollment or state. Its sibling oyzu.lock owns user-default tool pins. Unset the variable to return to the native user configuration location. Help/version do not read this setting. Managed state includes signed policy entries under the user state directory and integrity pointers/high-water state in the native credential store. Ordinary configuration edits do not change that state. Source capture enforces size/complexity budgets, including a 1 MiB file limit, and detects concurrent source changes rather than mixing revisions. This configuration format has no include mechanism or executable configuration language.

Native locations follow OEP-0002: Windows known folders, macOS Application Support, and Linux /etc/oyzu plus absolute XDG user locations. Protected files require administrative ownership and permissions. Windows uses native ACL/handle checks; Unix checks root ownership and write permissions; macOS also examines extended ACL entries on the opened object and rejects non-root mutation grants using the native descriptor ACL API. An insecure, unreadable or malformed enrollment never becomes standalone mode. admin-settings.json uses the same typed constraint evaluator as corporate policy. Locks, allowed whole values, numeric bounds and required sets intersect independently of ordinary precedence. Required checks cannot be removed by empty ordinary arrays. The build planner requires configured checks to have actual actions/report contracts; report collection enforces the coverage minimum, including missing/zero-denominator failures. config status reports enrollment and cached-policy status. config refresh performs a headless request to the enrolled platform's public configuration-context endpoint. Signed responses use pinned Ed25519 keys, canonical JSON, identity/context binding, monotonic sequences, expiry and explicit offline permissions. Cache entries are content-addressed and flushed before an OS credential-store pointer commits them. A corrupt entry can only be repaired from a newly verified online response. Windows Credential Manager, macOS Keychain and Linux Secret Service hold integrity state. If that service is unavailable, managed execution fails; standalone use does not need it. Transport backoff never extends signed deadlines. Server denial cannot become offline permission.

Rust targets can declare a finite rust object with optional features and a targets list of Cargo triples. Tool requirements remain in TOML and resolved identities in oyzu.lock; the YAML object rejects toolchain pins. It produces explicit native binary task definitions, described in Rust binary targets, including the unfinished locked-tool execution handoff. It cannot be combined with captured platform matrices. Isolated builds reject that native-only intent instead of dropping its requirements. build.yaml describes target intent separately from the TOML cascade. Its optional application container field is a boolean or a finite object with base, user, workdir and entrypoint; see Python application containers for types, defaults and current runtime support. Capture validates and freezes that object with the target inventory. config validate rejects malformed option values without resolving images or executing a build. The object introduces no task language or additional precedence layer. Administrative execution checks and resolved owner settings still apply to generated image actions.

The Docker adapter registers docker.apparmorProfile. It replaces direct adapter reads of OYZU_BUILDKIT_APPARMOR_PROFILE; the legacy environment variable remains a diagnosed invocation input and faces the same policy constraints. The default still detects the host's AppArmor user-namespace restriction. Builder namespaces stay behind the crate-private Builder contract. A frozen build configuration contributes its digest to target/action records. Formatting, profile names and presentation preferences do not affect that configuration digest. Policy revision and online/offline context remain separate evidence. No policy snapshot grants signing, publishing or credential issuance. Build preparation and planning require the resolved invocation snapshot and every selected target's snapshot, including inferred targets without configuration files. Missing internal snapshots fail with CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE; they never disable policy checks or cause adapters to recalculate defaults. Library callers must use discovery to obtain this state; serialized discovery JSON is an inspection result, not a resumable workspace. Rediscover the workspace if that state is missing. Docker reads its execution profile from the admitted snapshot before preparation starts. Later edits to live configuration files do not change an already frozen plan; start a new invocation to resolve them. The current native tool-store, authenticated platform-session, connector-binding and shell-secret-consumer implementations are not completed by this configuration change; the remote action cache is an experimental development-scope implementation that signs in only with a token from OYZU_CACHE_TOKEN or a CI job's ID tokens (see the action cache). Explicit tool requests that cannot be bound to a verified installation are rejected before builds. Enforced routes/catalogs requiring unavailable bindings fail before public acquisition. Managed builders that still require public dependency preparation are blocked; offline-capable local Docker and Helm preparation remains separate from those network paths. Development secret references require an authorized consumer and are not substituted into build literals. build.jobs bounds concurrent ready actions. The invocation uses the smallest admitted root/target ceiling; each target retains serial mutation and hook order. Targets have private workspaces and output roots. Dependency or deferred-report failure blocks consumers while independent targets can finish. ui.color controls human-readable task labels and outcome statuses: always emits ANSI color, never disables it, and auto enables it only when the relevant output stream is a terminal. Task-specific resolved preferences apply to that task; root tasks use root preferences. JSON output remains unstyled. Cache preferences do not grant cache credentials or trust: a remote hit is a development result. These boundaries are deliberate failures rather than claims that all OEP-0002 ecosystem and platform integration acceptance cases pass. Three-host ACL/keychain qualification, signed server interoperability, authenticated logout/account-switch flows, complete connector routing and tool-store integration remain release gates. Development execution checks tool eligibility, explicit tool requests and protected routing/catalog requirements before any prerequisite or hook runs. Managed host tasks remain blocked until approved development execution and connector bindings exist; the host runner cannot claim to enforce managed network routing. Task-specific and native-adapter environment additions must satisfy administrative environment restrictions. In a single-target nested project, the target's final task cascade determines whether a root operation is replaced or removed, consistently with inspection and build planning.

Diagnostic or symptom Recovery CONFIG_SYNTAX, duplicate keys Correct the source file's syntax/duplicate declaration, then validate CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE, CONFIG_SCOPE Use the registered type and permitted scope; ordinary set/unset can repair invalid values CONFIG_PROFILE_UNKNOWN Inspect profile declarations and select an existing name; use --no-profile only if policy permits Optional-setting warning / strict failure Correct the spelling or remove inert optional settings; ordinary validation does not execute unknown syntax Unsupported schema major or required capability Use a compatible client; do not remove a requirement unless the project no longer needs it CONFIG_POLICY_CONFLICT, CONFIG_OVERRIDE_DENIED Reconcile conflicting administrative constraints or choose an allowed value; unavailable execution bindings require their implementation/provisioning CONFIG_EDIT_CONFLICT Re-read the file and retry the intended edit; do not overwrite another writer's changes CONFIG_LIMIT Reduce file size, nesting or configuration entries, including inactive profile data POLICY_INVALID Inspect enrollment protection and policy/cache validity; an administrator may need to repair bootstrap permissions or signing configuration POLICY_EXPIRED, POLICY_UNAVAILABLE Restore endpoint/native credential-store availability and run config refresh; failure never converts an enrolled machine to standalone POLICY_CLOCK_UNCERTAIN Correct clock problems and reconcile online; do not erase rollback-protection state to bypass the error Offline execution requires explicit signed permission and remains bounded by both signed expiry and maximum offline age (at most 24 hours). CI requires online policy. Transport retry/backoff preserves these deadlines; denial and malformed responses do not authorize offline fallback. Explicit refresh can fail while an older valid cache remains stored. A corrupt cache entry requires a newly verified online response; damaged integrity-store state can require administrator intervention. Refresh rechecks time after I/O, so a request that finishes after a deadline does not extend authorization. Changing protected bootstrap pins invalidates the previous cache binding. Recovery requires an online response verified against the current pins with a strictly newer policy sequence; existing high-water state remains in force. Do not delete credential-store state as a key-rotation procedure. Cache commit ordering preserves the old committed pointer until the new entry has been flushed; full crash/reboot qualification remains a release gate. There are no login, logout or enrollment commands in this delivery. When authentication is designed, revisit session-to-policy identity binding, account/organization switching, logout invalidation, credential lifecycle, authenticated refresh and CI identity, plus end-to-end server interoperability. Configuration policy is not a login session and does not grant publishing/signing authority. Connector credentials, shell secrets, verified tool installation and remote action caching also remain separate integrations.

The implementation status records tested revisions and host coverage. The current contracts have focused coverage in resolution and editing tests, CLI tests, execution enforcement tests, and signed managed-policy tests. Agent transition tests beside the policy agent cover key rotation, elapsed deadlines and denial/clock behavior. These tests do not establish interoperability with a production authenticated service. Documentation structure is checked with node tooling/check-docs.mjs; that check does not validate product behavior. The quick-start command sequence and the provisioned-Node task example were separately exercised against the compiled CLI on Windows during this documentation update.

The project environment reference documents env._.path, its atomic replacement and file-relative paths. The optional compatibility capability is config.env-path/v1. This metadata is not exported into task/build environments.

Global verbosity and OYZU_LOG are typed invocation-only presentation inputs, resolved before any project session. They are not project keys and never enter effective execution snapshots or configuration digests. Explicit CLI controls override the complete environment filter. Help/version do not resolve it. See CLI diagnostic controls for grammar and errors.

[tools] declarations can also be written, replaced and removed with oyzu install SPEC, oyzu uninstall and -g/--local/--profile, which keep comments and lock the result; see tool commands. A declaration is a version string, or mise's option-table form with only a version key (node = { version = "22" }), which validation normalizes to that string so every consumer sees one form. Edits change only the table's version. Any other option key, or a table without a version string, fails with CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE naming the key; see option tables. tools.platforms is an optional project/profile string set consumed through the normal configuration cascade. It restricts Rust lock metadata coverage, not the artifact matrix or installation authority. When absent, pin uses the finite default metadata platforms. An empty or unsupported selection fails pin. Values are exact OS/architecture/ABI tuples; this setting is not a tool version request. No schema version changes.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/direct-tests.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. oyzu run test produces a test-only dist/ bundle for single-package Node projects and native npm/pnpm/Yarn workspaces using node:test, Jest, Vitest or Mocha, Python projects using pytest through pip, uv or Poetry, Go modules/workspaces using native testing, Helm charts using local validation and optional helm-unittest suites, Rust apps/workspaces using nextest and Cargo doctests, supported Ant assertion/JUnit targets, native Maven reactors, and Gradle multi-project/composite builds. Native dependencies and any required reporters must already be installed. Node itself is resolved during oyzu build preflight when the project has no pin (see below); oyzu run uses an existing selection. There is no Docker, desktop, sign-in or tool-installation prerequisite for this host workflow. See Python test reporting, Go testing and Helm testing for native prerequisites and coverage scope; the examples below use Node. oyzu run list oyzu run test oyzu inspect dist oyzu run test -- --test-name-pattern=greeting The builder recognizes the conventional runner or a supported exact test command and supplies native JUnit and applicable application coverage reporting. Helm records coverage as inapplicable, with one local-validation report and a separate native unittest report when detected. Host Helm tests require prepared chart dependencies, a provisioned Helm executable and the helm-unittest plugin when suites are selected. Their orchestration is compiled into Oyzu and requires no Python interpreter; they do not install tools or download dependencies. Existing npm pretest/posttest lifecycle behavior stays native. Qualified names such as api:test use that target's configuration and working directory; Oyzu pre_/post_ hooks and declared prerequisites follow the task engine's ordering. Forwarded arguments apply only to the requested task.

The invocation uses the same report binding, validation, collection and bundle transaction as captured builds. dist/manifest.json links current JUnit and coverage reports (LCOV for Node, Cobertura for Python, native statement profiles for Go), their summaries, the recorded plan, execution envelope and logs. It records no newly built application artifacts and does not run packaging, lint or formatting just because tests were requested. Use oyzu build for builder stages and snapshot artifacts. Local text-mode tasks inherit stdin and tee stdout/stderr live to the caller and the bundle's numbered log files, including on native failure. The child's output streams are pipes. An explicitly interactive = true task instead inherits real stdout/stderr descriptors in text mode; its output cannot also be retained and its bundle stdout/stderr logs are empty. JSON mode captures both streams even for interactive tasks, without terminal output descriptors. Native report files and their validation remain required independently of stream capture. See development task streams for empty-stdout checks, quiet mode, completion waiting and current verification limits. Native test failures, missing required reports, malformed reports and an unmet configured coverage minimum fail the command. Valid failed-test reports and bounded malformed report bytes are retained when available. Collection waits for the post-hook so that a report-transforming hook can finish. A failing pre-hook blocks its test; a failing test skips its success-only post-hook; a failing post-hook retains the test's available reports. A launch failure produces failed action evidence rather than success. Unexecuted actions are marked blocked. Default reports use a fresh private directory for every invocation. Custom commands are not parsed as arbitrary shell programs or replaced with guessed native commands. Hooks and commands receive OYZU_TEST_REPORT and OYZU_COVERAGE_REPORT for concrete assigned paths.

oyzu build and oyzu run <target>:test resolve the same task: an explicit Oyzu task, else the project's native package.json test script, else the builder default. Discovering a script does not by itself add it to the build lifecycle. The resolved task has one of three integration modes, shown in the human summary and in extensions."oyzu.dev/report-integration": builder-default: no native test override; the builder runs node --test with JUnit and lcov reporters, and the Node runner and coverage need no extra packages. native-runner: a package.json script that is exactly node --test followed only by plain --flag options. The script still runs through npm, so project config and pretest/posttest lifecycle behavior stay native and tests run once; reporter and coverage options are appended after --. Scripts that name paths, their own reporters, coverage or watch options are not instrumented, because flags after paths are silently ignored by Node. opaque: any other command is preserved verbatim, with nothing appended or guessed. Supported reports are collected only if the command writes them to the assigned OYZU_TEST_REPORT / OYZU_COVERAGE_REPORT locations (or a declared reports path) during this execution. Absent reports are recorded as status: missing. Each test action also produces a test-evidence record (manifest.extensions."oyzu.dev/test-evidence", the Test evidence block in human output and evidence in oyzu run --json outcomes) with separate command, test-results and coverage status, and an acceptance verdict: Case Outcome Builder default, reports collected accepted Native override, reports collected accepted Opaque command passed, reports absent, not required incomplete: "command passed; test results missing; coverage missing"; the build still succeeds Test command failed (any mode) command fails; partial reports are retained; rejected Report missing and required (checks.tests = "required" or checks.coverage = "required", checks.coverageMinimum, or an explicit task reports entry) report-missing error diagnostic; command fails; rejected Builder default but a report is missing fails Only reports produced by the current execution can satisfy a requirement; stale files are rejected. Oyzu does not edit package.json or checked-in configuration. A literal declaration can also redirect a supported exact command: [tasks."project:test"] argv = ["node", "--test"] reports = [{ kind = "test", format = "junit", path = "reports/junit.xml" }] The path is relative to the task's working directory. Oyzu creates missing parent directories for literal paths. A report declaration does not remove the other required report kinds. Explicit report paths or globs must have no existing matching output before the invocation; preserve or remove earlier files before rerunning. Oyzu fails rather than treating stale evidence as current. For a glob, the command remains responsible for producing matching files and directories; no single output path environment variable is inferred for multiple files.

Host tasks often build into dist/ before running tests. Direct tests preserve those files alongside their new evidence, recording paths, sizes and digests under extensions.oyzu.dev/host-outputs. Previous artifact bytes are preserved as ordinary host output; they are not listed as artifacts produced by this test invocation. Inspection verifies the preserved inventory. Earlier Oyzu reports, evidence and logs stay in history rather than becoming current test results. The previous directory moves to .oyzu/history/<new-run-id> through the shared transaction. Native output must use portable regular files/directories; links, reparse points and collisions with new evidence fail. manifest.json, plan.json, envelope.json and logs are reserved bundle paths. An application-owned manifest or other reserved-path collision needs to be preserved or relocated before this workflow can finalize. Failures during preflight or output preservation can leave the earlier bundle in place; check the command outcome and run identity instead of assuming any existing dist belongs to the latest attempt. See bundle retention and recovery.

The plan, envelope and manifest disclose oyzu.dev/invocation with kind: test, execution: host, isolation: none, source: observed-before-run and toolIdentity: unverified. Source identity is observed before executing against the live checkout; dependencies, ambient tools and subsequent source mutations are not captured. Actions declare network: host, are not cacheable, and disclose that sandbox resource limits are not enforced. Environment values in plan records are redacted. Native output/logs remain the output of the invoked programs; they are not a general secret-redaction service. CI detection gives ci-unverified, not a trusted producer identity. Effective configuration identity and available management metadata are recorded, but this test invocation does not satisfy unrelated full-build checks or grant publication/signing authority. Inspection checks integrity and agreement of invocation records, not authenticity. This is local development evidence, not hermetic or production provenance. Integrated profiles are single-package Node tests and npm workspaces (node:test, Jest, Vitest and Mocha), Python's pytest default, native Go module/workspace tests and Helm charts. Rust app/workspace native acceptance passed on all three CI hosts as described below. Ant tests and Maven reactor tests connect their native test and JaCoCo adapters to this collector. Gradle composite tests also supply named native reports. pnpm/Yarn workspace tests now use native membership with the shared package collector. Docker still lacks this test-only bundle integration. A supported test depending on an unsupported test profile fails before execution rather than claiming complete evidence for both. These are implementation gaps; the intended common builder reporting contract remains broader. The native probe is python tooling/test-direct-test-bundles.py --cli <compiled-oyzu-path>, with dependencies from tooling/design-requirements.txt. It checks real native tests, application coverage, lifecycle behavior, hooks, failed/missing/malformed evidence, redirected/stale reports, launch failures, native output preservation, history and inspection tampering. CI runs it after CLI compilation on Windows, macOS and Linux. Revision-specific results and remaining gaps are recorded in implementation status; CI wiring alone does not prove all hosts passed. python tooling/test-helm-direct.py --cli <compiled-oyzu-path> --helm <helm-path> exercises application and root library charts, qualified targets/hooks, native unittest, failed reports, coverage inapplicability and bundle inspection. The probe requires Helm 3.22.0, helm-unittest 1.2.0 and Python 3.11+; Python runs this repository's verification harness, not the product's Helm orchestration. The shared TaskPlan carries coverage applicability into target records, including after post-hooks; a positive coverage minimum cannot be satisfied by a chart without a coverage report. The Linux Helm suite runs this probe after downloading the compiled CLI. Windows native results and pending Linux execution are recorded in implementation status; macOS native execution is not yet qualified.
