Jest 29.7.0, Vitest 5.0.3 with matching @vitest/coverage-v8 5.0.3, and Mocha 11.8.0 with c8 10.1.3 are exercised by the direct framework probe. Provision project dependencies before oyzu run test. Mocha requires project-installed c8 10.x or explicitly provisioned fallback tools via OYZU_NODE_REPORTING_HOME; see Mocha reporting. Tests do not install missing reporters. Vitest's declared coverage provider must match its version; other framework major versions are not qualified by these checks. No test section is needed. Detection selects the implicit runner; exact native scripts (jest, jest --ci, vitest, vitest run, mocha) keep npm pretest/posttest behavior while the existing framework adapter adds JUnit and LCOV. Native configuration remains authoritative for test selection, reporters and coverage scope. Both implicit and scripted tests use the common bundle collector, with native failures retained in the manifest. Recognized command overrides retain report obligations; arbitrary script bodies must supply their assigned reports themselves. The framework wrappers resolve npm to its provisioned JavaScript entrypoint, preserving argument arrays and avoiding shell-dependent .cmd invocation on Windows. They retain native npm configuration. The three-platform CI probe covers implicit runners and npm scripts; pnpm/Yarn scripted host combinations are not yet qualified by this probe. Host tests retain ambient network access as disclosed in the invocation; they do not establish hermetic build evidence. Run python tooling/test-node-framework-direct.py --cli <compiled-path> after npm ci in tooling/fixtures/jest, tooling/fixtures/vitest, tooling/fixtures/mocha and tooling/images/node-quality, with tooling/design-requirements.txt installed. It invokes the real CLI and native frameworks, validates JUnit/LCOV bundles, checks native/Oyzu hook ordering and failed assertions, and calls oyzu inspect dist. Fixture copies preserve npm's executable symlinks: dereferencing Unix .bin entries breaks Vitest's relative imports before the native test command can run. The initial Linux/macOS probe exposed that harness error. The corrected probe passed on all three hosts at bfa2b7c in run 37049720609. npm workspace report ownership and native prerequisites are described in npm workspaces; pnpm/Yarn direct workspace integration is described in native workspace tests; Yarn and pnpm captured workspace builds are now implemented with isolated CLI acceptance pending. Rust app/workspace direct tests use the same collector with nextest JUnit, Cobertura and doctest invocation reports. The direct reporting step passed on Windows MSVC, Linux and macOS at bfa2b7c. The local Windows GNU toolchain lacks the required profiler runtime. See Rust prerequisites and current verification for measured scope and unsupported combinations. Workspace bundle publication holds an invocation lock through finalization and rollback. Completing or abandoning the transaction explicitly unlocks it so a transient inherited Unix file description cannot keep the next invocation locked out. Concurrent active invocations still fail with the workspace-lock diagnostic; this does not permit concurrent writes to one bundle.

With no configuration pin, oyzu build preflight requests lts whether or not engines.node is present: it selects the greatest release whose Node index lts field is a non-empty string and that satisfies every engine constraint. If no LTS release satisfies them, it falls back to the greatest stable release satisfying them; the requirement reason in the plan explains this fallback rule. With 24.x marked LTS and 26.x Current, >=22 selects 24.x and >=26 selects 26.x. Configuration pins, including latest, 26, exact versions and lts/<name>, keep their existing behavior and must satisfy engines. Preflight writes oyzu.lock and installs the selection before any action runs; it prepares tools only and never runs tests. See Node selection. oyzu build --connector-bindings <file> supplies host bindings for administrator-routed tool sources. .nvmrc/.node-version are not read yet. python tooling/test-node-test-reporting.py --cli <compiled-oyzu-path> [--store <dir>] [--lock <oyzu.lock>] creates temporary Git fixtures and runs oyzu build --full and oyzu run site:test for: builder default, native node --test --test-concurrency=1 with pretest/posttest (each runs once per invocation), opaque wrapper, a cooperative wrapper, failing default and native tests, and an opaque wrapper with checks.tests = "required". It asserts the integration mode, per-capability statuses, acceptance verdict, retained partial reports and the report-missing diagnostic. Qualification limits are recorded in implementation status.
documents.s: Node selection and the Node task probe

documents.t: CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/discovery-selection.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Experimental. Static discovery decides each exclusive role of a Node or Python target, such as its package manager or formatter, from native project files. It reads bounded metadata, never runs a tool, script or configuration file, and never breaks a tie silently. When native evidence settles a role, no Oyzu configuration is needed. When it does not, discovery fails and names both the conflicting inputs and the build.yaml declaration that settles the role. oyzu build --plan shows every decision with its reason.

Without build.yaml, discovery selects a native project at the root or searches below that root for targets. The inventory walk stops descending as soon as it finds a target; the selected native builder owns discovery within that target. Nested Git repositories and directories with their own build.yaml also stop the walk. Existing generated/dependency directory exclusions, the depth limit of 32 and the limit of 1,024 targets still apply. Ordinary files below an already selected target do not add inventory traversal work. These rules apply equally to human and JSON discovery output. The invocation's configuration boundary also bounds conventional target discovery. An empty or malformed ancestor .git marker does not select that ancestor as a workspace: for standalone sibling projects with no enclosing Oyzu configuration, oyzu -C first run list discovers only first's tasks. In a real Git workspace, discovery still includes its conventional targets, and an unqualified task exposed by several targets remains ambiguous. Use the target-qualified task named by the error, or --root first when deliberately selecting a narrower root. Gitdir-pointer repositories and linked worktrees follow the same boundary rules. Each detector reports a candidate with evidence of one strength. The strongest evidence wins: Strength Examples declared a test script that runs exactly one recognized test runner native a lockfile, package.json packageManager, a framework configuration file, a pyproject.toml tool table conventional a declared dependency, a settings-only pnpm-workspace.yaml, a uv.lock that locks no packages default the documented default when nothing else applies, such as npm, ESLint, Prettier, pip or Ruff Two different candidates with the strongest evidence are a conflict. A candidate the builder has no adapter for, such as packageManager: nub@0.8.3, is unsupported. Both fail discovery; neither registration order nor file order picks a winner. Native rules that settle a role without configuration: Lockfiles beat a settings-only pnpm-workspace.yaml. pnpm reads settings from pnpm-workspace.yaml and can write the file on its own; only its packages list declares a workspace (the pnpm adapter already treats a settings-only file as no workspace). A file without packages is conventional pnpm evidence, so package-lock.json (npm) outranks it, while with no lockfile it still selects pnpm over the npm default. A file with packages, or one that is not a YAML mapping, stays native and conflicts with another manager's lockfile. The runner a compound test script names. When the test script is not exactly a recognized command (jest, vitest run, mocha, ...) but its &&, ||, ; and | segments name exactly one of jest, vitest, mocha or node --test, that runner is declared evidence. Segments such as pnpm lint, npm run unit or yarn unit are followed into the referenced package script. Leading NAME=value assignments, cross-env, npx and <manager> exec are skipped. A script with quotes, $, backticks, parentheses, redirection or manager flags such as --filter is not read; its framework is then decided by the remaining evidence. The script itself still runs natively, without report instrumentation unless it is an exact recognized command. A uv.lock that locks no packages. uv records the project itself in uv.lock, so a lock without any [[package]] cannot belong to this project's manager. It is conventional evidence and yields to poetry.lock or [tool.poetry]. A uv.lock that does lock packages stays native.

When discovery fails, declare the target and add the selector the error names under with: pytest: uses: python/package with: formatter: ruff If native files identify more than one builder, select uses first. For example, the pinned Mermaid root contains both package.json and Dockerfile; its build.yaml needs mermaid: {uses: node/app} before the Node test-runner decision can be made. That choice does not require a with.test-framework selector: pnpm lint && vitest run selects Vitest from the native test script. Builder with key Values node/app, node/package package-manager npm, pnpm, yarn test-framework node-test, jest, vitest, mocha, custom linter eslint, biome formatter prettier, biome python/app, python/package, python/library package-manager pip, uv, poetry linter ruff, flake8 formatter ruff, black The keys match the role names in --plan and in the target's oyzu.dev/discovery plan extension. A selection wins over every observation; discovery still records the observations, and the selected value must be one of the listed values. Any other value, a non-string value or any other with key fails. A selection applies to the declared target's own root only; it does not change the decisions of packages inside a Node workspace. Tool versions are not selected here: they belong in oyzu.toml. Example errors: conflicting Python formatter candidates black, ruff: black via pyproject.toml tool.black; ruff via pyproject.toml tool.ruff; declare the intended one for this target in build.yaml with `with: {formatter: black}` or `with: {formatter: ruff}` conflicting Node package manager candidates nub, pnpm (nub unsupported): nub via package.json /packageManager; pnpm via pnpm-lock.yaml lockfile; declare the intended one for this target in build.yaml with `with: {package-manager: pnpm}` The suggestions list the supported candidates that were observed; when none was, they list every supported value. Selecting a manager or runner the project does not natively use can still fail later, in that tool's own preparation or test run.

oyzu build --plan shows a Discovered table per target with each role, the selected candidate and the reason. With --json, each entry of targets has a discovery object mapping the role to selected and reason. For example: package-manager npm native package-lock.json lockfile; outranks pnpm (conventional pnpm-workspace.yaml settings without packages) formatter ruff build.yaml with.formatter; discovery also observed black A reason names the strength and evidence of the winner and every candidate it outranked with non-default evidence. Executed builds keep the complete observations, detector registry and any selector in the plan's oyzu.dev/discovery extension.

The Rust builder reads rust-toolchain.toml and rust-toolchain in every form rustup accepts: the legacy rust-toolchain file holding only a toolchain name, such as nightly-2020-07-10, stable or 1.95.0; the TOML [toolchain] table, in either file, with channel (stable, beta, nightly, <major.minor>, <major.minor.patch>, optionally dated or with a host triple), components, targets and profile; a table without channel, which rustup resolves to the default toolchain: Oyzu then uses its own default (the [tools] rust selection in oyzu.toml, otherwise the adapter baseline) and keeps the declared components, targets and profile; path, a local toolchain directory. Oyzu cannot provision it, so oyzu pin and build tool resolution fail with toolchain.path names the local toolchain ...; select a Rust release in oyzu.toml with [tools] rust = "<version>". An explicit [tools] rust overrides it. An empty [toolchain] table, channel together with path, or an empty or whitespace-containing channel fails. Both files together still fail with both rust-toolchain.toml and rust-toolchain exist, although rustup itself prefers rust-toolchain. Reading a channel is not resolving it: the Rust tool backend currently resolves exact three-part stable versions, and other channels report that backend version selection is needed.

Selections are read once, at discovery, from the frozen build.yaml inventory. Captured workspace planning reuses the target's decisions for its root. The host development composition of npm workspace tests and quality checks re-detects each package, including the root, without them, so a root that needed a selection fails there. Node output profiles and the Python test framework have no selector. The six discovery stops in the feasibility corpus are covered by fixtures in tests/integration/discovery.rs; the shared resolver by discovery::detectors unit tests; Rust toolchain forms by builders::rust::requirement_evidence unit tests. The pinned-corpus qualification records a compiled-CLI Windows plan against all six real source commits, including required selector reruns and its limits. It does not qualify builds or other host platforms.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/example-collection.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. The public Oyzu examples repository owns self-contained native project candidates, canonical recipe instructions, four learning paths and a coverage inventory. Standalone examples need no platform account. Each entry states whether it is executable, blocked or planned; the collection does not imply that every registered adapter or provider is qualified. Each recipe separates the copied project/ from metadata and verification expectations. Use instructions and project files from the same exact commit. Native manifests and oyzu.toml own tool requirements, oyzu.lock owns resolved identities, and build.yaml declares only necessary build intent/relationships. The website imports selected recipes and actual source excerpts at an immutable commit, identified by its source links. Product support, example maturity and measured verification are independent. An executable recipe is not necessarily verified on your host/executor; old results apply only to their recorded subject. Unsupported capabilities remain explicit gaps with a next proof. The collection includes basic adapter/manager projects, package consumers, workspaces, generated sources, task hooks, affected selection, cache reuse, artifact materialization, local serving and file publication. Captured execution requires the named compatible executor; a controller's host is distinct from the artifact target. Follow the recipe's prerequisite and profile instructions. Recorded baseline consumers cover all ten existing builder families. That does not qualify every package manager, runtime, platform or provider. Yarn Classic is supplied by its captured executor. uv and Poetry examples use native Python manifests and provided runtimes; explicit Python tool-lock handoff is not proved. The complete Rust platform matrix remains a documented gap. The Windows pnpm workspace record requires the separately identified CLI correction and verifies both delivered archives through an independent offline consumer. Offline replay needs the selected sources and normal cached prerequisites. Publication/deployment additionally need scoped destinations and credentials. A successful build is not publication or observed deployment and cannot waive required evidence or organizational controls. The maintainer selected Apache-2.0 for first-party examples on 2026-10-17. Retain copied project licenses and applicable third-party notices. See the repository's contribution guidance and integration operations for selection, preparation, failures, release retention and verification limits.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/local-builds.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. The current implementation connects host-native Cargo, Go applications, npm dist applications and pip wheel builds to the local development proposal. Qualification is recorded by scenario in the tool user-flow record. Do not interpret the commands below as completed qualification of every platform or build mode. The host coordinator also admits existing captured docker/image workers, with per-target placement shown by --plan. See image workers and qualification limits. Host processes remain unrestricted; worker enforcement does not extend to the entire graph. BuildKit actions supervise both the docker exec client and the worker. A nonzero client exit reports BUILDKIT_BUILDCTL_FAILED; a stopped, OOM-killed or unreachable worker reports BUILDKIT_WORKER_UNAVAILABLE. Container state and daemon probes run every five seconds with individual two-second deadlines; the final check runs immediately when the client exits. An observed stopped or OOM-killed container fails immediately. Failed inspection or daemon probes need three consecutive failures; a successful check resets the count. A dead daemon therefore does not wait for the action timeout. Diagnostics retain the buildctl exit code/signal when available, container exit and memory limit. State.OOMKilled confirms OOM; exit 137 alone is reported as possible OOM or external SIGKILL. If the Docker client is still stuck, its exit is explicitly unavailable. Cleanup has a separate five-second bound. Retry after restoring the worker or providing enough memory; failed actions do not publish artifacts.

oyzu pin --dry-run previews requirements and lock changes without installing native tools or changing project files. For a new project or a version-1 resolution lock it resolves compiler metadata; --offline requires matching cached metadata. oyzu pin publishes complete resolutions, with conflicts and incomplete inputs reported as failures. See tool planning. All project locks use one version-1 contract. pin resolves requirements whether or not installation records already exist, and preserves those records when publishing resolutions. Incomplete resolution leaves the lock unchanged. Build preflight installs missing supported pinned tools; native host prerequisites still require external provisioning. Pinning itself does not install tools. When a selected builder admits automatic tool resolution and the project has no oyzu.lock, native build preflight resolves its requirements and publishes the lock without editing authored TOML. It captures the published lock before installing and activating the exact selection for native actions. This uses the normal acquisition verification and installation leases; an ambient compiler is not required for supported managed tool requirements. Existing locks remain frozen: incompatible or missing selections require an explicit pin update rather than silently resolving during execution. Offline preparation requires the existing metadata, archive or installation needed by the selected provider. The empty-store qualification and current platform limits are recorded in the fresh-checkout record. The initial adapter covers Rust: rust-toolchain.toml or the legacy rust-toolchain file, Cargo package/workspace rust-version minimums, declared components/targets/profile, and the tools/components required by the existing native build/test/lint/format stages. Every toolchain-file form rustup accepts is read; see Rust toolchain files. A file without channel keeps its components and uses the configured or default Rust; a local path toolchain fails resolution unless oyzu.toml selects a release. Both toolchain filenames together are an error. In the discovery inventory, no toolchain declaration means Rust is reported without a selected version; a build then locks the greatest stable release (pinning is optional). That inventory reports effective Oyzu tool settings separately without claiming resolution. The resolver resolves those inputs through the tool-planning contract described above. Each fact includes its source; repeated facts retain their sources. System linker/SDK requirements are explicit. Windows discovery uses the declared toolchain channel: windows-gnullvm identifies LLVM-MinGW UCRT, Clang linking and a Rust profiler runtime; windows-msvc identifies Microsoft Build Tools and the Windows SDK. A windows-gnu declaration explicitly calls for a coverage-capable alternative. An unqualified channel such as 1.95.0 lists GNU/LLVM and supported MSVC as alternatives, rather than assuming the user's rustup default. This static discovery does not run rustup, inspect PATH or install Windows components. Dependency build-script requirements, compiler/profile compatibility and inherited parent-directory toolchain files are not inferred in this slice. Node requirements are also resolved through the shared tool contract. For the native pip wheel path, CPython is resolved from requires-python or .python-version and installed from Python Build Standalone (details); uv, Poetry and legacy Python tools are not provisioned. Other unsupported requirements remain explicit. The command works offline in standalone mode; existing configuration loading and managed policy rules still apply. Pinning currently requires the workspace root. On 2026-10-03 the compiled discovery implementation inspected this checkout's requirements with PATH empty. Two integration tests passed for toolchain-free inspection, unchanged lock bytes and conflicting manifest rejection. Other hosts are unverified. Discovery evidence is available in pin JSON alongside the resolution preview. It is not installed-tool evidence. Unsupported prerelease lock versions are rejected; no legacy decoder or automatic migration is provided. Existing tool stores are left intact. See the lock contract.

Native Rust compilation retains compiler state under the original project's .oyzu/native/rust/<host>/, while source compilation runs in a private target projection. The Rust builder explicitly identifies its absolute cache and inventory arguments as host paths, including the separate test cache when quality stages are selected. These exact arguments retain their host locations even when a project is rooted under /workspace/, /out/ or /oyzu/. Captured workspace, output and runtime paths still translate into the source projection, report output and engine runtime. Path declarations do not relax native cache, binary inventory or artifact containment checks. Isolated execution reuses completed read-only tool restorations (Docker volumes or daemonless directories) under the existing restoration locks. A completed restoration is trusted as an installed tool, so reuse does not hash its source archive again. A new restoration verifies the archive before worker launch/extraction; incomplete restoration is never a hit. This does not change archive acquisition checks or current tool/catalog admission. Native Rust builds now project inferred snapshot package versions into the private manifests using the same resolver as captured builds. Each native member keeps its own package scope and tag baseline, augmented by the declared target prerequisite closure. Cargo reconciles only private workspace versions offline against the existing lock, preserving locked external packages. Compiled CARGO_PKG_VERSION, artifact version metadata and plan/manifest decisions use the projected version; executable filenames retain their native names. The original manifests and Cargo/tool locks remain unchanged. Conflicts and missing offline dependencies fail preparation with recovery guidance. This new Rust projection passes the Windows three-application pair with and without a declared producer edge, including native reports and independent compiled-version execution. This does not qualify other hosts or all native profiles; see version inference. This fixes issue #384, where an absolute host cache was mistaken for a captured /workspace/ mount and compilation failed with COMMAND_FAILED: No such file or directory after successful preparation. Retry the same native build with the corrected CLI; no project configuration or cache migration is required. python tooling/test-native-host-paths.py --cli <compiled-oyzu> --parent <writable-directory> checks two native binaries, repeat compilation, bundle inspection and unchanged source/configuration files. Use a parent under /workspace/ to exercise the original collision; --full additionally checks native quality-stage cache paths with provisioned test/coverage tools. This does not qualify captured builds or other operating systems.
documents.s: Host cache paths and source projections

documents.t: Native Rust builds now check the selected environment with a temporary, dependency-free Cargo compile-and-link probe before compiling project code. The probe honors Cargo linker configuration and Rust flags; selected test stages also request coverage instrumentation. Success verifies this basic capability, not every library needed by dependency build scripts. Temporary probe files are removed after success or failure. No OS components are installed. oyzu run performs the same probe before starting a Rust task that compiles or links (cargo build, test, install, check, clippy, doc, run, rustc), once per target and after tool preparation. Tasks that compile nothing, such as cargo fetch, skip it. Without a linker the task fails in under a second with the guidance below instead of a raw compiler error; a windows-gnullvm toolchain is told to put LLVM-MinGW's bin directory on PATH. Oyzu does not install LLVM-MinGW. A failure reports EXECUTOR_PREREQUISITE_UNAVAILABLE with the native cause and external provisioning guidance. Correct the selected toolchain/linker/SDK and rerun. Discovery and pinning remain static and report availability as not checked; only actual preflight executes the probe. Managed tools and executor prerequisites are separate categories in the inventory. Compile-only inventory omits automatic quality-stage helpers; explicitly declared components remain requirements. This check currently covers native Rust execution. It does not introduce remote executor probes, arbitrary system-package detection or OS provisioning. A ready host capability is not a claim of hermeticity or publication eligibility. Plain oyzu build selects native development execution when every selected target is native-eligible (Rust, Go, Gradle, Maven, npm node/app and pip Python, plus admitted image workers). Other builder/workspace shapes retain their existing captured behavior. oyzu build --isolated explicitly uses the existing captured container executor; --image also retains that path. --affected computes its selection first and then follows the same native-eligibility rules as a plain build, falling back to the captured path only where a plain build would. A failed native or isolated build never retries through another executor. CI detection does not change this selection. Plain local builds need pinned Rust/Cargo and provisioned native compilation prerequisites. Preflight verifies or installs the pinned tools before native dependency preparation. Declared platform relationships and target selection are validated before automatic pinning acquires tool metadata or publishes a lock. Invalid or ambiguous matrix relationships therefore fail without starting tool provisioning. Quality stages additionally need their tools: rustfmt for formatting, Clippy for linting, and nextest, cargo-llvm-cov and the compiler's LLVM tools/profiler runtime for tests with coverage. The Rust test prerequisites describe report tooling. Native dependency preparation first checks the Cargo cache and acquires missing locked inputs when online, as described below. The existing historical Windows coverage qualification includes the MSVC toolchain/linker/SDK. The locally provisioned windows-gnu 1.95 compiler failed a coverage probe with missing profiler_builtins on 2026-10-03. A separate Rust 1.95 x86_64-pc-windows-gnullvm experiment on 2026-10-04 passed two tiny-project tests through cargo-llvm-cov 0.9.1 and nextest 0.9.146, producing a Cobertura report with five of six lines covered using LLVM-MinGW UCRT 20260616 and Clang linking. The compiled CLI also passed oyzu run test on that probe; oyzu inspect dist confirmed both tests and the same collected coverage counts. This required no Microsoft Build Tools installation. It proves direct test and coverage execution, not the complete Oyzu self-build or automatic tool provisioning. The full Oyzu checkout also passed cargo check --locked --offline --bin oyzu with GNU/LLVM, Clang and native CMake/Ninja; final executable linking was not tested by that check. Coverage remains required when the test/coverage stage is selected; plain local compilation does not select it automatically. The native path builds development-profile binaries unless the build is optimized: oyzu build --optimized, build.optimized = true, or a build whose artifacts leave the machine (a slice, a shared remote cache write, a packaging target, the release context) runs cargo build --release instead; see optimized builds. Tests keep Cargo's test profile. Plain local oyzu build automatically schedules compilation and any check at level required. oyzu build --full, the pr, ci and release contexts or the CI profile also schedule test/JUnit/coverage/doctest integration, Clippy and read-only formatting checks, except those whose check level is off. Required checks, hooks and task prerequisites remain enforced in fast mode. Binaries are collected only after the selected stages succeed. oyzu run test, oyzu run lint and oyzu run format-check remain explicit task entry points. Native build overrides are currently rejected with an explicit diagnostic. Ordinary hooks and task prerequisites use the shared task graph. Required configuration checks remain enforced; unsupported managed host execution fails before native preparation. This repository sets Cargo's development and test profiles to debug = 0, omitting generated debug information while retaining debug assertions. The development profile optimizes the direct SHA-256 dependency (sha2 0.10.9) at level 3; the test profile inherits that package override. Oyzu's own code and other dependencies retain their existing optimization settings. This reduces the CPU cost of full tool-payload and evidence hashing without caching or skipping verification. Dependency upgrades must keep this version-specific override aligned with the direct sha2 dependency. Release settings are unchanged. Windows worker tests relaunch their own test executable; embedded debug information previously grew that executable beyond the worker's 512 MiB image limit and caused TOOL_WORKER_IMAGE_INVALID before launch. Source-level debugger information is unavailable in these default builds. Profile overrides that restore debug information can reintroduce this failure; rebuild with the repository defaults to recover. The image limit, integrity checks, test/report gates and scenario timeouts remain unchanged. Other projects retain their own native Cargo profile settings. --all-platforms requests the declared matrix through the existing captured executor; it requires its provisioned Docker environment. Native execution does not cross-compile or confer production publication eligibility. Native development output is a runnable binary, not a versioned source distribution; use the isolated path for the existing packaging contract. Its manifest record still carries the bundle's required version: the builder's own artifact version where it has one, otherwise the target's resolved version. A consumer that declares a platform other than the host, such as a docker/image with platforms: [linux/amd64] that materializes a Go binary on a Windows host, does not use the native path, because native producers are built for the host only. Plain oyzu build (and --plan) then selects the captured executor, which builds each producer for the platform its consumer requires, so the binary is a Linux executable. When the consumer's platform is the host's, the native path is unchanged. A pinned Go, Node or helm is restored from the lock in that captured worker (see Go, Node and Helm); any other pinned tool the worker cannot yet take from the lock is still refused there.

oyzu build --plan previews the same execution-path selection as a build: local host when supported, otherwise the captured executor. --isolated, --all-platforms, named targets, profiles and --full keep their normal selection meaning. The preview itself needs neither Cargo nor Docker installed. The preview reads configuration and native manifests, applies the shared target, matrix and task-selection rules, and shows each target's discovery decisions with their reasons, selected/skipped stages, declared task ordering and consolidated tool requirements. See discovery decisions and selectors. It does not install tools, fetch packages, execute build tools or project scripts, create a lock, open a tool store, write a source snapshot, or create/replace a build bundle. Application dependencies are acquired only by an actual build's preparation. --affected additionally hashes local source and reads the local Git baseline using Git; its existing conservative fallback rules still apply, with no network or checkout writes. A preview is deliberately incomplete: installed-tool availability, executor capabilities, dependency cache readiness, exact commands, native-generated stages, artifact names and report bindings remain unresolved. A selected stage means configuration requests it, not that its prerequisites have passed. Dynamic target relationships may add work during real preparation. Success means the static preview was produced; it does not certify build success or publication eligibility. Live build output shows one plan table once, before work starts: targets by stages with run, skip or - cells and one footnote per skip reason. A single target built for several platforms pivots to one row per platform; above twelve rows targets with identical stages share a counted row (-v lists every target). See Result output. Matrix expansion (--all-platforms, --isolated) can yield targets that differ only by platform. In the live build output a single target built for several platforms is one plan table with a row per platform; the requirements table shows "all N targets" when every target shares a requirement. --json still reports every target individually. Targets whose plans differ keep their own sections. Human output uses stage/requirement tables with semantic color on capable terminals (or CLICOLOR_FORCE=1); NO_COLOR preserves plain text. Owned styling is emitted once, after escaping project-controlled values. --json returns a version-1 build-preview record with resolved: false, selection, targets (each with a discovery map of role to selected and reason), tasks, requirements, unresolved details, effect flags and timings. It is not the executable build-plan retained by actual builds in dist/plan.json. The former captured --plan behavior that acquired dependencies is superseded; use an actual build and its retained plan for execution-level evidence. No schema version was bumped. timings reports where the preview spent its wall-clock time, in milliseconds: totalMs and phases, in order discovery (configuration and target discovery), selection (selection, variants, task graph and requirements), source (inventorying the working tree for analysis from file metadata; no file is read until analysis asks for it), analysis (with targets, one entry per analyzed target, then finishMs for merging facts and rulesMs for the diagnostic rules) and planning (stage and task listing). source and analysis are absent when analysis is disabled or fails. Timings describe one run only and are never part of the analysis record, which stays identical between runs.

oyzu build --remote --plan previews what oyzu build --remote would run on a platform pool, without contacting the platform or needing its settings or token. It is the same read-only preview with the pool's selection: isolated execution, full checks, and the ordinary isolated platform selection. --remote does not imply --all-platforms or introduce additional platform variants. Named targets and --affected <base> select as the remote run does; --affected compares with the merge base of <base> and HEAD. The record's execution is remote. The platform's planner runs this command with the project's pinned Oyzu on a checkout of the exact commit to learn each job's requirements before it is queued. The preview reads the working tree, so local uncommitted changes are included even though a remote run never sends them. --isolated, --all-platforms, --image, --check and --download are refused with --remote. Every preview target carries these placement facts: Field Meaning platform The artifact platform. From the target's variant when it declares one; otherwise the executor's own platform decides, shown as unresolved until executor selection. platformSource variant, executor or host (a development-mode host target). executionPlatform The platform an executor must run on, or null when any executor works. A Rust cross-compile runs on linux/amd64 whatever it targets. A Docker image needs its own platform when its reachable final stage has RUN; a clearly independent final stage ignores RUN in unused earlier stages. Ambiguous stage relationships retain the conservative whole-file requirement. needsDaemon, daemonReason Whether the selected work needs a Docker engine on the executor, and why. false for development-mode host targets, Node targets that can use the daemonless sandbox, and admitted image assembly with only its native build task selected. Selected quality tasks or hooks can make an image target require Docker. isolation What the executor must provide to run the target: host (development mode), crun (Linux with unprivileged user namespaces, or a Docker engine), in-process (Oyzu's native OCI assembly and output copy), or docker (a Docker engine). id, logicalTarget, variant Concrete target ID, its original logical name, and its expanded axes. IDs may be normalized and hashed; clients must use the returned ID rather than construct one. A logical dependency waits for every selected variant; a concrete dependency names that variant only. dependsOnTargets Concrete declared ordering and artifact-input dependencies. Cross-target tasks[].dependsOn edges also contribute to the graph. sliceable Whether the static preview finds no reason this target cannot be reused by another slice. false means include it in the consumer's slice, not a separate handoff producer. Runtime preparation, invalid output writes or storage failures can still prevent reuse. sliceReason, sliceDetail Stable refusal code and human explanation when sliceable is false; otherwise null. Codes: ALWAYS_RUN_HOOK, UNCACHED_TASK, UNSCOPED_INPUTS, UNBOUNDED_OUTPUTS, SECRET_ENVIRONMENT, CACHE_DISABLED, SOURCE_PROJECTION. Platforms are written in OCI form (linux/amd64, darwin/arm64), as variants and pool facts name them; a development-mode host target reports the host that way too. OYZU_NO_DOCKER=1 does not alter preview selection or placement facts. Plan-only requests never enable the execution guard. Remote planning needs no credentials. Hooks always run, including hooks declaring outputs. Authored tasks need both cache = true and valid declared outputs; inputs outside their target cannot be cache scoped. Static analysis can identify native stages with unbounded outputs (omitted with --no-analysis). Secret environments and disabled local caching prevent storage. Image builders currently use source projections the action cache declines to store. sliceable describes upstream reuse, not whether a target may execute as a slice. Failed builds and runtime output-contract violations are not predictable by this read-only preview and still fail downstream reuse safely. The top-level placement object names which facts are final and which can grow. Each target's platform, executionPlatform and needsDaemon are final, as are the tool requirements of targets whose requirement status is discovered. The selected targets, the task graph, each target's stages and the requirements of unsupported targets can grow: dynamic target relationships found during preparation can add targets, and each added target brings its own facts. The Dockerfile analysis uses the Docker builder's native assembly grammar to identify a clearly independent final stage. Unsupported syntax, stage references and ambiguous dependencies fall back to a whole-file RUN check, which can over-require but never under-require native execution.

oyzu build --no-docker, or OYZU_NO_DOCKER=1 in the environment, is for executors that have no Docker engine, such as a container or Kubernetes pool. In this mode Oyzu runs no Docker command at all. Before anything is prepared or run it works out the same preview as --plan for the build's selection; if any selected target has needsDaemon: true, the build stops with exit status 3 and nothing runs. Any other value of the variable than empty or 0 enables the mode. oyzu build --isolated --no-docker --json {"error":"NEEDS_DOCKER_DAEMON: cli need a Docker engine, which this executor does not provide (--no-docker); nothing was run","reason":"NEEDS_DOCKER_DAEMON","targets":["cli"],"exitCode":3} Exit status 3 signals a placement mismatch, so a runner can tell it from a failed build (1) or a refused invocation (2) and requeue the job on a pool that has Docker. Placement normally comes from --remote --plan; this is the guard for when that plan was wrong. Node targets run in the daemonless sandbox in this mode. An admitted RUN-free Dockerfile with FROM scratch or a digest-pinned base can build in process with --isolated --no-docker; it needs no crun or user namespaces. A final stage independent of an unused earlier RUN stage can also use this path; see Docker image assembly. --full selects Dockerfile lint and format checks that still need the Docker worker, so the guard refuses that selection rather than skipping checks. Unsupported Dockerfile work such as RUN also requires Docker. Development builds of host targets run. --no-docker cannot be combined with --remote.

Unchanged captured npm builds can reuse verified script-free dependency acquisition before action lookup. Current tool admission and the offline install, lifecycle scripts, hooks and report gates keep their existing rules. See acquisition reuse for invalidation, offline behavior and cache controls. On Linux, the isolated steps of a Node target (npm, pnpm or Yarn) can run under crun, a rootless OCI runtime, instead of docker run. The step gets the same sandbox: no network, a read-only image root, no capabilities, no-new-privileges, a seccomp filter, Docker's masked and read-only /proc paths, the same mounts and the same tmpfs sizes, inside a user namespace that maps the workspace owner to itself. The image's root filesystem is unpacked once per image digest under the image cache and shared by every build on the host. The backend is not part of the action key: both backends produce the same keys and outputs, so a result cached by one serves the other. The build.isolation setting selects the backend: auto (default) uses Docker when an engine answers and crun otherwise, docker always uses Docker, and crun uses crun for Node targets even with Docker present. --no-docker and OYZU_NO_DOCKER=1 select crun for Node targets whatever the setting says. oyzu install downloads a pinned crun release (1.24), checks its SHA-256 and keeps it in the user data directory; OYZU_CRUN names a crun the executor already provides instead. Images come from their published, digest-pinned source, or from a local Docker engine's copy when one is running; a tag-only local image with no engine has no source and the build fails before running anything. Before running anything, a build that selected crun checks that crun runs and that the host lets an unprivileged process create user, mount, network and PID namespaces. When it cannot, the build stops with NEEDS_USER_NAMESPACES, exit status 3 like NEEDS_DOCKER_DAEMON, naming what failed (for example kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns=1, a seccomp profile that blocks unshare, or cgroups mounted in hybrid mode). Oyzu never runs the step without the sandbox. {"code":"NEEDS_USER_NAMESPACES","error":"NEEDS_USER_NAMESPACES: the daemonless sandbox (crun) cannot run on this host: cgroups are mounted in hybrid mode, which crun does not support; nothing was run","exitCode":3,"nextStep":"Run on a Linux executor that allows unprivileged user namespaces and has crun, or on one with a Docker daemon.","reason":"NEEDS_USER_NAMESPACES"} crun runs without a cgroup of its own, so the executor pool's limits bound the step rather than per-step memory and CPU limits. Each action in the build manifest records how it was sandboxed in sandbox: backend (docker or crun), the crun runtime version, and resourceLimits (cgroup or pool).

A build can be split into jobs queued along the target graph, each reusing the results its predecessors built. Each job runs a slice: a build of the named targets in which every other target the build needs may only be reused, never built. The pinned worker's private admitted preparation and execution operations use the same executor preflight as ordinary builds: no-Docker refusal, resolved build.isolation selection, then the required sandbox probe before native preparation. They honor the existing OYZU_NO_DOCKER control. A read-only public preview still performs no executor preparation. Private assigned execution emits its completed manifest even when the build fails, then returns the ordinary failure status: 1 for failed/interrupted work, 4 for unavailable upstream reuse or 5 for failed handoff publication. A failed manifest cannot appear to the worker as successful execution. Native admission still requires exact selected records; mismatch diagnostics name the record and changed field names without printing command/environment values. oyzu build --slice --handoff oci://registry.oyzu.dev/acme/web/ci web Input Meaning Target arguments One or several logical target names or concrete preview targets[].id values. A logical name uses the same variant selection as a whole isolated build: runtime variants remain selected, while declared platforms use the normal host filter unless --all-platforms is given. A concrete ID builds exactly that variant, including a non-host platform. Upstream dependencies remain reuse-only unless explicitly named too. --slice-plan <target-id> Requires --slice; repeat once per concrete ID in the original preview, including folded upstreams and unrelated jobs. This is the client contract for inPlan; pass the complete original set unchanged to every slice and retry. Without it, inPlan uses this invocation's selection before preparation and cannot detect growth since an earlier preview. --slice Build only the named targets (at least one is required). Every action of any other target the selection needs (the named targets' depends_on, materialize and task prerequisites, transitively) is looked up in the local cache and the remote tiers; one that is missing fails with UPSTREAM_NOT_CACHED instead of running. A slice runs the captured (isolated) path, as pool jobs do. With --plan it prints the isolated preview of that selection, with the same needsDaemon and isolation as --remote --plan. With --no-docker (or OYZU_NO_DOCKER=1) it is judged as an isolated build: a Node target runs in the daemonless sandbox, and any other target stops it with NEEDS_DOCKER_DAEMON (exit 3) before anything runs, so a pool without Docker requeues it rather than failing it. It cannot be combined with --remote, --affected, --check, --no-cache or --verify-contract, and it needs an active action cache when any selected upstream is unnamed. With cache.local = false, naming the entire selection permits a folded slice to run without reuse or handoff writes; an unexpectedly unavailable cache still fails admission. --handoff <oci-url> Requires --slice. The OCI repository (oci://host/path, the same form as cache.remote) read first for upstream results, before cache.ciRemote and cache.remote, and written with every result this slice produces whatever cache.read and cache.write say. The registry decides whether the job may write there, with the credential an ordinary remote uses (OYZU_CACHE_TOKEN or the job's ID token). A URL this client cannot use is refused (exit 2) before anything runs. None of these inputs changes a key: a slice derives every upstream key exactly as a whole build does, from the outputs it restores, so per-target slices of a commit produce the same action keys and artifact digests as one whole build. A producer that built something else than this checkout expects therefore shows up as a miss, never as a wrong reuse. The entries are the frozen OEP-0011 entries every remote tier holds; a handoff hit is verified and materialized like any remote hit. Reason codes, each with its own exit status so an executor can act without parsing text: Reason Exit Raised when UPSTREAM_NOT_CACHED 4 An action of a target the slice does not build was not restored from any cache. It is recorded as failed, everything that needs its output is blocked, and nothing of it runs. HANDOFF_PUSH_FAILED 5 A result of a named target could not be written to the handoff repository (refused, unavailable, or the repository was switched off after an earlier failure). The build is failed even when every action succeeded, because the jobs after it would miss. Exit status 1 stays a failed build and 2 a refused invocation; 3 is NEEDS_DOCKER_DAEMON or NEEDS_USER_NAMESPACES. When both happen, UPSTREAM_NOT_CACHED wins. A failed slice prints one JSON line last on stderr, in human and --json mode alike, so an executor that forwards only the tail of the output can act without --json. It has the shape of NEEDS_DOCKER_DAEMON's error plus the failure's fields (below): {"action":"app:package","error":"UPSTREAM_NOT_CACHED: app:package of upstream target app (key sha256:…) is not in the local cache or oci://registry.oyzu.dev/acme/web/ci; a slice reuses upstream targets and never builds them","exitCode":4,"inPlan":true,"key":"sha256:…","reason":"UPSTREAM_NOT_CACHED","repositories":[{"location":"oci://registry.oyzu.dev/acme/web/ci","status":"active"}],"target":"app","why":null} The build record (dist/manifest.json, printed by --json) carries an oyzu.dev/slice extension: Field Meaning targets The concrete targets this slice built (requested targets and their variants). upstream The other targets it reused. handoff The --handoff location, or null. written One entry per result of a built target that is in the handoff repository: target, action, key and outcome (pushed, converged when an identical entry was already there, conflicts when a different one held the key and was kept). The runs service keeps these on the job, so a later miss can tell a producer that wrote a different key from one that wrote none. misses Every upstream action that was not restored: target, action, key, repositories (each remote asked, with status active or unavailable and why), inPlan, and why when the action was never looked up (for example an authored task without declared outputs, which is never cached). notWritten Every result of a built target that did not reach the handoff repository: target, action, key, repository and status (the registry's answer). failure null, or the first miss (reason: UPSTREAM_NOT_CACHED, exitCode: 4) or else the first unwritten result (reason: HANDOFF_PUSH_FAILED, exitCode: 5), with that entry's fields. inPlan tests membership in the original set passed with --slice-plan. false means a missing producer was absent from that preview, including a dependency added between preview and execution. That is an explicit plan mismatch; it does not authorize a whole-build replay or repetition of effects that may have occurred. true means an expected producer did not leave a reusable result. Both exit 4; neither permits the slice to execute an unnamed producer. The action cache's summary gains a handoff section beside ciRemote and remote, with the same fields. A result restored from the handoff repository is not a CI result: a later CI build that finds it in its local store looks it up again, as it does for a development remote's. An upstream marked sliceable: false must be named alongside its consumer, for example oyzu build --slice --handoff oci://localhost:5000/demo/ci generate web. If several consumers require its live state or its effects are not known safe to repeat, keep the coupled work in one engine invocation. Transferability and repeatability are separate facts; cache ineligibility does not authorize one execution per consumer. An unnamed unreusable upstream still fails with UPSTREAM_NOT_CACHED and its why. Every upstream target is prepared (its dependencies acquired) because its keys include the prepared dependency identity. Verified with the slice-handoff build scenario against zot on Linux (OYZU_ZOT_BINARY=<zot> python tooling/test-build-scenarios.py --cli <oyzu> --suite node --only slice-handoff): per-target slices of a two-target project match one whole build key for key and digest for digest with no upstream action run, a deleted upstream entry exits 4, and refused handoff writes exit 5; see implementation status. The expanded scenario adds concrete matrix IDs, folded hooks and graph growth. --suite rust --only slice-corpus adds the pinned serde and regex workspaces, three declared crate targets each, checking every action key and cached output tree digest plus artifact digests from fresh local stores. A slice hands its results off and so builds the optimized profile; slices and the reference whole build are compared at the same profile, so the reference runs with --optimized. These additions await execution with Docker; the earlier two-target proof does not qualify them. Invalid configuration, unknown targets and statically invalid relationships fail normally. Configuration is opened offline to preserve the no-network contract; managed configuration that cannot resolve offline fails closed rather than bypassing policy. Correct the reported configuration or run a normal build to perform the preparation needed to resolve remaining details. Native macOS runtime qualification remains pending.
