documents.t: Successful binaries are collected in dist/<target>/<platform>/ (the host platform, such as dist/cli/windows/x86_64/; see the bundle layout) with their normal native names, then exposed at .oyzu/bin/<name>[.exe]. Outputs labels each one with the profile it was built with, development or, for an optimized build, optimized; each binary is statically verified as an executable for the host before it is collected (executable verification). The shared bundle store retains manifest, plan, envelope, reports and action logs. These disclose host execution, observed source and unverified tool identity; they do not confer production eligibility or assert enforced isolation. Rust state lives under .oyzu/native/rust/<compiler-host>/: target holds native compilation state and tests holds separate instrumented/test state. Cargo owns native invalidation. Prepared package bytes remain in the already provisioned native package cache; this slice does not implement an acquisition proxy, import unmanaged caches as trusted evidence or add a shared artifact cache.

After tool admission, the Rust builder tries locked offline Cargo metadata. If the cache is sufficient, it proceeds without fetching. Otherwise an online build runs cargo fetch --locked through the host executor with live, labeled preflight output, then resolves metadata offline again. Cargo owns registry/Git downloads, checksums and its cache; Oyzu does not rewrite Cargo.lock. Compilation remains offline. oyzu build --offline never takes the fetch path and reports missing inputs with guidance to run an online build or correct the manifest/lock. This is the standalone native path: Cargo uses its configured repositories, credentials and network settings. It is not a broker-controlled acquisition or network isolation guarantee. Managed host tool admission remains unavailable; this does not enable it or change captured-build acquisition. Native preparation failures retain a safe category and recovery guidance even when credential-bearing native details are withheld. Warm-cache qualification alone does not prove cold repository self-building; see the recorded qualification results. Previous claimed artifacts move to bundle history on either successful or failed native builds; unrelated dist files stay protected. See bundle finalization and recovery. Failure returns a nonzero exit and leaves .oyzu/bin at the last successful generation. Treat it as stale relative to the failed attempt. Promotion renames the previous image before replacing the stable name, avoiding direct overwrite of a running Windows image. An image that cannot yet be deleted may remain as a hidden previous generation; repeated Windows self-rebuilds still require proof.

Build the initial executable with cargo build --locked --release --bins, then copy target/release/oyzu[.exe] and target/release/oyzu-shim[.exe] together to a dedicated user PATH directory outside the checkout, preserving any existing installation. This independent fallback must not point back into the compiler output or .oyzu/bin. Check the build exit status before copying, verify the copied binary, and retain a rollback copy. Release builds avoid installing the much larger development/debug executable; the initial release build can be substantially slower than an incremental local build. On Windows, saving a directory in the user PATH does not update an already-open terminal or its parent application. Update the current PowerShell session explicitly, substituting your fallback installation directory: $fallbackBin = 'C:\path\to\oyzu-bootstrap\bin' $env:Path = "$fallbackBin;$env:Path" oyzu --version New terminals inherit PATH from their parent process, so opening another tab in an already-running terminal application may still inherit the older value. The repository configuration contains: [env] _.path = ["./.oyzu/bin"] Activate the shell through the fallback as described in project environments. For PowerShell 7.5+, use oyzu activate pwsh | Out-String | Invoke-Expression. Run oyzu build, then _oyzu_hook if an explicit refresh is needed. Get-Command oyzu -CommandType Application (PowerShell), type -P oyzu (Bash), or whence -p oyzu (Zsh) should resolve to the project output. Ordinary oyzu invocations use the activation wrapper, which dispatches to that application; an unqualified command lookup can show the wrapper function instead of its destination. Leaving the project restores the baseline PATH. Merely writing TOML does not activate an existing terminal. Oyzu's repository configures +crt-static for x86_64-pc-windows-gnullvm in .cargo/config.toml. This links the compiler's unwind runtime into the Oyzu executables so workers can start without LLVM-MinGW's libunwind.dll on PATH. It does not install an OS component or relax the worker's explicit environment. Other targets retain their native defaults. Compiler flags supplied explicitly through Cargo's environment can override this repository configuration; preserve the static-runtime setting when building this target.

Fresh-store installation and a small native Rust build --full have passed on Windows GNU/LLVM, including automatic helper installation, JUnit and coverage collection, formatting and linting, followed by offline reuse. Use oyzu build --store <path> to select the same store as oyzu install --store <path>. The default remains the shared user store. Relative overrides resolve against the invocation directory (or global --root), before workspace-root discovery. The selected store is used for native installation and verification and captured-build tool preparation; it never changes pins, tool identities, checks or image policy. A missing or invalid installation in that store does not fall back to another store. --offline requires its cached inputs; use the same override on install, build and tool-inspection commands. Repository test fixtures explicitly select their intended profile, and doctest compilation no longer has a private two-minute timeout. Git and Windows PowerShell must be available for the repository's own tests. See commands, measurements and qualification limits. Native execution inherits host capabilities. Cargo's offline mode is not network denial for arbitrary build scripts. New process/network isolation and approved broker routes remain future work. An installed fallback, local successful build or local isolation flag cannot grant production publication authority. Current implementation verification and missing end-to-end evidence are recorded in implementation status. The intended host matrix is Windows/macOS/Linux, but no new host is qualified by this document.

Rust discovers an explicit install task; no custom bootstrap task is needed. See Rust executable installation. With the required tool environment available, run from this checkout: oyzu run install -- --bins --force --root "$env:LOCALAPPDATA/Oyzu/bootstrap" The destination is machine-local, not committed task configuration. Windows self-installation stages the Cargo result before replacing the running bootstrap. This invokes Cargo installation, not the full Oyzu build quality gates. Cargo uses release compilation by default; add --debug after -- for a development installation. These profiles use different compiler caches. Run oyzu install first to materialize the pinned native toolchain and its verified installation receipt. An outdated bootstrap can initially be replaced by invoking Cargo directly with the provisioned toolchain: cargo install --path . --bins --locked --force --root "$env:LOCALAPPDATA/Oyzu/bootstrap" oyzu run fetch prepares Cargo dependencies; oyzu run install installs project executables; oyzu install provisions development tools. They remain distinct.
documents.s: Updating this repository's bootstrap with Cargo

documents.t: The Windows task flow uses a pinned MSVC installation, which needs Visual Studio Build Tools (C++ workload, no IDE) installed first: oyzu pin, oyzu install, then oyzu run install. A checkout whose oyzu.lock was installed with the earlier GNU/LLVM default holds a stale Rust-only installation record that conflicts with the new selection (TOOL_LOCK_AMBIGUOUS); delete that oyzu.lock and rerun oyzu pin and oyzu install. Ordinary tool installation does not provision Docker or a Linux worker. Keep machine-specific linker/CMake paths and Cargo cache locations in ignored oyzu.local.toml, using [env] and _.path. Cargo's CARGO_INSTALL_ROOT selects the bootstrap prefix (the binary goes under its bin directory); this setting also applies to oyzu run install. The selected verified Cargo/compiler remain owned by Oyzu, while LLVM/MinGW, CMake and dependency-specific native prerequisites are provisioned separately. Do not commit one developer's absolute machine paths. See native Rust task execution. The Oyzu executable explicitly links its existing unwinder statically on Windows GNU/LLVM. Rust 1.95 otherwise emits a libunwind.dll import, causing startup to fail before CLI code runs when LLVM is absent from PATH. See the upstream Rust explanation. This binary-only link declaration does not change downstream project profiles or install a compiler runtime globally. The local bootstrap retains the provisioned LLVM license next to its installation; packaging remains subject to the existing third-party distribution review, not cleared by this development proof. On Windows, the inferred Oyzu Cargo install task stages installation under the explicit destination root (CARGO_INSTALL_ROOT or forwarded --root). Cargo compiles and installs into staging while the existing bootstrap remains callable. Only after Cargo succeeds does execution publish binaries with Windows file replacement, retaining one .NAME.previous backup per replaced file. Cargo's installation bookkeeping is staged and published too. Cancelling compilation or a native install failure leaves the installed bootstrap unchanged. A forcibly terminated process may leave its private .oyzu-install-* staging directory; do not remove one belonging to an active installation. Publication is per file, not an atomic transaction across the CLI, shim and Cargo metadata. On a publication error, inspect the named file and adjacent backup; close processes still holding an older backup before retrying. Concurrent Oyzu installs to this root serialize; a simultaneous direct Cargo install is outside that coordination. Other packages and non-Windows installs retain native Cargo behavior. Without an explicit root, Oyzu leaves Cargo's destination selection alone and does not move the running executable out of the way. Native builds acquire the same verified configured tool environments as tasks before invoking builder metadata. Leases are retained and reused by all stages with the same frozen target configuration. No tool verification gate is bypassed. Repeated successful native builds replace artifacts recorded by the prior bundle at the newly collected artifact paths. Test-only runs continue preserving those files without claiming them as new build artifacts. Unclaimed native files still cause a collision rather than being overwritten; prior bundles remain in history. Build output starts with Building <directory name> (or Planning for --plan), followed by host platform or the requested matrix, local/isolated execution, and the requested fast/full mode. Relative . paths resolve to the actual directory name. This initial summary does not override configuration or policy; preflight establishes the selected targets and required checks. JSON emits a structured heading event on stderr; quiet mode suppresses it and stdout remains unchanged. Build output follows Preflight → Build → completion summary. Preflight includes configuration, target discovery, pinned tool preparation, native dependency metadata and planning. These internal steps are not competing top-level phases. The default view shows tool, requested version and observed installation status on the same row. Missing tools report acquisition/installation, followed by verification; reused tools report verification before receiving a success mark. The Rust component installer currently reports downloading and installing as a combined step; it does not invent byte percentages. A success mark requires the existing installation verification to finish. Errors stop preflight and remain visible. External SDK/linker prerequisites explicitly remain unchecked until the native tools run; discovering them does not establish availability. Optional formatting, linting, testing and coverage tools are omitted from the fast-build summary unless quality stages are selected. The full declared inventory remains in detailed logs; this presentation does not change pins, installation recipes, enabled stages or enforcement. Additional environment, execution and source context is available with p, rather than repeating it in the default view. Native execution does not imply isolation or verified commit identity. Auto and plain modes use a linear, scrollback-preserving build flow. They do not open an alternate screen or maintain panes. Color is independent of interaction: ui.color=auto colors terminal output unless NO_COLOR is set to a non-empty value; always also colors redirected text and never disables color. A terminal is capable when TERM is not dumb and, on Windows, when the console accepts virtual terminal processing, which the CLI switches on for its own stdout and stderr; a console that refuses gets plain text and no line clears. Active tools and build subprocesses show eight dimmed output lines beneath their headers on capable terminals. Success collapses those lines; failure retains them. Redirected output appends each update. --output interactive retains the old dashboard as an explicit opt-in. JSON remains structured and unstyled; raw child output and retained evidence are unchanged. See build logging. Native builds automatically install missing configured and builder-required tools from existing pins using the shared user store, then verify the selected environment before compiling. Builds never update pinned versions or write a new lock: run oyzu pin for missing or stale resolutions. --offline forbids acquisition and requires the installer's cached inputs. Small terminals retain detailed logs (d) for values outside the visible area. Automatic installation uses the same acquisition, checksum, installation lease and policy checks as oyzu install, consuming the configuration snapshot selected for the build target. Installation errors stop execution before native metadata or compilation. A denied or corrupted selection is not replaced by an unverified PATH tool. This applies to the supported native build path; isolated builds retain their provisioned image contract. Provisioned builds without a portable pin retain their existing behavior. With a portable pin, selected tests include the pinned nextest and cargo-llvm-cov helpers automatically; ordinary fast builds omit them. System linkers and SDKs remain external prerequisites. See helper installation. Native Rust preflight names linker/runtime prerequisites from the selected compiler's reported host (GNU/LLVM, MSVC, MinGW, Apple, or Linux). The actual prepared Cargo environment performs the compile/link probe, including inherited linker configuration and coverage instrumentation when selected. Ready means that probe succeeded using executor-provided facilities; it does not claim that Oyzu installed an OS SDK or independently identified every library's version. Pin's executor table omits tool-version and installation-backend columns because those prerequisites are externally provided and are not probed by pin.

Native host execution records an observed source identity. It validates and hashes source files using the captured-source exclusions, path/type rules and change detection, but does not write an unused temporary source copy. The native compiler still reads the checkout; this does not provide a frozen filesystem or isolation. Captured/container execution still creates its required input copy. Preflight names output-bundle opening, compiler-cache retention, source hashing, CLI identity hashing and report preparation. Each running operation has an explicit completion or failure; report contracts and binding readiness share one completion row. Source and CLI identity completion include measured durations. Slow operations retain named activity updates. See linear logging. The 2026-10-06 provider-identity refresh passed the actual Windows repository bootstrap → pin/install → fast build → local-CLI self-install loop, plus a fresh Linux fixture's install/build/offline/activation flow. See the commands, fixture corrections and limits. Subsequent qualification passed the Windows repository build --full, the Linux repository host build inside Docker, and a deliberate failed-test fixture with retained reports and no published artifacts. See the measured results and cache baseline.
documents.s: Local source evidence and startup progress

documents.t: Rust source refresh and version projection preserve the modification times of final Cargo.toml files and Cargo.lock when their newly reconciled bytes are identical to the previous projection. This keeps Cargo and its build scripts from treating unchanged versions as changed source. Each current file is hashed before its time can be retained; changed bytes keep their fresh time. Expendable digest/time hints live in manifest-projection.json beside the native compiler cache. Missing, damaged or unwritable hints fall back to ordinary Cargo fingerprinting. Source admission, Cargo resolution/version decisions and action keys still run. This also applies with --no-cache, which disables Oyzu action reuse while retaining native compiler caches. Oyzu's own build script watches existing Git metadata and the current loose ref or its existing parent. An absent optional path such as packed-refs no longer forces a build-script run on every invocation; unborn and packed branches still refresh the compiled identity when commits change. Native Rust oyzu build retains at most cache.nativeMaxMiB MiB across its selected host's declared compiler caches after normal completion. The default is 8192 MiB (8 GiB). Configure it through the ordinary configuration cascade: [cache] nativeMaxMiB = 8192 Eviction runs Cargo's own cargo clean on the declared cache directory. Oyzu first marks that directory with the standard CACHEDIR.TAG, because current Cargo refuses to clean a target directory without one; a cache created before the tag existed would otherwise fail every build once the budget was exceeded. The setting accepts 1–1048576 MiB, supports ordinary policy numeric constraints, and applies identically online and offline. It is separate from remote result cache preferences. Progress reports the measured size and any reclaimed roots; JSON builds keep those diagnostics on stderr and the result on stdout. The build holds the workspace transaction lock while checking the budget before execution and after collecting artifacts and reports. If over budget, execution runs the selected Cargo's clean --offline --target-dir <validated-directory>. Cargo retains ownership of compiler-file cleanup and its own cache locking. Whole roots are evicted in this order until under budget: the obsolete separate doctest target, coverage target, ordinary build target. Under budget, no native cleanup runs. Doctests now reuse the ordinary build target; instrumentation keeps coverage in a separate target. A budget below the working set trades incremental reuse for space and can cause a cold compile on every invocation. This is a retained-size policy, not a peak disk quota: compilation can temporarily exceed it, and a crash or full disk before collection may leave oversized state until the next invocation. End-of-build cleanup failure emits NATIVE_CACHE_RETENTION_FAILED without discarding build evidence or changing its result; the next pre-build check retries, and a failure there stops execution. Root/entry symlinks and Windows reparse points are rejected rather than followed. Use a normal directory or remove the redirection before retrying. No claim is made of protection against a hostile concurrent filesystem writer. Only builder-declared roots under the selected target's .oyzu/native are eligible. Installed tools, downloads, .oyzu/bin, dist, history/recovery, proof files, other platform roots, direct Cargo's project target, and arbitrary oyzu run tasks are outside this policy. No schema changed and no legacy data was relabeled. The regression entry point is python tooling/test-native-cache-budget.py --cli <compiled-oyzu> with this checkout's pinned Rust/check tools and native linker prerequisites. It proves small-budget rebuilds, retained warm state, doctests, report inspection and failed-build preservation through the compiled CLI.

Run oyzu build or oyzu build --plan from a nested project containing its own build.yaml; no --root is required. Source subdirectories select their nearest ancestor declaration. Repository configuration continues to inherit, while the selected build owns its lockfile and outputs. Parent builds do not automatically include nested build inventories. See configuration boundaries for the configuration contract.

A project whose selected profile has a native host build runs on the machine without Docker: Oyzu resolves missing tools, installs them into the shared store, then invokes the ecosystem's own tools. Other profiles use the isolated executor and fail with a message naming that requirement when Docker is unavailable. Profile Host build Unpinned tool selection Rust (Cargo) Yes Automatic (greatest stable release; must satisfy Cargo rust-version; a rust-toolchain.toml channel or explicit pin wins; see Rust installation) Node node/app with npm and a dist/ output Yes Automatic (greatest LTS satisfying every engines.node constraint; greatest matching stable release if no LTS matches; selection) Go go/app: one module, no go.work, exactly one package main Yes Automatic (greatest stable release satisfying the go directive minimum) Python pip with pyproject.toml Yes (wheel) Automatic (greatest stable CPython satisfying requires-python; see Python installation) Java Maven reactor (readable jar names; a committed mvnw is run) Yes (jars; tests run in verify) Automatic (JDK from the declared level, Maven 3.9 unless a wrapper supplies it; see Java installation) Java Gradle build (a committed gradlew is run; jars from Gradle's model; tests run in build) Yes Automatic (JDK from the declared level, Gradle 8 or 9) Go libraries, workspaces, several binaries; Ant and other Java; uv/Poetry/requirements-only Python; other Node profiles No: isolated executor Not applicable Package tools that a builder detects (for example protoc for a Rust project whose Cargo.lock has prost-build) follow the same rule without a pin: the version is the folder pin, else the detection's version hint, else the latest stable catalog release; preflight locks it with the other requirements and installs it, and oyzu pin records the same selection. A tool with no catalog entry, no usable checksum, or that cannot be resolved or installed is left as an attention row and the build continues (tools.ignore silences it); only a tool you pinned in oyzu.toml fails the build when it cannot be verified or installed. Verified on Windows: a Rust project whose Cargo.lock lists prost-build resolved protoc 36.2, locked it for every platform and installed it on the first oyzu build; the second showed it already installed. oyzu pin is optional for Rust, Go and Node. With no oyzu.lock, preflight resolves the requirement, writes oyzu.lock and installs from it; commit that file to make later builds reproducible, or delete it to re-resolve. An explicit [tools] go = "1.24" takes precedence. The Go build runs go build -trimpath -buildvcs=false -o <private output> with GOTOOLCHAIN=local, so only the locked toolchain compiles and none is downloaded mid-build, and GOPROXY=off under --offline. Compiler diagnostics are shown with their file and line, the exit status is preserved and no previous binary is republished. The artifact is the executable <target>-<version>; --full adds go test -json with coverage, go vet and gofmt -l. Dependencies use Go's module cache in the user's Go environment (not isolated per project). Evidence: fresh-checkout qualification.

The host coordinator selects declared targets and their dependency closure, prepares verified configured tools, asks each builder for its native build contract, and executes one shared task graph into one evidence bundle. Before preparation, host execution and --plan share logical selection, prerequisite/hook expansion and cycle validation. The executable host plan retains those dependency edges; the shared scheduler runs independent targets concurrently up to the resolved build.jobs ceiling. Build YAML depends_on gates consumers on the producer's selected stages. A failed dependency blocks its consumers while unrelated targets may finish. Stages within one target remain ordered to protect their shared native workspace. It does not claim process/network isolation or production eligibility. Explicit --isolated retains the isolated path and its existing tool-identity admission limits. Native and captured builds use the same executable-action description and shared operation/hook/report composition. Native artifact locations remain machine-local collection bindings to the plan's logical outputs. This changes no executor selection or fast/full default: native build commands retain their own lifecycle, including Maven tests within verify. Internal action boundaries do not imply a separate native invocation for each module or more precise cache inputs. Required reports and successful collection still gate artifacts; private workspaces alone do not establish enforcement. See task composition. Native support includes Cargo, Maven reactors producing jars, single-binary Go applications, explicit npm dist applications, and pip pyproject wheel distributions. Other Node/Python profiles retain the existing isolated path and its admission limits. npm uses npm ci for declared dependencies and requires a lockfile. Installation is the native target's prepare action: it runs before pre_build hooks on a cache miss, and an unchanged whole-target cache hit reuses it with the build. A failed installation blocks hooks/build and publishes no artifacts. --no-cache runs installation again. npm lifecycle scripts and offline behavior stay native; no node_modules directory is retained in the source projection. pip uses its native PEP 517 wheel builder, including build-backend acquisition. Offline adds npm offline/pip no-index behavior and may fail when native prerequisites are unavailable. CPython is provisioned as a managed tool (Python installation); pip is the one bundled with it. pip performs build-backend acquisition during its wheel command; this is visible native preparation output, not a separate Oyzu dependency graph. Host wheels are distribution artifacts, not a bundled runnable Python application. The build performance assessment records the reviewed paths, measured repeated-build timings and remaining preparation costs. Reproduce its bounded npm checks with python tooling/test-build-performance.py --cli <compiled-oyzu>; both modes require the pinned Node and the provisioned npm worker image. Use --mode native for host checks alone. The probe checks reuse, source edits, fresh-output equivalence, native hook ordering and install failure propagation; timings are observations, not portable pass/fail thresholds. First functional proof: run oyzu build from examples/tasks/grouped-targets/project without root overrides, produce the Python wheel and Node dist directory in one dist/manifest.json, then validate the bundle with oyzu inspect dist. Target selection, failure handling and a repeated invocation close the remaining functional checks. Broader native profiles remain separate follow-ups. Native builds now use private target workspaces and explicit artifact transfer. An ordering edge alone does not copy files. Additional shared-source inputs currently require the native host path. Windows verification: the grouped API/web build and oyzu inspect dist succeeded with both artifacts. python tooling/test-native-multi-build.py --cli <compiled-oyzu> verifies real npm multi-target builds, a selected target, repeated publication, missing-fresh-output rejection and a native child failure that blocks dependent tasks. The concurrency proof uses a two-process rendezvous, and the dependency proof checks producer completion before consumer execution. Native executable filename collisions are rejected before build actions. These checks do not qualify full-quality dependency availability for every ecosystem.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/node-applications.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. The experimental node/app builder declares a versioned directory artifact for a recognized Vite build or an explicitly selected application with a custom native build script. No output section or new Oyzu setting is required. This supports standalone package roots, including native Vite 8 configurations and the conventional dist/ contract below; native workspace application outputs and automatic custom-script output inference remain unfinished. Platform matrices can select matching provisioned Node images through toolchain selection; the Docker suite has verified the authored EX-050 graph with amd64 and ARM execution.

For a project whose native script writes dist/, application intent is sufficient: frontend: uses: node/app path: frontend The authored directory example uses "build": "node build.mjs". Oyzu runs the native script through its selected manager, then stages the contents of frontend/dist/ as the primary directory artifact application-<snapshot-version>. A consumer using materialize: [{from: frontend, to: site}] receives site/index.html, without a nested dist directory. This is a documented convention selected by explicit application intent, not static interpretation of arbitrary JavaScript. Custom scripts retain native lifecycle semantics and can use compound commands supported by their manager. The output must be a freshly produced contained directory. Missing output, a file in place of the directory, linked entries or special files fail packaging; previous bundle contents cannot satisfy the new build. Build/test/lint/read-only format gates still apply, and the default quality checks exclude the generated dist. Browser globals are not inferred merely from the application selection. Static content alone does not prove platform independence: the current artifact retains its execution platform, and multi-platform reuse remains unimplemented. The npm builder's own fixed dist collector has a native read contract for that tree and stages its artifact under the engine-owned output mount. On supported hosts it can run confined; a project command, another manager or a different output directory cannot borrow that model. Distributed safe repetition still requires every executed action's admitted facts, rather than inferring it from directory output or a successful cache lookup. Discovery exposes builder_selection: explicit and the dist-application output profile. A recognized framework such as Vite has stronger output evidence and keeps its native adapter and validation. Explicit node/package retains native archive packaging. For compatibility, an automatically inferred Node target with an unknown custom script still uses native package output; add uses: node/app only when the script follows this directory convention. A custom non-dist output requires further native output integration; no new general-purpose output configuration is introduced here. Node workspaces continue to use native workspace package planning rather than this single-root application profile.
documents.s: Custom build scripts and the dist convention

documents.t: A package with a captured vite dependency and "scripts": {"build": "vite build"} uses Vite's native dist output. Ordinary package discovery selects node/app, so a standalone project needs no build.yaml. The authored frontend/image variant demonstrates a grouped consumer: frontend: uses: node/app path: frontend image: uses: docker/image path: image materialize: - from: frontend to: site The image's Dockerfile can use COPY site/ /site/. It receives site/index.html and the generated assets, with no extra dist layer. The consumer uses the producer's recorded artifact identity and matching execution platform. The executor assembles the private BuildKit context from selected source files plus explicit materializations. Directory inputs retain all artifact descendants, including empty directories and names such as dist that source capture normally excludes. It rejects linked inputs, collisions and paths outside the image target; combined inputs are bounded to 100,000 selected entries and 10 GiB of file bytes. Directory copying uses the shared snapshot traversal and verifies that its content identity did not change during the copy. Native source ignore rules do not filter explicit artifact inputs. For a different directory, use the native script vite build --outDir public-site. The currently recognized grammar is exactly vite build with an optional literal --outDir <path>. Paths must be contained, portable and use ASCII letters/digits, slash, underscore, hyphen or dot; parent/dot segments, absolute paths, shell expansion, quoting and compound commands are not interpreted. Vite defines the native default and outDir option; Oyzu does not assume that every Node build script follows that convention. Static discovery records the output profile and configuration-file evidence without executing project code. Unsupported Vite flags still fail captured planning with an explicit diagnostic. Unknown custom scripts follow the intent/convention rules above, and explicit node/package retains a package archive even with a Vite script. These are compatibility limits, not complete application packaging support.

Existing vite.config.js, .ts, .mjs, .mts, .cjs and .cts files use Vite's own loader. For example, the configuration overlay selects web/production from the native mode and emits an extra asset through a Vite plugin. Neither discovery nor dependency acquisition evaluates that configuration. After dependency installation in the private offline workspace, preparation replaces the private package's build script with an Oyzu wrapper. The native manager still invokes its prebuild/build/postbuild lifecycle. The wrapper calls Vite 8's native builder API and observes its resolved configuration and written output. The original checkout is unchanged. A literal --outDir retains native precedence over the configuration's output directory. Package-manager behavior still determines which lifecycle hooks run. The plan names application-<snapshot-version> before execution. Native configuration determines an intermediate output location during execution; after a successful build, packaging copies that directory into the planned artifact. The second artifact, build-metadata, is vite-output-<snapshot-version>.json with media type application/vnd.oyzu.vite-output.v1+json. Its bounded record includes schema version, kind, Vite version, snapshot version, native root, output directory and mode. Both artifacts participate in bundle integrity checks. Consumers that omit an artifact name still select primary. The current adapter requires one finite client environment and directory output. Native root/output must remain within the captured target without linked parents. Library/SSR builds, multiple environments, watch mode and write: false fail explicitly. Bundler output options must agree with the resolved directory; the adapter checks before writing and again when observing written output. Native plugins remain executable project code subject to the sandbox, not trusted release evidence. A failed build does not produce a successful output record. Missing, malformed or version-mismatched metadata fails packaging; correct the native configuration or failed operation and rerun the build. Vite versions outside major 8 require another qualified API adapter.

oyzu run list exposes native build and test scripts, inferred lint/read-only format checks and explicit mutating formatting. oyzu build retains the existing dependency preparation, native build, test, lint and format-check gates before packaging. For recognized Vite projects, fallback ESLint includes browser globals alongside Node globals. The selected native output directory is excluded from implicit quality traversal; supplied native scripts/configurations remain authoritative. After a captured build, implicit quality tasks use its recorded output. Before that record exists, explicit quality execution resolves native configuration in production build mode; this can execute configuration code on the host for development tasks, or inside the sandbox for captured tasks. Listing tasks remains non-executing. See Node quality. Native Node tests produce JUnit and LCOV through the existing reporting adapter. The versioned primary artifact appears beneath dist/<target>/<platform>/application-<snapshot-version> in the build bundle, for the platform the target was built for (see the bundle layout); consult its manifest path rather than constructing this path in consumers. Only the selected native output tree is staged. Source, dependencies and tests are not automatically copied into that artifact. Failed tests or quality checks block artifact publication to the bundle; collected failure reports remain available. The manifest records kind: directory, version, producing action, complete inventory and logical tree digest. Collection and oyzu inspect dist use the shared directory integrity contract. Missing output, links, special file types and oversized staging fail packaging. A failed operation can leave partial unrecorded output; it is not a valid artifact. materialize copies verified content into a fresh consumer context and retains producer evidence references. This does not prove platform independence or production release eligibility.

Oyzu can resolve and install Node and supported npm/pnpm releases through shared tool management. Automatic native build preflight is currently limited to npm node/app targets with the conventional dist-application profile; other application profiles retain the captured path. Development tasks require an existing compatible tool selection, native project dependencies and quality tooling. Installing Node does not install every project's test or quality dependencies. See native local builds for selection, offline behavior and admission limits, and fresh-checkout qualification for measured empty-store results. The authored variant pins Vite 8.3.2 and npm 11.11.0, with Node >=22.12. Captured acceptance uses the provisioned Node 22/npm image, the quality image, Docker metadata tooling and the isolated BuildKit worker described in builder verification. CI provisions those tools explicitly before invoking the already compiled CLI; automatic acquisition covers only the published toolchain images. Dependencies are acquired through the selected native manager's existing broker/capture flow before isolated execution. Build actions replay prepared dependencies offline; this output integration introduces no new download route or credential channel. Native project build scripts remain executable project code and receive the existing sandbox restrictions. Vite SSR/library modes and compound Vite-command recognition, native workspace application output and cross-platform directory reuse need further integration. Windows transfer of Unix executable directory metadata retains the shared directory limitation. python tooling/test-node-conventional-application.py --cli <compiled-oyzu-path> exercises the custom script's actual native build/test/quality tasks and directory staging on the host, including missing/wrong-kind output failures. The captured Node suite also builds the authored frontend target, then a single-platform consumer variant, checks versioned directory and OCI contents, repeatability and missing-output failure. These are separate scopes: host staging does not prove isolated execution, and the single-platform variant does not establish full EX-050 matrix acceptance. See implementation status for revision-specific results. Rust checks cover non-executing discovery, literal output arguments, package/application distinction and configured output declarations. tooling/test-node-application.py --cli <compiled-path> executes native Vite development tasks and staging, including browser lint, native configuration/plugin assets, npm lifecycle hooks, output overrides, quality exclusions and rejected failures. CI runs that probe on Windows, macOS and Linux. The Docker acceptance suite builds the plain and configured variants, verifies actual image bytes against the directory manifest, JUnit/coverage, repeatability, custom outDir, metadata, tampering and failed-producer rejection. The configured native probe uses Vite 8.3.2 with an ESM config; every supported native loader form and package manager still needs equivalent qualification. See implementation status for checks actually completed; test registration alone does not establish acceptance. The original custom script's two-platform execution is covered separately below. The Docker suite additionally runs the original EX-050 two-platform configuration with matching provisioned amd64/ARM Node images. It requires independently executed tests/coverage and quality, two directory snapshots, exact Docker copies, a complete OCI index and repeatability. These checks passed at revision ad6cbf1 in Docker job 110868387899. This does not establish platform-independent directory reuse or complete every authored negative case.

A project that pins Node ([tools] node = "22.12", locked with oyzu install node@22.12) runs on that exact Node in the captured worker, not the image's copy. Preparation reads the Linux (linux/amd64/gnu) archive recorded for the pinned version in oyzu.lock, downloads it through the tool broker unless a copy cached under the user data directory still matches the locked SHA-256, verifies the bytes against the locked digest and restores them read-only at /scratch/nodetool. The directory is added to PATH just before the image's system directories, so the package manager the image provisions (its pinned npm, pnpm or Yarn, found earlier on PATH) keeps running and only the runtime changes; the same environment applies to preparation and every build action. The plan records the archive under oyzu.dev/locked-tool, so a different pin or archive changes the action identity. Without a pin, the Node that build preflight locks using the LTS preference and engine constraints described below is used the same way; an engine range with no matching LTS release can select a newer stable runtime even though the image carries Node 22. A project whose existing oyzu.lock has no Node entry, a matrix.node runtime axis, a managed build or a non-Linux worker uses the image's Node. Combining a pin with a matrix.node runtime axis is refused, because each would select the runtime. Oyzu's own test reporting passes Node 22 flags (--test-coverage-exclude), so a pin older than Node 22 builds but its native test stage fails with bad option. Pin Node 22 or later when tests run. Verified on Windows 11 with Docker Desktop and the npm image (Node 22.23.3, npm 11.11.0): with node = "22.12" locked, preparation observed Node 22.12.0 under npm 11.11.0 and the native test stage ran on it (a test asserting v22.12. passed and one asserting the image's v22.23. failed); with no pin the image's Node was observed; a changed lock digest was refused; the cached archive was reused. Only the npm image was exercised: the pnpm and Yarn images are not provisioned on that machine, so their PATH handling is untested. Only linux/amd64 workers are admitted, and offline builds need the archive already cached. Without a configuration pin, the default request is lts whether or not engines.node is present. It selects the greatest stable release with a non-empty string in Node's index.json lts field that satisfies every engine constraint. If no LTS release satisfies them, it falls back to the greatest stable release satisfying them. For example, with 24.x marked LTS and 26.x Current, >=22 selects 24.x and >=26 falls back to 26.x. The preference follows publisher data without a compiled-in major. node = "latest", node = "26", exact pins and lts/<name> retain their existing selection behavior and must satisfy engines. .nvmrc and .node-version are not read yet. build --plan explains the LTS default and fallback rule in the requirement source; pin previews and locks retain the lts request. A matching lock keeps its exact version, including a stable fallback, without consulting today's LTS metadata; engine constraints still validate offline. A previous default * request does not match the new lts default; preflight must resolve the new request online before an offline build can use it. Standalone indexed resolution uses the same publisher selection, then looks for that exact release in the signed index. Under an organization catalog the signed index currently has no LTS markers: use an approved exact version or named line such as lts/krypton; the moving alias fails with TOOL_LTS_METADATA_UNAVAILABLE without contacting a publisher outside the catalog. All repository Node image definitions (quality, npm, pnpm and Yarn) and the builder-worker image install Debian libatomic1, needed by newer Node binaries. Rebuild provisioned images to pick this up; existing tags and published digest pins do not change when a Dockerfile changes. Node 26 execution and worker-death qualification remain pending for the #289/#290 fix; see the qualification record.

documents.t: A locked npm or pnpm release, selected under [tools] or by an exact packageManager, runs in the captured worker in place of the image's manager, on the same Node the section above selects. It is restored read-only beside Node and recorded under oyzu.dev/locked-manager. See npm and pnpm installation for the paths and limits.

documents.t: See native local builds for the bounded host profiles, prerequisites, artifact differences and multi-target evidence behavior. This is separate from the isolated packaging contracts above.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/project-environments.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Every Oyzu build includes the mise library integration. Build with Rust 1.95 using cargo build --locked --bins; no integration feature flag exists. This page describes the experimental environment implementation, not a production-qualified release. Its scoped lifecycle checks passed on Windows PowerShell and Linux/macOS Bash and Zsh. See implementation status for measured results. The opt-in OCI session prototype adds Unix launch shims for provisioned Helm/BuildKit clients. Activation itself does not contact its agent; the native invocation requests a session using its current context.

An environment-only project needs no tools, lock, install or account. Shell activation and oyzu exec apply its environment after the folder is trusted; explicit project tasks and builds always apply it: [env] APP_MODE = "development" _.path = ["./bin", "./node_modules/.bin"] The array prepends directories in order. To append as well, use this alternative: [env] _.path = { prepend = ["./bin"], append = ["./scripts"] } The reserved env._ table is metadata, never an exported variable. Values and paths are literal: no variable expansion, scripts, dotenv discovery or command substitution. Plain env.PATH assignments are rejected with a migration message. Relative paths belong to the file declaring them, including local/profile files. They do not change when you enter a subdirectory. Missing directories are allowed. Empty entries, NUL, unknown controls and an embedded host PATH separator are errors. Use "." explicitly for the declaring directory. Normal configuration precedence applies. Each winning _.path declaration replaces the entire inherited control; [] clears project additions. Arrays preserve order. Selected tool shims precede project prepends, inherited PATH, then project appends. Existing occurrences are preserved rather than claimed as project-owned insertions. Projects within Git use the repository root unless --root is explicit. Outside Git, the outermost applicable ancestor Oyzu configuration establishes the root. Nested files affect only their subtree. Installed tools live in the shared user store, independently of the project owning the configuration and lock. Activation can select an explicit store with --store; relative store paths resolve against the invocation directory. Use the same store for installation and activation. Relative parent components such as ../tools are normalized lexically on every host before the store's existing no-follow filesystem checks; normalization does not create directories or relax symlink/reparse-point validation. Development tasks can select that store with oyzu run <task> --store <path>. The path follows the same invocation-directory resolution as build and install, and applies to the whole task sequence, including hooks and prerequisites. Tasks verify installed selections; this option does not install missing tools or fall back to another store. Preparation failures retain their original error and causes; shared stderr diagnostics give recovery guidance without replacing the error code. oyzu run list --store <path> remains discovery-only and does not open or create the store. Place task arguments after --; a --store after that separator is forwarded to the task instead.

In PowerShell 7.5+: oyzu activate pwsh | Out-String | Invoke-Expression Set-Location ./project-a Set-Location ../project-b oyzu deactivate In Bash or Zsh: eval "$(oyzu activate bash)" # substitute zsh for Zsh cd ./project-a cd ../project-b oyzu deactivate Activation can start outside any project. Directory hooks apply before the next command; configuration edits refresh at the next hook. Call _oyzu_hook to refresh explicitly in an activated shell. Hooks never install tools, run tasks or access the network. Tools declared in [tools] must already have a usable frozen selection. Profile installation is explicit: oyzu shell install SHELL --profile-path PATH. Removing that profile block changes future loads; deactivate the current session separately. See the profile instructions. Each activated terminal owns its state. A nested shell can call activate to obtain its own record and change projects without modifying its parent's record. Deactivation restores its inherited baseline. No shared global tool selection is changed.

Switching first reverses the prior project delta. A scalar restores only when it still equals Oyzu's applied value; user edits and deletions are preserved. A new project's explicit assignment temporarily overrides that edited baseline, which is restored afterward. Empty strings and absent variables remain distinct. Explicit removals use the existing configuration control: [overrides] remove = ["env.APP_MODE"] The variable is unset for that project and restored on unload if the user has not changed it. PATH restoration preserves unrelated additions and removes owned unique entries even after reordering. Ambiguous duplicate edits are retained with a diagnostic. Invalid configuration or unavailable required selection unloads the previous project's changes and reports OYZU_TOOL_STATUS=unavailable. Fix the configuration or explicitly install/update tools; the next hook retries. No failing project is partially applied. A usable environment reports ready. Managed environments and development secret references remain unsupported in this milestone and fail explicitly. Hooks do not authenticate, refresh credentials or fall back around authorization. Applying project/local literal values through activation, hooks, shims or exec requires folder trust, because shells, loaders and interpreters can execute the contents of environment variables.

Review the checkout's environment settings, then run oyzu trust [path]. With no path, this trusts the current project's root. oyzu trust --revoke [path] removes the record; oyzu trust --list lists records. Every form supports --json and human output. Trust is keyed by the canonical root folder, including resolution of symbolic links, and survives edits to oyzu.toml. It never writes into the checkout or contacts a service. Records live under trusted-projects in the native user state directory. Untrusted folders never prompt or block tool selection: activation still exposes the tools but skips project/local [env], env._.path, and their removals. User/global environment values remain effective. Prompt hooks, shims, exec and one-shot env --shell use the same rule. A short stderr hint names oyzu trust once per invocation, or once per activated shell session. run, build, build planning and the build configuration digest always include project/local env and PATH settings under normal configuration precedence, regardless of folder trust. These commands explicitly execute or plan the repo's declared code and must agree with CI. config inspection also retains the configured environment. User/global or administrative configuration can set [trust] enabled = false to disable the check, or parents = ["/absolute/projects"] to trust projects beneath selected canonical parent folders (for example E:\\CodexData\\projects on Windows). The default is enabled with no trusted parents. Project/local files cannot set these controls. OYZU_PROJECT_TRUST=false disables the check for an invocation; true enables it and overrides ordinary files. CI context is automatically trusted, including a true CI marker; platform executors run in that CI context. Local coding agents receive no exemption. Revocation removes only the explicit record: a parent rule, disabled check or CI exemption can still trust the folder. This changes earlier literal-environment behavior. Trust existing checkouts once, or configure their parent directory in user scope. Dedicated regression coverage tests scope rejection and the compiled CLI trust lifecycle; Windows native state and real shell qualification still require running the checks on that host.

oyzu env displays configuration sources, effective variable names and selected executables in separate tables. Names such as CARGO_HOME and cargo-llvm-cov are preserved literally. Configuration sources include env._.path, which is PATH metadata rather than a separate exported variable, and identify the winning source and profile from the resolved cascade (including oyzu.local.toml). Ordinary values are visible in human and JSON inspection. Credential-like names (including token, secret, password, API key, authentication and private-key names) and values rejected by the shared diagnostic sanitizer remain redacted. This is heuristic protection, not secret discovery: do not put secrets in innocuously named literal variables. Configuration/log inspection retains its separate, conservative redaction contract. Human output lists PATH entries in search order and removes Windows extended-path prefixes from displayed source paths. Tool-provided variables and inherited PATH also contribute to the composed environment. Inspection does not modify the calling shell. In an untrusted folder, oyzu env still shows configured values and provenance, with project entries marked skipped until trusted for activation, hooks, shims and exec. The displayed PATH describes the configured composition, including those entries; it is not a claim that activation has applied it. oyzu env --json lists inspected environment values and selected commands, with configuration provenance in the configuration array. projectEnvironmentSkipped reports whether shell/exec use withholds project environment, and affected configuration rows carry the same skipped until trusted status as human output. To apply directory changes in an existing PowerShell session, run oyzu activate pwsh | Out-String | Invoke-Expression. Then where.exe oyzu includes the project-local executable before the bootstrap if env._.path contains its directory. Leaving the project restores the prior PATH. For future shells, use the explicit shell profile installation. On Windows, directories Oyzu adds to PATH use ordinary drive or UNC notation, not the \\?\ prefixes used by internal filesystem canonicalization. Inherited PATH entries retain their original spelling for restoration. Windows PowerShell 5.1 can apply the initial activation, but the upstream directory-change hook requires PowerShell 7 or newer; use a supported PowerShell version for automatic switching (including the empty-variable requirement noted below). oyzu exec -- /absolute/path/to/program applies the trust-filtered environment, including unsets, to a child without changing the caller. Bare commands retain the existing declared-tool requirement. oyzu env --shell SHELL emits one-shot changes without installing lifecycle hooks; use activate for automatic rollback. PATH metadata does not become a task environment variable or a hermetic build input. The existing build/task contracts still own their explicit execution environments.

The repository's .oyzu/bin PATH declaration supports the in-development native CLI bootstrap workflow. Environment activation alone does not prove successful native compilation or repeated self-replacement. The activation wrapper dispatches ordinary CLI commands to the first oyzu application on the active PATH, falling back to the activating executable when none is found. Environment hooks and shell lifecycle commands retain the activating executable. This permits a successful local build to take over ordinary commands without reinstalling activation. The PowerShell lifecycle fixture verified this dispatch on Windows with the compiled limited-debug CLI on 2026-10-03. Native self-build and promotion remain separately unverified. Run python tooling/test-project-environments.py --cli PATH --shell pwsh or select bash/zsh. The fixture exercises real shell entry/switch/leave, nested scopes, unset/restore, config refresh, failure cleanup and child-session independence. It provisions no tools and checks that no project lock or tool store was created. The native CI workflow also compares ordinary and no-default-features command help. The intended shell matrix is Bash on Linux/macOS, Zsh on Linux/macOS and PowerShell 7.5+ where available. PowerShell 7.5 introduced support for preserving empty environment values; earlier versions cannot satisfy this environment contract (Microsoft documentation). Evidence is recorded separately; a test definition is not proof that every host passed. Additional shells, managed/secret integration, general shim expansion, active-installation retention, crash recovery, stress testing and performance tuning remain outside this environment milestone.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/publish.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Status: experimental OCI and GitHub Releases publication. The standalone path distributes selected finalized files without a platform account, requires preexisting signed provenance, signs publication intent, and retrieves the registry objects to verify their bytes. Native npm, Python, OCI image archives and mutable OCI tag publication remain outside this slice. Authored code and tests are not a deployed-provider qualification; measured evidence belongs in implementation status.

Run oyzu publish --manifest dist/manifest.json --destination sandbox, or omit --destination to use publish.default. Repeat the option for several named destinations or select a configured set. All selected destinations are required. The complete selection and evidence are checked and all publication signatures are verified before the first distribution. A later destination failure leaves earlier successful publications intact and reports unfinished destinations. Configure through the ordinary configuration cascade: [publish] default = "sandbox" [publish.destinations.sandbox] kind = "oci" # Optional when the build bundle has exactly one artifact: artifacts = ["app/archive"] registry = "https://registry.example.com" repository = "team/artifacts" usernameEnv = "REGISTRY_USERNAME" passwordEnv = "REGISTRY_PASSWORD" [publish.sets] release = ["sandbox"] [publish.requirements.provenance] bundlePath = "evidence/build.sigstore.json" publicKey = "<base64 raw 32-byte Ed25519 public key>" builderId = "https://ci.example.com/builders/release" [publish.requirements.signing] keyEnv = "PUBLICATION_SIGNING_SEED" publicKey = "<base64 raw 32-byte Ed25519 publication public key>" This is an illustrative configuration: supply your own accepted public roots, preexisting signed evidence and independently provisioned credentials. Secret values never belong in the TOML. PUBLICATION_SIGNING_SEED contains a base64 32-byte Ed25519 seed. Its derived public key must match the configured public key. Registry username/password references are optional and must appear together. The same-origin registry bearer challenge flow is supported. HTTPS is required, with plain HTTP permitted only on loopback for local proof registries. kind is optional and defaults to oci. Explicit kind = "oci" uses the same publication path and normalized request as an existing destination that omits it; existing configurations need no migration. GitHub Releases uses the native adapter described below. npm, pypi and unknown kinds fail configuration validation with CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE before evidence loading, credentials or network access. Remove the unsupported kind only when the destination is actually an OCI registry; omitting it does not enable a native package protocol. Unknown destination fields also remain errors. publish.destinations, publish.sets and publish.requirements each resolve as one atomic value: a later cascade source replaces that entire map/object. They do not merge nested entries. Profiles and existing mandatory configuration constraints apply. An evidence path is relative to the source declaring the effective requirements. Artifact paths are relative to the build manifest's bundle. Each destination may select distinct exact build output IDs with artifacts. The ID is the target for its primary output, otherwise target/name; it is not the file's basename or the manifest's internal artifact id. For example, artifacts = ["app/archive"] selects target app, output archive, while artifacts = ["app"] selects that target's primary output. Omission is valid only when the manifest contains one artifact. Empty or duplicate selectors fail configuration validation with CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE. Unknown or ambiguous output IDs or omitted selection in a multi-artifact bundle fail with PUBLISH_ARTIFACT_SELECTION_INVALID before evidence loading, signing or upload. Correct the exact IDs in each selected destination. Explicit entries support several files and different files per destination, without implicit Cartesian fan-out. A selector may name one platform: output-id@os/arch, such as cli/bin-oyzu@linux/x86_64. The platform is the one the builder recorded for the file (its oyzu.dev/artifact-compatibility fact), written in the canonical spelling x86_64/arm64; amd64 and aarch64 are accepted and normalized. An unqualified selector such as cli/bin-oyzu selects every platform of that output in the bundle, each as a separate file with its own evidence, so a single-platform bundle keeps working unchanged. A qualified selector whose platform the bundle lacks fails with PUBLISH_ARTIFACT_SELECTION_INVALID and lists the platforms present; so does a qualified selector for an output without a recorded platform, and two artifacts of one output and platform (another variant axis), since variant selection is unsupported. Listing an output both unqualified and qualified, or the same platform twice, fails configuration validation with CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE. A bundle holds several platforms of one output only when its manifest lists them; today oyzu build writes one platform per bundle, and the release workflow publishes each platform's bundle to the same release. The manifest must record a succeeded build. The selected artifact must be a finalized regular file; its bytes and size must match its SHA-256 identity. Other outputs retain manifest validation but their files are not read or distributed. Publication never builds, scans, repackages, executes project hooks, or creates missing historical evidence. The evidence profile is a Sigstore v0.3 bundle carrying one DSSE application/vnd.in-toto+json envelope, an in-toto Statement v1 and SLSA build provenance v1, verified against an independently configured Ed25519 public root and exact accepted builder identity. This self-managed-key profile makes no transparency-log, trusted-time, keyless identity or SLSA-level claim. For a build with different provenance per output, replace the single [publish.requirements.provenance] fields with an exact output-ID map: [publish.requirements.provenance.byArtifact."app/archive"] bundlePath = "evidence/app.sigstore.json" publicKey = "<accepted base64 raw Ed25519 builder public key>" builderId = "https://ci.example.com/builders/package" [publish.requirements.provenance.byArtifact."cli"] bundlePath = "evidence/cli.sigstore.json" publicKey = "<accepted base64 raw Ed25519 builder public key>" builderId = "https://ci.example.com/builders/cli" These illustrative entries use the same output IDs as destination artifacts; only the selected output's profile is used. Its bundlePath stays relative to the source declaring the effective requirements, and its exact subject, public key and builder are verified before signing or distribution. Unselected bundle files are not read. The existing single form remains supported; it still must cover the selected file. Combining that form with byArtifact, using an empty map/ID, or supplying malformed profile fields fails with CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE. A missing selected entry fails with PUBLISH_EVIDENCE_MISSING; add its exact profile rather than substituting another output's evidence. Mapping several profiles requires exact-subject evidence for each selected file. Signing settings are unchanged. byArtifact keys use the selector grammar above. Provenance is one bundle per file, so an output selected on several platforms needs one bundle per platform: either a qualified key per platform ("cli@linux/arm64"), or one unqualified key whose bundlePath contains the {artifact.platform} placeholder. The placeholder renders as the canonical platform, which is also a relative path: [publish.requirements.provenance.byArtifact."cli"] bundlePath = "evidence/{artifact.platform}/cli.sigstore.json" # evidence/linux/x86_64/cli.sigstore.json publicKey = "<accepted base64 raw Ed25519 builder public key>" builderId = "https://ci.example.com/builders/cli" {artifact.platform} is the only placeholder; any other { or } in bundlePath fails configuration validation. An unqualified key without the placeholder that would cover several selected platforms, or a placeholder on an output without a recorded platform, fails with CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE before evidence loading. Qualified and unqualified keys for the same output together fail configuration validation. A missing bundle for one platform fails the whole plan with PUBLISH_EVIDENCE_MISSING naming the qualified key; nothing is published. Standalone publication rejects --no-upload and the governed --provenance and --policy-evidence options before configuration or network access. It takes existing evidence only from the resolved publish.requirements.provenance.bundlePath setting. The separately signed publication intent binds the exact artifact identity, media type, native coordinate, provenance digest, canonical plan digest, evidence placement and effect targets to the operation publish. It cannot assert a historical build origin or completed upload. Its deterministic contents exclude the invocation identifier, allowing identical republishing to reuse the native OCI coordinate. The signature is verified before distribution. The OCI artifact contains the unchanged file plus the preexisting provenance bundle and publication-intent bundle as retrievable layers. The coordinate is registry/repository@sha256:<manifest-digest>. Tags are unsupported: a mutable tag's preflight read cannot prevent a concurrent writer from replacing it. Matching existing content is already-present; a wrong digest header, manifest, layer or declared artifact identity is a conflict. Success requires independent native GETs of the manifest, config and all layers with digest/size checks. Upload acknowledgements and HEAD responses alone never establish success. Human output identifies the operation, selected artifact output ID, each destination outcome, exact reference and retrieved artifact digest. --json returns a v1alpha1 receipt with operationId, status, planDigest, artifacts and destinations. Each destination has kind and entries with artifact ID, coordinate, reference, payload/native-asset outcomes and evidence storage/verification. Artifact id is the exact selection key: output-id@os/arch for a file with a recorded platform (cli/bin-oyzu@linux/x86_64), the output ID otherwise. Such an artifact also carries compatibility (kind target, native or independent, and the canonical platform), which the signed intent binds. When other outputs exist, unselectedArtifacts lists their keys in sorted order. Human output lists them as unselected and not published. Each destination distinguishes published, already-present, failed and unfinished, and records the manifest/artifact/evidence digests actually verified. A failed or unfinished receipt exits 2; successful publication exits 0. Retry the unchanged plan after resolving the failure; successful destinations are reconciled by their digest. Preflight operation errors such as missing evidence, a wrong subject or a conflicting existing asset exit 1 through the shared CLI error path; JSON diagnostics carry the same exitCode. Invalid command syntax exits 2. Publication needs network access. There is no offline publication success. Artifacts and GET responses are currently held in memory; streaming and larger artifact qualification are deferred. The implementation is shared across host platforms; only explicitly recorded native runs establish platform coverage. The Linux standalone selection proof built two real binaries and verified the selected output, its original provenance and signed intent through a disposable OCI registry. It also verified that the unselected payload was absent, matching repeat/recheck behavior and early refusals. That anonymous loopback run does not qualify authentication or governed execution.

The GitHub adapter uses the same configuration, whole-plan evidence acceptance, signing and restricted worker as OCI. The bounded GitHub.com proof passed on Windows x64, including native downloads, exact evidence/signature checks, matching/conflicting assets and controlled partial recovery. The GitHub qualification record records exact revisions and limits; broader hosts, enterprise routes and deployed platform execution remain unqualified. Replace the destination in the preceding example with this illustrative entry: [publish.destinations.sandbox] kind = "github-release" apiUrl = "https://api.github.com" repository = "your-owner/your-test-repository" tag = "existing-test-tag" tokenEnv = "GITHUB_SANDBOX_TOKEN" artifacts = ["app/archive", "cli"] [publish.destinations.sandbox.evidence] mode = "destination" Provision the tag/release separately and supply a repository-scoped Contents read/write credential by environment reference. The adapter never creates refs or releases, finalizes releases, changes metadata or deletes assets. It freezes the API root, observed repository/release IDs, resolved tag commit, upload route, draft/prerelease state and exact filenames, then refuses changed identity before writes. Reported draft/private visibility does not imply public distribution. Asset names are derived at publication from the file's local name and the compatibility its builder recorded, so one release holds several platforms of one operating system family. Bytes and local dist/ filenames never change: Recorded compatibility Asset name Example target (built for one platform) <stem>-<os>-<arch><ext> oyzu for linux/x86_64 → oyzu-linux-x86_64; oyzu.exe for windows/x86_64 → oyzu-windows-x86_64.exe; app.tar.gz for linux/arm64 → app-linux-arm64.tar.gz independent (no platform restriction) the filename site.tar.gz native (a package whose own name encodes the platform, such as a wheel) the filename pkg-1.0-cp312-cp312-manylinux_2_28_x86_64.whl pending, unknown or missing refused with PUBLISH_ARTIFACT_SELECTION_INVALID the builder must record what the file is for The platform uses the canonical spelling (x86_64, arm64, never amd64); an ABI would appear only when the builder records one, and no builder records one today. ext is the longest case-insensitive match from .tar.gz, .tar.xz, .tar.zst, .tgz, .zip, .exe, .msi, .dmg, .pkg, .deb, .rpm, .dll, .so, .dylib, keeping its original case; without a match the platform is appended. A target file is qualified even when the release holds one platform, and names carry no version, so releases/latest/download/oyzu-linux-x86_64 stays stable. Extending the extension list renames matching assets. Derived names must use ASCII letters, digits, dot, underscore or dash, at most 220 bytes, without a leading dot, and must not end in a reserved evidence suffix. Reserved evidence names follow the derived name: <asset>.provenance.sigstore.json and <asset>.publication.sigstore.json. Two planned names that are equal ignoring ASCII case collide. These checks fail with PUBLISH_ARTIFACT_SELECTION_INVALID before evidence loading, signing or network access. The plan freezes each derived name in the coordinate's assetName, which the signed intent binds; the worker re-derives it from the frozen artifact facts and refuses any other name. Earlier assets under unqualified names (oyzu) are left alone; they are never renamed or removed. Before any upload, the complete plan checks planned name collisions, aliases and independently retrieved existing assets. Matching content is reused; different bytes fail with PUBLISH_CONFLICT without overwrite or deletion. Original provenance and verified signed intent are uploaded and retrieved before their corresponding payload. Success requires exact native GET bytes, sizes/digests and evidence claims, rather than an upload acknowledgement. The default and only supported evidence placement for both OCI and GitHub is evidence.mode = "destination". receipt and managed cannot be used to weaken remotely retrievable evidence requirements. This does not imply npm/PyPI support. GitHub.com admits the configured API origin, exact release upload route on uploads.github.com and asset downloads on release-assets.githubusercontent.com. API path prefixes are preserved. Same-origin requests stay within that prefix; upload routes bind the repository and release ID. Redirected asset downloads remain anonymous, including a return to the API origin. Tokens never follow arbitrary redirects. Enterprise endpoints are initially limited to same-origin routes within the API prefix; translating /api/v3 to /api/uploads is unsupported. No enterprise, GitHub Actions artifact or GHCR qualification is implied. An uncertain upload can leave a remote asset. Receipts retain verified completed, failed and unfinished native asset outcomes. Retry the unchanged plan under current authority: matching assets remain, and only missing work is attempted. Changed subjects, coordinates or evidence require a new plan; same-name different evidence is a conflict, not permission to replace it. Release metadata remains mutable by other writers; read-back is an observation, not permanent immutability. The unreleased v1alpha1 worker, receipt and intent evolve in place to file sets, typed coordinates and entries. Old singular-subject worker bodies are rejected; there is no parallel legacy protocol. Existing OCI configuration still defaults to oci, but derived wrapper coordinates can differ because intent claims changed. Use a fresh proof namespace when comparing historical OCI qualification. Release asset naming changed every destination kind, not only GitHub: when a file has recorded compatibility, its receipt artifacts[].id, entry artifactId and unselectedArtifacts use the qualified key (cli/bin-oyzu@linux/x86_64), and its artifact identity, plan digest and signed intent include compatibility. An OCI destination still accepts files without recorded compatibility.

For preparation without publication, see the native Linux candidate review record. Its private covered-source rebuild proof demonstrates changing an embedded shell component and emitting it from a rebuilt CLI, with exact source/material identities and explicit cache/delivery limits. CLI distribution remains subject to the compliance gate; the workflow below does not grant distribution clearance. Publishing a GitHub release triggers .github/workflows/release.yml. It runs one job per platform runner; each job downloads the newest earlier release's oyzu for its platform (tooling/bootstrap-oyzu.sh --release), builds the release tag with it natively (oyzu build cli), signs provenance and publishes its own platform's executables to the same release with oyzu publish. Asset names carry the platform, so jobs never collide and may run in parallel. Each of the six declared platforms has a GitHub-hosted runner that builds it natively (ubuntu-24.04, ubuntu-24.04-arm, macos-15-intel, macos-15, windows-2025, windows-11-arm); the repository variable OYZU_LINUX_RUNNER (a JSON runs-on value) moves Linux x86_64 to another runner. Paid hosted minutes are used for releases only; pull request and push checks stay on the self-hosted runner. A job whose platform's payload and both sidecars are already on the release skips itself, so re-running the workflow only builds the platforms still missing. When no earlier release has the qualified executable for the runner's platform, the workflow builds oyzu from the tag's source instead; that happens once per platform. The bootstrap maps the host to its asset and verifies the digest GitHub reports before installing it as .oyzu/bin/oyzu (or oyzu.exe) with mode 755, since raw downloads lose the executable bit: Host Asset Linux x86_64 / aarch64 oyzu-linux-x86_64 / oyzu-linux-arm64 macOS x86_64 / arm64 oyzu-darwin-x86_64 / oyzu-darwin-arm64; under Rosetta (sysctl.proc_translated is 1) it takes arm64 Windows x86_64 / ARM64 (MSYS/MINGW) oyzu-windows-x86_64.exe / oyzu-windows-arm64.exe, read from PROCESSOR_ARCHITEW6432/PROCESSOR_ARCHITECTURE because uname -m reports x86_64 under emulation tooling/bootstrap-oyzu.sh --print-asset prints the name for the current host. It does not look up the unqualified oyzu/oyzu.exe names of earlier interim releases; without a qualified asset it builds from source. Sidecar verification in the bootstrap is later work. Create and publish the release (and its tag) first: the adapter attaches assets to an existing release found by tag, and GitHub's tag lookup does not return a draft, so a draft fails with PUBLISH_GITHUB_API: inspection returned HTTP 404.
