A prerelease on a private repository is visible only to collaborators and its assets need a token to download. Re-run a release with gh workflow run release.yml -f tag=<tag>. Until a protected builder exists, the evidence comes from a local test-builder witness, tooling/release-witness.mjs. It signs SLSA provenance for the built outputs with a self-managed Ed25519 key. It is not a protected build, a trusted timestamp or a SLSA level claim. The accepted public keys are in oyzu.toml; the seeds are the repository secrets OYZU_RELEASE_BUILDER_SEED and OYZU_RELEASE_PUBLISHER_SEED in CI, or files in a directory outside the checkout: node tooling/release-witness.mjs keys --key-dir <dir outside the checkout> # once gh secret set OYZU_RELEASE_BUILDER_SEED < <dir>/builder.seed gh secret set OYZU_RELEASE_PUBLISHER_SEED < <dir>/publisher.seed To release by hand, build, then sign with --started/--finished timestamps taken around the build (without them the witness falls back to approximate dist/ file times), then publish: oyzu build cli node tooling/release-witness.mjs sign --key-dir <dir> --artifact cli/bin-oyzu --artifact cli/bin-oyzu-shim node tooling/release-witness.mjs publish --key-dir <dir> --arg --manifest --arg dist/manifest.json --arg --destination --arg github The witness takes the same selectors as oyzu publish (cli/bin-oyzu signs every platform of that output in the manifest, cli/bin-oyzu@linux/x86_64 exactly one) and writes each bundle to .oyzu/release-evidence/<os>/<arch>/, the path the {artifact.platform} placeholder in oyzu.toml renders. Signing the same bundle again yields byte-identical evidence: the invocation ID derives from the manifest and artifact digests, and the build times and source state are recorded once per manifest in .oyzu/release-evidence/witness-run.json and reused. A retried publish over the same bundle therefore reuses the sidecars already uploaded. Limitations: Optimized executables are not yet observed in a release run. The workflow's build step sets OYZU_CONTEXT=release (a release event's tag already implies it; a workflow_dispatch re-run runs on a branch ref), and since build intent slice 5 a release build is optimized (cargo build --release). No release has run with this yet; earlier published executables were development builds and report debug in --version. Optimized is not a publication-eligibility claim. Hosted platforms are not yet qualified. Linux arm64, macOS and Windows jobs are configured for GitHub-hosted runners but have not completed a release run; until one does, treat those platforms as unqualified. Linux x86_64 has run on the self-hosted runner. A partial platform conflicts on rebuild. A platform is skipped only when its payload and both sidecars are present. If an earlier attempt uploaded part of a platform, the re-run rebuilds different payload bytes under the same asset name, which is PUBLISH_CONFLICT; publish the same bundle again by hand, or delete the partial assets before re-running. Publishing a combined bundle handed off from build jobs is later work (build intent slice 6).

With explicit --server, --account, --project (or the corresponding environment selection), the CLI stages/registers the build, then submits a durable publication operation. Pass --provenance FILE with the preexisting Sigstore bundle. The platform selects requirements and destinations centrally; caller-selected roots or signing credentials cannot grant governed authority. --destination cannot be combined with governed routing. The first slice requires one staged file artifact; --no-upload cannot satisfy this path. Optionally pass --policy-evidence FILE with an existing signed policy report bundle when the central policy requires one. The CLI reads UTF-8 JSON and sends the original string unchanged as policyEvidence.bundle; omitting the flag omits that optional object. It does not verify the report signature, evaluate customer facts, select trusted roots, or treat report contents as approval. Central admission determines accepted producer, predicate, root and account/subject scope. A report that observes an issue is open is an observation, not an approval claim. The operation POST is /publish/v1/accounts/{account}/projects/{project}/operations, carrying schemaVersion, registrationBuild, exact staged artifact identity/reference, and provenance.bundle. The CLI follows GET /operations/{operationId}. Build registration or staging success alone is never presented as completed distribution. The durable operation remains inspectable when following it times out; inspect that operation before submitting another request. Server URL path prefixes are preserved for staging, registration, operation submission and status following, with or without a trailing slash. The complete governed flow and publisher isolation qualification are deferred by the maintainer's 2026-10-17 implementation-merge decision and tracked in issue #541. The standalone proof and component checks do not establish those governed guarantees in a live deployment. Protected workers invoke the same built-in implementation through the hidden __publication-worker --request FILE bridge. This is an internal fixed contract, not a plugin ABI. The request freezes the exact file set, entries, native coordinates, evidence, signing references and operation/executor authority. Before signing and each registry mutation, the worker requests current central authorization bound to the exact operation, executor, subject, destination, provenance and signing intent. Mutation requests have no automatic transport replay. Roots and secrets are provisioned by the protected host, never returned to the caller. The following sections document the existing registration/staging transport used before that operation, including its CI credential discovery.

In CI, governed oyzu publish first reads the completed build manifest (dist/manifest.json), stages its file artifact and registers its outputs and component versions. This registration uses the same output contract as platform build completion. The command then requests publication with the preexisting provenance and follows the durable operation. Its final result reports that operation's decisions, execution and verified receipts. Registration alone does not authorize external distribution. Publishing is optional. oyzu build and everything else stay local and work without an account.

A finished oyzu build whose manifest records status: succeeded. A failed, cancelled or interrupted build is refused before anything is sent (PUBLISH_BUILD_NOT_SUCCEEDED). The platform URL, account and project, as flags or environment variables. A credential the project accepts: the pipeline's OIDC token for a trusted CI connector, or a publish token issued on the project's CI connector. See credentials. Registration routing uses flags/environment; commit, repository and ref come from the CI system's environment or flags. Standalone publication uses the cascade above.

oyzu build oyzu publish --server https://oyzu.example.com --account acme --project web --provenance evidence/build.sigstore.json Flag Environment Default Meaning --server URL OYZU_URL required The platform's URL. Must be https, except http://localhost, http://127.0.0.1 or http://[::1] for a local devstack, so a token never crosses a network unencrypted (PUBLISH_INSECURE_SERVER). --account ID OYZU_ACCOUNT required The account to publish to. --project ID OYZU_PROJECT required The project to publish to. --manifest FILE dist/manifest.json The build manifest, relative to the directory (-C). --provenance FILE required for governed publication Original preexisting signed provenance bundle, read as UTF-8 without rewriting its bytes. --policy-evidence FILE omitted Optional original signed policy report bundle for central admission; governed only. --version VERSION none The build's version, when the pipeline names one. --commit SHA from CI The built commit. --repository OWNER/NAME from CI The repository the build came from. --audience AUDIENCE OYZU_AUDIENCE oyzu The audience requested for OIDC tokens the CLI asks a CI system for. --token-env NAME none Read the OIDC token from this environment variable instead of discovering one. --no-upload OYZU_PUBLISH_UPLOAD=0 upload Historical registration-only transport control. Governed publication requires staging and rejects an artifact without an immutable staged reference. A flag wins over its environment variable. Account and project identifiers follow the platform rule: lowercase letters, digits and inner hyphens, 1 to 63 characters, starting and ending with a letter or digit. The global --json flag prints the final operation record with registrationBuild. If following the operation times out, the CLI reports status: "unfinished" and a recovery message; the platform operation remains inspectable. Transport errors follow the usual {"error": …, "exitCode": 2} shape.

jobs: build: runs-on: ubuntu-24.04 permissions: contents: read id-token: write # lets oyzu publish request an OIDC token steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - run: oyzu build - run: oyzu publish --server https://oyzu.example.com --account acme --project web --provenance evidence/build.sigstore.json

oyzu publish uses the first credential it finds, in this order: --token-env NAME, else OYZU_ID_TOKEN: an OIDC token the pipeline already holds. A --token-env variable that is unset or empty is an error, not a fall-through. GitHub Actions: when ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_URL and ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_TOKEN are set (the job has permissions: id-token: write), the CLI requests a token for the audience (GET $ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_URL&audience=oyzu, authorized by the request token) and uses the answer's value. Bitbucket Pipelines: BITBUCKET_STEP_OIDC_TOKEN (a step with oidc: true); CircleCI: CIRCLE_OIDC_TOKEN_V2, then CIRCLE_OIDC_TOKEN. Buildkite: when BUILDKITE is set and buildkite-agent is on PATH, buildkite-agent oidc request-token --audience oyzu. OYZU_PUBLISH_TOKEN: a scoped, revocable publish token (oyzp_…) issued on the project's CI connector, for CI tools without OIDC. A source that is present but fails (GitHub refuses the token request, the Buildkite agent fails) stops the command (PUBLISH_CREDENTIAL_UNAVAILABLE) instead of falling through to another credential. With none found the command fails with PUBLISH_NO_CREDENTIAL and, in GitHub Actions, names the missing id-token permission. The Buildkite helper has a fixed 30-second deadline, including output capture. If it stalls, Oyzu attempts to kill the local helper and returns PUBLISH_CREDENTIAL_UNAVAILABLE with external command deadline exceeded; it does not wait indefinitely for a descendant holding an output pipe open or fall back to the publish token. Token output stays in memory and is not included in timeout diagnostics. There is no timeout setting or automatic helper retry. Check the Buildkite agent and its OIDC service/policy, then rerun oyzu publish, or explicitly select an already issued credential with --token-env. An absent agent still allows the normal discovery fallback. Killing the local helper does not guarantee remote work or descendants stopped, and the helper deadline does not bound the complete HTTP publication flow. Offline publication is unavailable. Deadline-runner regressions are authored but unexecuted on this desktop; see verification status. How each CI system provides its token: CI system How GitHub Actions permissions: id-token: write on the job; discovered automatically. GitLab CI/CD id_tokens: on the job, for example OYZU_ID_TOKEN: {aud: oyzu}; read from OYZU_ID_TOKEN (or name another variable with --token-env). Bitbucket Pipelines oidc: true on the step; BITBUCKET_STEP_OIDC_TOKEN is discovered. Its audience is fixed by Bitbucket; the project's trust must accept it. CircleCI CIRCLE_OIDC_TOKEN_V2 / CIRCLE_OIDC_TOKEN are discovered. Their audience is the CircleCI organization; for an oyzu audience, mint one with circleci run oidc get --claims '{"aud":"oyzu"}' into OYZU_ID_TOKEN. Buildkite Discovered through buildkite-agent oidc request-token; the pipeline's OIDC policy must allow it. Jenkins with the OIDC provider plugin Bind the plugin's credential to a variable and pass --token-env (or bind it as OYZU_ID_TOKEN). Jenkins without OIDC, TeamCity OYZU_PUBLISH_TOKEN from a credentials store / secure parameter. Which tokens a project accepts is the platform's decision (the trusts on the project's CI connector), not the CLI's. The token is sent only in the Authorization header of the publish request. It is never printed, logged or written to disk; progress names only where it came from (for example "a GitHub Actions OIDC token").

Before the build is POSTed, every artifact without an oci_digest (anything but an OCI image or index) is uploaded to the platform's registry as an OCI artifact, unless --no-upload or OYZU_PUBLISH_UPLOAD=0 is given. Images and indexes are not uploaded by the CLI; they keep their oci_digest. Check the files. Only an artifact whose path is a regular file in the bundle, of the recorded size and SHA-256 digest, is uploaded. A directory artifact is skipped with one warning and published without an oci_ref. A missing file or one whose bytes changed since oyzu build stops the publish with PUBLISH_ARTIFACT_CHANGED before any credential is requested. With no artifact left to upload, steps 2 to 4 are skipped. Upload grant. POST {server}/publish/v1/accounts/{account}/projects/{project}/builds/uploads with the same credential and headers as the publish: {"artifacts": [{"path": "artifacts/api/default/binary/server", "media_type": "application/octet-stream", "digest": "sha256:…", "size": 123}]} path is the artifact's path in the bundle as the manifest lists it (1 to 1000 entries, only the artifacts being uploaded). The platform answers 200: {"registry": "https://registry.example", "repository": "acme/web/artifacts", "token": "<jwt>", "expires_at": "2026-10-11T12:00:00Z"} 404 means the platform has no artifact storage: one warning is printed and the build is published as without upload, with no oci_ref. 401, 403 and 422 fail the publish with the platform's problem, as for the publish itself; 502, 503 and 504 are retried the same way. Registry sign-in. The standard registry token flow: GET {registry}/v2/ answers 401 with WWW-Authenticate: Bearer realm="…",service="…"; the CLI calls the realm with ?service=<service>&scope=repository:<repository>:pull,push and HTTP Basic authentication (user oyzu, password the grant's token) and uses the answer's token (or access_token) as the bearer. The realm must be on the registry's own origin (scheme, host and port), so the grant token never goes elsewhere. The registry must be https, except plain http on loopback. Push. The empty config blob {} once (application/vnd.oci.empty.v1+json, sha256:44136fa355b3678a1146ad16f7e8649e94fb4fc21fe77e8310c060f61caaff8a, size 2), then for each artifact: its file's bytes, uncompressed, as one blob whose digest is the artifact's digest, after HEAD /v2/<repository>/blobs/<digest>; a 200 skips the upload; this manifest, serialized once in exactly this form and put to /v2/<repository>/manifests/sha256:<SHA-256 of those bytes> with Content-Type: application/vnd.oci.image.manifest.v1+json (never a tag): {"schemaVersion":2,"mediaType":"application/vnd.oci.image.manifest.v1+json","artifactType":"<media_type>","config":{"mediaType":"application/vnd.oci.empty.v1+json","digest":"sha256:44136fa355b3678a1146ad16f7e8649e94fb4fc21fe77e8310c060f61caaff8a","size":2},"layers":[{"mediaType":"<media_type>","digest":"<digest>","size":<size>,"annotations":{"org.opencontainers.image.title":"<file name>"}}],"annotations":{"dev.oyzu.output":"<output name>"}} <output name> is the target for its primary artifact and target/name otherwise, as components name build outputs. Registry requests that fail with a server error or in transport are retried up to three attempts; any other refusal fails the publish with PUBLISH_UPLOAD_FAILED and nothing is published. Each uploaded artifact's output then carries "oci_ref": "<registry host[:port]>/<repository>@sha256:<manifest digest>" (no scheme).

POST {server}/publish/v1/accounts/{account}/projects/{project}/builds with Authorization: Bearer <credential>, Content-Type: application/json and Accept: application/json: { "version": "1.4.2", "commit": "0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef01234567", "repository": "acme/web", "ref": "refs/heads/main", "run_url": "https://github.com/acme/web/actions/runs/42", "outputs": [ {"path": "dist/manifest.json", "kind": "manifest", "media_type": "application/vnd.oyzu.build-manifest.v1alpha1+json", "digest": "sha256:…", "size": 2101}, {"path": "dist/image-index/any/image.oci.tar", "kind": "artifact", "media_type": "application/vnd.oci.image.index.v1+json", "digest": "sha256:…", "size": 123, "target": "image-index", "name": "primary", "version": "0.1.0-dev.g111111111111", "oci_digest": "sha256:…"}, {"path": "dist/api/linux/x86_64/server", "kind": "artifact", "media_type": "application/octet-stream", "digest": "sha256:…", "size": 123, "target": "api", "name": "binary", "version": "0.1.0-dev.g111111111111", "oci_ref": "registry.example/acme/web/artifacts@sha256:…"} ] } Optional fields are omitted when unknown. outputs matches a platform runner's FinishOutput (runner contract): one manifest output for the manifest file itself: its media type, the SHA-256 of its bytes and its size; one artifact output per artifact the manifest lists, with the manifest's path, mediaType, digest, size, target, name and version, plus oci_digest (the manifest's ociDigest, the digest a registry addresses it by) for oci-image and oci-index artifacts only, or oci_ref for an artifact the CLI uploaded. oci_ref is the one field beyond the runner's FinishOutput. Directory artifacts carry their tree digest. Paths are relative to the checkout root, as a runner reports them: the manifest's directory relative to -C (dist/ by default) followed by the artifact's bundle path. A --manifest outside the directory reports paths relative to its own bundle. Artifact digests are the ones oyzu build recorded; files that are uploaded are checked against them, and oyzu inspect checks the whole bundle. The CLI checks the platform's limits before sending (PUBLISH_MANIFEST_INVALID): at most 1000 outputs, paths up to 1024 bytes, media types 255, targets 256, names 64 and versions 255; every artifact has a target, name and version, a sha256 digest, a safe relative path and, if it is an OCI image or index, a sha256 ociDigest. Commit, repository, ref and run link come from the first CI system that announces itself: CI system commit repository ref run_url GitHub Actions GITHUB_SHA GITHUB_REPOSITORY GITHUB_REF $GITHUB_SERVER_URL/$GITHUB_REPOSITORY/actions/runs/$GITHUB_RUN_ID GitLab CI_COMMIT_SHA CI_PROJECT_PATH refs/tags/$CI_COMMIT_TAG or refs/heads/$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH CI_PIPELINE_URL CircleCI CIRCLE_SHA1 CIRCLE_PROJECT_USERNAME/CIRCLE_PROJECT_REPONAME CIRCLE_TAG / CIRCLE_BRANCH CIRCLE_BUILD_URL Buildkite BUILDKITE_COMMIT (not HEAD) from BUILDKITE_REPO BUILDKITE_TAG / BUILDKITE_BRANCH BUILDKITE_BUILD_URL Bitbucket BITBUCKET_COMMIT BITBUCKET_REPO_FULL_NAME BITBUCKET_TAG / BITBUCKET_BRANCH https://bitbucket.org/<repo>/pipelines/results/$BITBUCKET_BUILD_NUMBER Jenkins GIT_COMMIT from GIT_URL GIT_BRANCH without origin/ BUILD_URL TeamCity BUILD_VCS_NUMBER (use --repository) none none

The platform answers 200 with the build, its eligibility (candidate or snapshot), one entry per component and the outputs that belong to no component: Build registered · 01jab7v3k9m2q8r4t6w0y1z5c7 (candidate) ✓ published api 1.4.2 (candidate) = already published web 2.0.0 ! skipped worker 0.3.0: the build did not publish [worker/config] Outputs in no component (never shipped) web/build-metadata This registration response describes recorded components and does not establish external distribution. The public command proceeds to the durable publication operation; its final receipt and independently verified outcome control success. The displayed final result is the operation result described above. A successful HTTP status alone is insufficient: the response must name the build, use candidate or snapshot eligibility, and provide components and unassigned outputs arrays. Every component names its component and version, uses published, already-published or skipped, and includes a reason when skipped. Malformed responses fail with PUBLISH_RESPONSE_INVALID in human and JSON modes. The server may already have published the build; inspect its state and check platform/client compatibility. Retrying the same build is safe.

Every failure exits 2 and prints one diagnostic; nothing is retried that the platform refused. Code Meaning PUBLISH_NOT_CONFIGURED A server, account or project is missing or malformed. PUBLISH_INSECURE_SERVER The server uses plain http and is not localhost. PUBLISH_MANIFEST_MISSING / PUBLISH_MANIFEST_INVALID No manifest at the path, or it breaks a rule above. Nothing is sent and no token is requested. PUBLISH_BUILD_NOT_SUCCEEDED The manifest records a build that did not succeed. PUBLISH_ARTIFACT_CHANGED An artifact to upload is missing, not a regular file, or no longer has its recorded size or digest. Nothing is sent; build again. PUBLISH_UPLOAD_FAILED The registry refused or failed a sign-in, blob or manifest request (after retries for server errors). Nothing is published. PUBLISH_RESPONSE_INVALID The platform's upload grant or answer is malformed, or names a registry that is not https (plain http only on loopback). PUBLISH_NO_CREDENTIAL / PUBLISH_CREDENTIAL_UNAVAILABLE No credential found, or a CI system did not issue one. PUBLISH_UNAUTHENTICATED (401) The platform did not accept the credential: expired, wrong audience or revoked. 403 (PUBLISH_<code>) "Oyzu refused this pipeline's token": the token is valid, but no trust on the project's CI connector accepts this pipeline (repository, branch or workflow). other PUBLISH_<code> The platform's RFC 9457 problem: its detail, each errors[] entry as field: message, and the platform request id. PUBLISH_UNREACHABLE The platform could not be reached after retries. Connection failures and 502, 503 and 504 answers are retried up to five attempts with backoff, honoring Retry-After (at most 30 seconds).

Not qualified against a deployed platform; the endpoint is being built. The first explicit publication slice accepts one finalized file. OCI images, indexes and directory publication require later native destination support. Each uploaded file is read into memory for its push; very large files need that much memory. Streaming is a later refinement. A registry whose token endpoint (realm) is on another origin is refused. Commit, repository and ref are what the CI system says; the platform decides what it trusts from the token's claims. Windows and macOS runners use the same code; the integration test runs on Linux CI.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/remote-runs.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Status: experimental client. oyzu build --remote and oyzu run <task> --remote implement the CLI side of the draft remote runs contract (design page). They are verified against a scripted local server and the contract's mock; no platform service implements the contract yet, so they are not qualified against one.

--remote runs the same invocation on a platform pool instead of this machine: the pool checks out the exact pushed commit, runs oyzu build or oyzu run <task> there with full checks in isolation, and streams the output back. The CLI follows it to the end and exits with the remote exit code. Everything else Oyzu does stays local and works without an account; --remote is the optional platform path.

A Git checkout whose HEAD is pushed to a github.com repository linked to a project in your platform account. git must be on PATH. platform.url and platform.account in user/global, machine or administrative configuration. Project/local scope is rejected with a diagnostic naming the key: oyzu config set --global platform.url https://platform.example.com oyzu config set --global platform.account payments CI can supply OYZU_PLATFORM_URL and OYZU_PLATFORM_ACCOUNT through the configuration contract. These invocation sources override ordinary files and remain subject to administrative constraints. A checkout cannot redirect a developer's platform credential, even when its environment is trusted. An access token in OYZU_PLATFORM_TOKEN. Interactive login from the authentication contract is not implemented yet; the token is a credential, so it is read from the environment and never from a configuration file.

Command Runs remotely oyzu build --remote Every target oyzu build cli web --remote Targets cli and web (and what they depend on) oyzu build --affected origin/main --remote Targets affected since the merge base of origin/main and HEAD oyzu run policy-check --remote Task policy-check (target:task also works) … --remote --download out The same, then downloads every output into out/ oyzu build --remote --plan previews a remote build locally without creating a run; see planning a remote run. The CLI resolves the repository from the current branch's remote (else origin), the full HEAD commit and the checked-out branch ref. For --affected it sends the full merge-base commit, never a local ref name.

Text mode uses the same linear view as a local build. Each log line the pool streams is attributed to the target or task that wrote it (scope in the contract), so task starts, native output and task results look like local ones. The runner's own lines (checkout, start, finish) appear under runner. The receipt on stdout leads with the outcome, then the run id, commit, project, Oyzu version, portal link when there is one, and the outputs the run produced: ✓ Remote build succeeded Run 01jab7v3k9m2q8r4t6w0y1z5c7 Commit 3f2a9c1d4b5e (main) Project oyzu/platform Oyzu 0.9.0 Outputs manifest dist/manifest.json 4.0 KiB sha256:aaaaaaaaaaaa report dist/cli/linux/x86_64/reports/junit.xml 2.0 KiB sha256:bbbbbbbbbbbb Use --download <DIR> to fetch outputs; nothing was written locally. With --json, stderr carries the same structured events a local build emits (output events keep the remote scope as operationId) and stdout carries one remote-run record: run (the final run resource), result (state, exit code, reason and outputs), downloads (path, digest, local file) and cancelled. The record also contains invocationId, the exact submission body (repository, commit and selection), observation and a cancellation object. After a run has been created, failure to follow or retrieve its result produces an unknown outcome with the last observed run state/time and log position; it does not assert failed remote execution or start local work. The last run-resource state can predate subsequent scoped task log events. Known log gaps remain explicit in the result even after a connection recovers. Complete observation means the client received terminal records, not that every log entry or required artifact transfer is complete. Bounded retry notices describe observation loss and recovery. Submission, observation and requested artifact transfer are distinct phases. The current public contract supplies queued/running/final states and scoped task lifecycles; worker identity, assignment and detailed worker preparation/transfer telemetry are unavailable and are not inferred from illustrative studies.

Remote outcome Exit code Succeeded 0 Oyzu exited non-zero on the pool That exit code Failed before Oyzu ran, skipped, cancelled, timed out, or an unknown state 1 Refused before or while creating the run (configuration, Git, platform problem) 2 Interrupted with Ctrl-C 130 An unknown remote outcome after submission exits non-zero (1); an interrupt retains exit 130. Use the supplied Web link, or check the run ID with the platform operator when no link was supplied, before starting a replacement run. Reattachment and CLI retrieval of a previous remote run are not implemented.

The first Ctrl-C asks the platform to cancel the run and keeps following its log while the pool stops it; a second Ctrl-C exits at once with 130. The observer keeps following beyond the local cleanup grace period so it can retain the execution owner's confirmed outcome. Cancelling is retry-safe, so a cancel that races the run's own finish is harmless. There is no confirmation prompt, so cancelling works the same in CI. Closing the terminal (SIGHUP) is not a cancellation: it ends only the local follower, and the remote run continues on the pool. cancelled records that this invocation requested cancellation. It is not confirmation that execution stopped. cancellation.requested, acknowledged and confirmed expose separate facts; confirmation follows a terminal cancelled result. A finished-run conflict is followed to its actual outcome. The receipt preserves pending or unknown cancellation and any known log gaps. Assigned native workers use the same cooperative interruption lifetime as a local captured build. A running cancellation acknowledgement requires the execution owner's normal process wait and fresh finalized native build record; revoking a lease or receiving a success response alone is insufficient. Forced or unconfirmed stops remain explicit failures. The real Linux service/worker proof passed cancellation during the shared native action: the observer retained all three cancellation facts and exited 130 after confirmed cleanup. A second real run preserved an already accepted shared contribution while stopping API and preventing the final bundle from starting; see the distributed qualification record. resultAvailable distinguishes a fetched result from a partial observation. When the final run resource is already confirmed, losing access to its result retains that execution outcome and identifies unavailable metadata/outputs. The invocation still fails if requested observation cannot complete. Last-observed timestamps advance on actual responses; elapsed waiting is not execution progress.

Outputs are listed by digest and never written into dist/. --download <DIR> fetches each one through the platform's short-lived download link, which receives no platform credential, verifies its SHA-256 digest before writing, and writes it at its recorded path under DIR. A path that would leave DIR is refused. For accepted native split builds, these are the manifest, artifacts and required reports. The output projection excludes the private admitted plan, execution envelope and logs; it is not a complete local build bundle for oyzu inspect. The existing run log view retains remote observation separately. Native contribution validation precedes final platform success; downloaded file digests are checked again by the client. Reported native success does not guarantee platform acceptance. If the complete transferred contribution cannot be verified, the run fails with CONTRIBUTION_UNVERIFIED and no accepted outputs. This does not turn successful native actions into failed tests or grant permission to replay their commands. Inspect the run's diagnostic and retained native evidence before retrying. The result must contain an outputs array, including an empty array when there are no outputs. Every output supplies its kind (manifest, report or artifact), media type, nonnegative size, path and digest. A missing or malformed array or missing output metadata fails with REMOTE_RESPONSE_INVALID before downloads start, in human and JSON modes, even when the platform reports that the run succeeded. Check the platform's result and client compatibility; the remote run itself is not restarted.

Refusals never fall back to a local build. Platform problems keep their stable code with a REMOTE_ prefix and the platform request id, for example REMOTE_UNAUTHENTICATED (set a current token), REMOTE_REPOSITORY_NOT_LINKED, REMOTE_COMMIT_NOT_FOUND (push first) and REMOTE_VALIDATION_FAILED. Local checks fail before any request: REMOTE_NOT_CONFIGURED, REMOTE_NOT_A_CHECKOUT, REMOTE_REPOSITORY_UNSUPPORTED (not github.com), REMOTE_COMMIT_NOT_PUSHED (HEAD is on no branch of the remote) and REMOTE_AFFECTED_BASE_INVALID. Uncommitted changes produce a warning: they are not part of the run. Requests that fail in transport or answer 503 are retried up to five times with backoff, honoring Retry-After. Creation is retried under the same Idempotency-Key, so a retry never starts a second run. Logs are followed with 30-second long polls over plain HTTPS and resume from the last cursor, so the client works through proxies (HTTPS_PROXY, NO_PROXY, SSL_CERT_FILE) with outbound access alone.

The token is sent only to platform.url as a bearer credential. platform.url must be HTTPS; plain HTTP is accepted only for a loopback host, for local development against a mock. Run ids and digests from the platform are validated before they are used in a URL or a file name, and log text is escaped before it reaches the terminal like local child output.

The #479 implementation candidate connects internal admitted native preparation and assigned-plan verification separately from public read-only preview. This has passed the connected real-service flow on Linux, including distinct API/Web workers, an independent whole-build artifact/report comparison, cancellation, retained-byte upload retry, safe worker replacement, coupled prerequisites and required output/report/contribution refusals without implicit replay. The agreed finite cases and exact qualification limits are recorded in distributed build completion. No interactive login; the token comes from OYZU_PLATFORM_TOKEN. GitHub repositories on github.com only, matching the contract's github provider. Task arguments (-- args) are not supported remotely. --detach, listing runs and re-attaching to a run are not implemented. Broader platform/host qualification remains incomplete; see the linked distributed qualification record and RUNS-08/RUNS-09 in the design page.

oyzu exec -- cargo test --locked --test integration remote_runs: the compiled CLI against a scripted server for a successful build with scoped log replay and verified download, a failing task's exit code and JSON event stream, an expired token and an unpushed HEAD. python tooling/check-runs-contract.py: the contract and its mock, including scoped log entries. python tooling/test-remote-cli.py --cli <compiled-oyzu>: the compiled CLI against the contract mock end to end.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/rust.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. The in-development native local build is selected by plain oyzu build for one inferred or explicitly declared Rust target. Use oyzu build --isolated for the captured behavior below. Adding --plan produces a read-only preview, not dependency capture. The native bootstrap milestone is not yet acceptance-verified. Rust build, test, doctest and packaging orchestration runs in compiled Oyzu adapters. Host and isolated plans select the private compiled entry point; the former Python adapter files have been removed. Rust requirement discovery does not list Python. Cargo, Nextest, LLVM coverage tools and the applicable linker/SDK remain prerequisites. Explicit task overrides retain their own requirements. Broader host report-gate and rebuilt isolated-suite qualification remain pending; the registry-backreference corpus proof below qualifies that specific rebuilt flow. See the migration checkpoint. The experimental Rust builder discovers Cargo.toml without Oyzu configuration. Cargo owns workspace membership, native package metadata and dependency resolution. Captured builds currently support single packages and contained local workspaces, including libraries, binaries, proc macros and build scripts. Locked crates.io dependencies are captured before execution. Private/alternate registry and Git acquisition, and cross-compilation, remain unfinished. Artifact version selection now uses the shared version inference resolver for native, exact-tag and nearest-tag/commit snapshots. Release authorization remains separate and unimplemented. Workspace members resolve independently using their native path-dependency closure. A relevant dependency commit participates in the consumer's version analysis; an unrelated member's commit does not. Root workspace inputs conservatively affect all members. Private manifests and packaged local dependency requirements use each member's selected version; equal native version strings do not establish a release group. Captured builds preserve a member's original declared version when Cargo's resolved registry graph contains a dependency on a registry package with that member's name. Cargo package verification re-resolves through the workspace's private packaging registry; a projected prerelease can otherwise conflict with the registry dependency's release range. Only affected members retain declared versions, and local path requirements use those retained versions. Unaffected members still receive their normal snapshot versions. Inactive dependency declarations alone do not trigger preservation. These artifacts remain snapshots. The existing oyzu.dev/versioning evidence records reason: cargo-registry-backreference, the source digest and captured Git/input-scope facts, intent: snapshot and productionEligible: false even when the archive uses a release-shaped declared version. Use the build bundle's source identity and artifact digest to distinguish snapshots with the same native version. This correction does not authorize publication or repair other Cargo dependency cycles. See native qualification. Local development-dependency cycles can be packaged in captured builds when their ordinary and build-dependency edges remain acyclic. Oyzu groups only members involved in a development cycle and asks native Cargo to package that group together. Its provisional package command uses --locked --offline --exclude-lockfile --no-verify; the provisional archives are admitted only to an invocation-private registry after native index identities and archive checksums match. Oyzu then packages every member separately with native verification enabled, --locked --offline --exclude-lockfile, and requires each final archive to be byte-identical to its provisional counterpart before admitting any group member as a final artifact. Acyclic members retain ordinary per-member packaging and their existing archive contents. Affected cycle archives omit Cargo.lock, so a consumer cannot use cargo install --locked against such an archive; use the source workspace with its original lock or resolve the published package normally. Declared versioned development dependencies remain in the normalized manifest. Ordinary/build dependency cycles, unsupported registry backreferences in a cycle group, changed external identities and native verification failures still stop packaging. See the measured qualification. When the original lock contains a different registry version of an affected member, the packaging adapter lets native Cargo align its invocation-private lock with checksum-verified workspace archives after their promotion. It uses the original native registry package IDs and precise retained versions, offline; package verification remains --locked --offline. Every resulting identity must be an original captured input or a verified owned archive. Native pruning is reported, and the execution copy's original lock/configuration are restored on success or failure. Source checkout files and the captured registry remain unchanged. Same-version archive collisions, incompatible native ranges or uncaptured external changes still fail and block final artifacts. Native Windows drive/UNC path prefixes are translated only at the Cargo configuration boundary; non-UTF-8 registry paths fail rather than losing identity. The pinned clap corpus now completes oyzu build --isolated --full using the rebuilt worker image and exact image override recorded in qualification, delivering eight native crates, a working Linux binary and all three required reports. Installed/default images and public distribution were not updated. Three members retain their declared versions while five retain normal snapshot projection; all eight decisions retain snapshot identity and no release authority. Coverage collection passed at zero of 73 lines, which is not positive application coverage. See the commands, artifacts and limits. Plain local oyzu build selects the host and retains quality gates. Use --all-platforms for the declared matrix through the captured executor. See build selection and checks.

A [tools] rust = "1.95.0" declaration in oyzu.toml selects the matching oyzu.lock environment for the captured target scope and profile. The current container worker consumes a linux/<architecture>/gnu installation from the workspace's .oyzu/tools store. This is the compiler's execution platform; artifact platforms in build.yaml do not change it into a macOS or Windows tool. Only a Rust-only declared tool selection is supported by this initial handoff. Before package acquisition or Cargo execution, OYZU verifies the locked request, current backend/installer identity, complete installation receipts and payload contents. It leases the installation while copying it into the private dependency snapshot, then verifies the copied tree against the receipt. Preparation and build actions use its Cargo, rustc and rustdoc; the plan fixes their command environment. The dependency evidence records the request, selection, installation, backend, lock and copied-tree identities. The live tool store is not mounted in containers. Missing or stale locks, missing worker distributions, absent installations, unsupported layouts and changed payloads fail without falling back to image Rust. This path does not resolve versions, install tools, edit the lock or use the network for tool restoration. Provision the matching worker installation first. Existing oyzu install currently provisions its host only; installing Linux compiler selections from a Windows host is still unfinished. No new project-specific build flag is required. Builds without explicit tool requests retain the existing provisioned-image behavior. The image continues to provide native OS prerequisites, format/lint and reporting utilities; this handoff does not qualify those as locked tools or establish cross-compilation support. On Unix controllers, the Linux restoration container runs as the owner of its private input directory, following the shared executor's user mapping. Its input remains read-only and private; restoration keeps networking disabled, a read-only root filesystem and all capabilities dropped. This avoids permission failures when the controller's temporary files are inaccessible to the image's default user. Windows retains its existing Docker user behavior. A bounded Linux Rust 1.99.1 app proof passed two full isolated builds, native crate verification, JUnit 1/1 and application coverage 6/9 lines. The delivered binary ran read-only without networking and printed Hello, Oyzu!; both artifact digests and original source bytes were unchanged on repeat. The flow reused a previously verified packaged compiler, then restored it into a read-only action volume. The new controller and unchanged worker have separately recorded source identities. See the qualification and limits; this does not establish fresh installation on every build, the full Rust corpus or Windows/full-Bookworm worker qualification. Verification: on a Linux controller using the local Docker engine, python3 tooling/test-build-model.py --cli <compiled-cli> --locked-rust <Rust-1.95-sysroot> uses a real compiler with explicitly synthetic test lock/receipt provenance. It proves plain oyzu build produces and executes the feature-enabled binary, records compiler 1.95 despite image Rust 1.94, and rejects missing/stale locks and a corrupted payload before actions. This fixture does not prove installation or download provenance. Native Windows cannot attest the Linux executable modes in its NTFS store; automatic Linux worker provisioning remains unfinished.

The CLI accepts builds.<name> with uses, path, platforms, materialize and builder-owned with. bindings can be inspected during discovery but still fails captured-build admission until implemented. Rust currently accepts with.features, a list of unique Cargo feature names. Features apply to native metadata resolution, builds, lint, tests, doctests and package verification. Native default features remain enabled. Unknown options fail; options are not arbitrary command strings. builds: cli: uses: rust/app platforms: [linux/amd64] with: features: [integration] Run oyzu build for the native host, or oyzu build --all-platforms for the declared matrix. The existing captured execution path still requires the provisioned Linux Rust builder image described below and captures crates.io inputs before offline execution. Outputs and reports remain in the verified dist bundle. An omitted platform uses the existing executor platform; an explicit list expands every declared platform on the captured path. The native local default selects the current host from that list. This parser migration does not add cross-compilation or a new compatibility baseline. Explicit Rust requests now use the locked-tool handoff below. Pinned public GitHub acquisition is implemented through the scoped broker; private Git remains unsupported. The repository's six-platform self-build is not yet working. Other proposed shared fields and other builders' with options fail explicitly until their adapters implement them. The historical flat inventory remains readable for regression compatibility. New named builds reject legacy language objects, tool versions, runtime matrices, unknown shared fields, and empty, repeated or suffixed platform declarations. tooling/test-build-model.py --cli <compiled-cli> exercises the new authoring through a real Linux build, feature-required compilation, reports, packaging, bundle inspection and execution of the collected binary. It is not six-platform self-build evidence.

Work in progress: the root CLI binary matrix is not yet an end-to-end locked tool self-build. Its initial YAML toolchain pin was removed following the maintainer's tool-ownership correction. Tool requirements belong in oyzu.toml, and resolved identities in oyzu.lock. Build discovery/planning must consume those sources as facts; it must not add a second tool-version source. The root CLI build.yaml uses the builds / shared platforms / with model now accepted by the parser. The captured executor still cannot complete that declaration. Its six OS/architecture strings follow the agreed authoring model; the planner must resolve qualified compatibility baselines. That resolution remains pending. The following legacy rust example documents the existing experiment only, not the current root file or recommended authoring: cli: uses: rust/app path: . rust: features: [mise-integration] targets: - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu - aarch64-unknown-linux-musl - aarch64-apple-darwin - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc Declare the compiler requirement separately in oyzu.toml: [tools] rust = "1.95.0" features defaults to []; the example's feature belongs to OYZU. targets requires 1–64 unique Cargo triples, at most 58 characters each, containing lowercase letters, digits, hyphens and underscores. Cargo owns native target and feature support. Unknown Rust fields (including toolchain), duplicate features/triples, non-Rust builders and combining this object with captured platform/matrix intent are rejected. Discovery adds cli:build-<triple> tasks. They invoke native cargo build --locked --release --workspace --bins --target <triple> --target-dir target/oyzu-binaries with the declared features. Cargo emits binaries beneath target/oyzu-binaries/<triple>/release, with .exe on Windows. All Cargo binary targets are included, including separately declared helpers; OYZU's current shims are links/copies of its own executable. Triples distinguish GNU/musl and MSVC/GNU. No compiler version is encoded in the task argv. Shared task overrides, hooks and policy admission apply. Current oyzu run still rejects explicit tool requests until it can bind a verified locked installation. Consequently the root oyzu.toml correctly exposes a remaining integration blocker: task execution must consume the existing tool-lock and lease contract before this repository's self-build can run. Do not remove the requirement or bypass admission to make it pass. No oyzu.lock has been invented for this change. Tool installation must generate it through the native flow. Projects with externally provisioned tools and no explicit tool requests can exercise the generated native tasks under the existing development contract. This proves native target/feature argument handling, not locked tool execution. Missing compilers, SDKs or target libraries fail through Cargo; cross-compilation does not prove target execution. Cargo may leave older output after failures. Extra task arguments such as --offline retain native Cargo behavior. The draft matrix workflow and artifact driver remain incomplete pending that handoff and platform tool-lock qualification. The driver derives requirements through configuration inspection and labels them as requests, not resolved identities. It collects only successful Cargo-reported binaries, with hashes, and explicitly labels engineering artifacts non-isolated and unapproved. oyzu build separately rejects this native-only intent. Isolated Git capture and non-Linux isolated execution are still unfinished.

oyzu run list oyzu run build oyzu run test oyzu run lint oyzu run format-check oyzu build --plan oyzu build oyzu inspect dist Development tasks use already provisioned Cargo, rustfmt and Clippy on the host. Static task listing reads native manifests without executing Cargo. Implicit tasks include fetch (cargo fetch --locked), executable installation (cargo install --path . --locked), workspace build/test, Clippy, formatting, formatting checks and archive. Fetch and install are explicit development tasks, not automatic build stages. oyzu run format modifies source; captured builds use read-only format-check. Direct test execution now uses native host state and the shared test-only dist/ report collector; its full native acceptance is pending on the CI toolchains described below. Native Cargo workspace ownership is distinct from separate Oyzu target groups. Captured builds require Docker and this explicitly provisioned Linux amd64 image: Run the following from the repository root: the image build copies Cargo.toml, Cargo.lock and src/ to compile its worker. The repository provisioning script uses the same root build context. Host development execution does not use this image. docker build -f tooling/images/rust.Dockerfile -t oyzu-toolchain/rust:1.99.1-nextest0.9.146-llvmcov0.9.1 . The image recipe selects Rust 1.99.1, rustfmt, Clippy, LLVM tools, cargo-nextest 0.9.146, cargo-llvm-cov 0.9.1 and the compiled Oyzu worker at /usr/local/libexec/oyzu/oyzu. Its separate image-build stage compiles that worker with Rust 1.99.1; Python is not installed. Custom --image cargo=<image> profiles must supply the same capabilities, including a compatible worker. Rebuild older images before using these plans. Tool/image provisioning is explicit and separate from project execution. Oyzu does not download a missing toolchain image. The updated image recipe has not yet completed isolated-build qualification. Docker dependency contexts use the narrower rust/cargo provider. Its standard Rust 1.94.0 consumer image needs no Python, nextest or llvm-cov. It validates the original lock/workspace and exports only the native registry, without artifact version projection or report setup. The tool requirements above still apply to ordinary rust/app and rust/library builds. The CLI supports Windows, macOS and Linux; that does not imply a native captured-build executor on each host. Current isolated Rust acceptance runs on Linux with Docker. The native artifact probe also runs separately on all three CI hosts. See implementation status for revision-specific evidence.

documents.t: A checked-in Cargo.lock is required. Preparation admits its complete registry inventory before issuing any requests. The current standalone source profile permits crates.io index entries through https://index.crates.io/ and archives through https://static.crates.io/crates/, using the shared host transport and its redirect/size/request limits. A different registry or an unsupported Git host fails explicitly; there is no direct Cargo network fallback. This fixed public profile is not yet enterprise connector routing or private Cargo authentication. Public GitHub sources must carry a full commit identity in Cargo.lock. Native Cargo and Git fetch through repository-scoped broker routes inside a container with networking disabled. The broker admits only smart-HTTP discovery and upload pack requests, with the existing size, redirect and request limits. Cargo checks out the pinned objects and resolves the package graph; OYZU captures the bare object database and reconstructs checkouts privately for offline build actions. This preserves Git repositories containing Unix symlinks on Windows controllers. Git evidence records object identity, not a publisher signature. Private Git, other hosts, submodule routing and Git LFS are not qualified. Private binary packages (publish = false packages that declare any binary target) produce executable artifacts without requiring a publishable .crate archive. A declared binary counts even when its required-features are off, so a private crate whose only binary is feature-gated (a test fixture or development tool) is neither archived nor shipped. Publishable packages retain native Cargo packaging and verification. A publish = false library that declares no binary target is still packaged and verified into a .crate, but Cargo does not register unpublishable packages in its packaging registry, so Oyzu does not promote them for dependents; a package that depends on such a library cannot be archived and fails with Cargo's own message. The archive inventory excludes the same binary-only packages that planning excludes. tooling/test-build-git.py exercises a real dependency from the pinned mise fork, compiles offline, executes the resulting binary and checks the build bundle. The Windows-hosted proof produced the binary and three reports; it is not evidence of the complete CLI platform matrix. Each locked registry package must have a SHA-256 checksum. Acquisition requires matching index metadata and archive bytes, then captures the archive and only the locked version's index entry in Cargo's native local-registry format. If a cached index entry omits a locked version, online preparation fetches that entry once through the approved broker source and checks it again. Offline preparation fails with a hint to rerun online; it never refreshes from the network. Duplicate matching entries and checksum disagreements remain errors. Cargo owns extraction, checksum revalidation, resolution and compilation. No project code runs during host acquisition. This avoids implementing a second Cargo resolver or unpacking untrusted crates on the host. When the lock contains only local workspace packages, preparation writes no registry replacement into the private Cargo home. Locked offline execution still applies. This preserves Cargo's native temporary registry for packaging unpublished workspace dependencies; replacing crates.io with an empty registry prevents that resolution. Single packages with captured registry dependencies retain source replacement. For a workspace combining local path dependencies and registry inputs, the Rust adapter packages acyclic members in dependency order using a private writable copy of the captured registry. Each acyclic member runs native cargo package --locked --offline --allow-dirty --registry crates-io --package <name> with verification enabled. Cargo generates the normalized archive and its temporary registry entry; the adapter checks their planned name/version and matching SHA-256 before admitting them into that private copy for dependent members. It does not generate Cargo index entries or resolve dependency versions. Local ordering uses native manifest paths, including renamed/optional dependencies. Development-cycle groups use the conditional native staging and verification flow described above. Ordinary/build dependency cycles and paths without a workspace owner fail planning explicitly. The original captured registry is immutable. The adapter restores the action's Cargo source configuration and removes its temporary registry on ordinary success or failure; sandbox cleanup owns abrupt termination. Captured packages remain inputs, while only the workspace's planned artifacts can reach dist/. Identity/checksum conflicts, a collision with an already captured name/version, an index over 4 MiB or an archive over 128 MiB fail packaging. Repair the native package input or manifest and rebuild; there is no network fallback. The conditional provisional native command skips verification only while staging an affected development-cycle group; every final member archive must pass native verification and byte comparison before admission. Registry publication restrictions in native manifests still apply to this explicit crates.io packaging profile; private-registry publication remains unfinished. Preparation then checks the original lock using native offline Cargo resolution, projects workspace package versions and contained workspace dependency requirements into private manifests, and regenerates the private lock with Cargo. Source files remain unchanged. Unresolved paths and paths outside the captured target fail preparation. Registry packages keep their locked versions and remain inputs; they do not become this workspace's published artifacts. Prepared input records contain each archive's name, version, digest and size. digest-only verification means matching recorded content, not a publisher signature or release authorization. Dependency edges and per-package purpose distinctions are not yet modeled in this inventory. Acquisition currently requires the approved upstreams to be reachable on each fresh preparation; persistent offline acquisition reuse is not implemented. Once preparation succeeds, build execution reads the captured registry with network access denied. Versions retain each package's base version and use a source-derived suffix, such as 1.2.3-dev.g<source-prefix>. Different workspace packages retain their individual base versions. These are snapshot versions; they do not establish release eligibility or production trust. Build execution runs workspace release compilation, native tests with reporting, Clippy, rustfmt checking, native verified crate packaging and final collection. Commands use locked offline inputs and the shared executor denies networking. Build scripts and proc macros execute inside that environment and must work with the captured inputs. The selected compiler host target, .oyzu-build/target output root, private Cargo home and offline setting are fixed plan facts; a task environment cannot redirect them. The owned command wrapper installs captured source configuration into that private home so Clippy, nextest and coverage subprocesses inherit it. Custom native source overrides are not supported by this public profile and can fail offline resolution; other native Cargo settings remain in the captured project. Tests run through cargo llvm-cov nextest; native JUnit and Cobertura are retained under dist/ and indexed with paths, digests and summaries in dist/manifest.json. Test execution and coverage generation retain independent failure outcomes. Missing or invalid required reports fail collection. inspect dist checks bundle integrity, not release authorization. Cargo doctests run as part of the same implicit test gate because nextest does not execute them. Prepared native Cargo metadata selects workspace packages with a doctest-enabled target, honoring native doctest = false. Each selected package runs cargo test --doc --locked --offline --package <name> in the captured workspace. Binary-only targets and registry dependencies do not create doctest invocations. Preparation layout version 5 retains the native doctest selection and relocatable binary inventory; old prepared metadata must be regenerated. The additional required doctest.xml report has one case per Cargo invocation, identified by package name, with bounded native diagnostics. Its suite properties explicitly describe this scope. Counts are invocation outcomes, not the number of individual documentation examples: a doctest-enabled package with no examples can have a successful invocation. Stable Cargo owns assertion semantics; Oyzu does not parse human console text into invented case counts. Native nonzero exits produce failures; launch errors produce errors. Native doctest stdout and stderr stream through the host executor while the report retains bounded diagnostic prefixes. Compilation and doctest execution have no separate per-package timer; any enclosing executor deadline still applies. Other selected packages still run after a package fails. Each invocation starts with fresh report output; prior success cannot satisfy a failed launch. Doctest failures block artifact collection even if nextest and coverage generation succeed. Inspect the named report and native diagnostics to repair the example, compilation or provisioned rustdoc/linker environment, then rebuild. Task replacement retains this additional report obligation. The existing coverage report measures nextest execution only: doctest coverage and individual doctest JUnit cases remain unfinished, as do every custom nextest configuration and broader framework support. Compilation, tests, lint, formatting and archive verification are required gates. Their failures block final artifacts. Native logs and available reports explain the failed stage. Repair the native input and rerun; an earlier successful bundle is retained under .oyzu/history, not reused as this build's successful output.

oyzu run test produces nextest JUnit, native LLVM Cobertura coverage and Cargo doctest invocation reports, followed by oyzu inspect dist. The real app/workspace reporting step passed on Windows MSVC, Linux and macOS in run 37049720609 at bfa2b7c. This verifies the direct reporting step, not the entire still-running workflow. The local Windows GNU Rust 1.94.0 compiler lacks profiler_builtins; its earlier coverage failure remains a toolchain limitation. Provision Rust/Cargo with its llvm-tools-preview component and compiler profiler runtime, cargo-nextest 0.9.146 and cargo-llvm-cov 0.9.1. Existing Windows product qualification uses an MSVC compiler and its native linker/SDK for coverage; the local windows-gnu compiler is not supported by this flow. A separate windows-gnullvm tiny-project coverage experiment succeeded without MSVC; see native build prerequisites for its scope and remaining qualification limits. Dependencies must already be installed for locked offline Cargo resolution. Tools are not installed by the product. Missing LLVM tools fail before llvm-cov can request a download; explicit LLVM_COV/LLVM_PROFDATA paths can identify provisioned binaries. After shared task admission, Cargo's native metadata --no-deps --locked --offline supplies workspace membership and doctest-enabled packages. Static run list never invokes Cargo. The exact implicit cargo test --locked --workspace command receives automatic instrumentation. Arbitrary task replacements retain their bodies and required JUnit/coverage/doctest obligations; they do not waive evidence collection. No Oyzu build/test configuration is needed for the default flow. A temporary nextest profile inherits the project's default configuration and supplies fresh JUnit output; the native .config/nextest.toml is not edited. This uses nextest's native profile inheritance. Project coverage/reporting state is not reused: compilation and coverage use private temporary target directories. Native nextest may retain its ordinary store output on the host. Extra command arguments go to the nextest invocation; doctest selection remains the metadata-selected workspace packages. Alternate nextest profiles, arbitrary Cargo test argument compatibility and filtered doctest selection are not implemented by this initial direct adapter. The compiled Rust adapter is shared by captured and direct execution. It runs nextest, attempts coverage generation independently of a failed test, and runs stable Cargo doctests. Any failed phase fails the task. Doctest reports count package invocations, not individual examples, and doctest execution is not included in nextest coverage. Custom native settings, build scripts and proc macros retain their normal execution semantics. Direct reports disclose host execution and unverified tool identity; Cargo's offline flags are not a host network sandbox. See direct test bundle boundaries. python tooling/test-rust-direct.py --cli <compiled-path> uses EX-021 and EX-022: implicit task listing, default-profile settings, native JUnit/Cobertura, successful and failed tests, independent doctest failure, unchanged source/configuration and bundle inspection. It requires tooling/design-requirements.txt for report-contract validation. CI explicitly provisions the pinned reporters with tooling/provision-rust-reporting.py after downloading the compiled CLI. The three-host direct-reporting steps passed at bfa2b7c; broader native profile and argument combinations remain outside that probe.

Each selected package produces a native <package>-<selected-version>.crate. Each enabled binary additionally produces <binary>-<selected-version>-<compiler-host>. The selected version is normally a projected snapshot; resolved registry backreferences retain the affected member's declared version as described above. Manifest names use the existing scoped crate- and bin- identities. A library-only package has a crate artifact without an invented executable. Duplicate binary names currently fail planning instead of colliding in the output bundle. Cargo's resolved features determine whether a binary with required-features is enabled. An unmet feature gate omits that binary from the artifact plan; enabling the feature through native defaults includes it. No Oyzu-specific switch or new build YAML is needed. This increment does not add a feature matrix or new CLI feature-selection syntax. Cargo documents required-features as native target selection. The build adapter consumes Cargo's JSON compiler messages. It matches opaque package IDs and binary target names against a prepared inventory and takes executable paths from native compiler-artifact events. It accepts fresh Cargo cache results as well as newly compiled binaries, requires a successful native process and build-finished event, rejects missing/unplanned/conflicting outputs and verifies each executable is a regular file contained in the target root. It does not guess executable filenames or publish intermediate test binaries. The adapter clears its reserved staging directory before invoking Cargo. Only after all expected binaries are verified does it stage them for the shared final collection step. This prevents a previous executable from satisfying a disabled feature or failed compilation. Native source archive contents are checked in the scenario harness to exclude private .oyzu-build files. Cargo does not automatically exclude arbitrary custom output directories; the captured profile fixes its private output location. Exhaustive custom Cargo include/exclude packaging behavior remains unverified. Task overrides and pre/post hooks retain their existing shared owners. Replacing a native build task must still satisfy its planned artifact obligations; an override does not waive collection checks. No registry publication, signing or promotion is performed by this builder increment.

python tooling/test-rust-artifacts.py --cli <compiled-oyzu> --cargo <provisioned-cargo> python tooling/test-rust-doctests.py --cli <compiled-oyzu> --cargo <provisioned-cargo> python tooling/test-rust-packaging.py --cli <compiled-oyzu> --cargo <provisioned-cargo> These Python programs are repository test harnesses, not shipped runtime adapters. They invoke the compiled CLI; --cli defaults to target/release/oyzu (with .exe on Windows). Historical results below predate the compiled migration; current qualification is recorded in implementation status. The artifact probe checks gated binaries disabled/enabled by Cargo defaults, exact executable bytes, launching collected executables, fresh cache results, source archive exclusions, missing outputs, redirected output paths and compiler failures. The Rust example variants supply the native inputs. Rust planner checks cover per-package versions, feature resolution and fixed output facts. The doctest probe runs real stable Cargo against a local workspace, checking successful examples, assertion/compile failures, independent package outcomes, missing-tool stale-report replacement and unchanged inputs. Its --cargo option accepts a command on PATH or an executable path; relative paths are anchored before changing into the fixture, and symlinks retain the Cargo invocation name required by rustup. Unix probes additionally execute through a temporary Cargo symlink. Windows verification passed with Rust 1.94.0; the local GNU toolchain required its provisioned linker setting in RUSTDOCFLAGS as well as RUSTFLAGS. Run 36971869232 passed all three CLI jobs, including the corrected native doctest probe and local-workspace packaging test. The captured Linux suite requires failed doctests to block artifacts despite successful nextest results; isolated doctest acceptance is still pending. The Rust test suite also gives native Cargo a fresh home and an acquired fixture registry, then runs tests, Clippy and verified packaging offline. It checks unchanged source lock bytes and rejection of corrupted archives from a fresh cache. Acquisition checks reject unsupported sources before fetching and mismatched index/archive checksums. The mixed-packaging probe uses native Cargo to create a registry fixture, then packages a three-member snapshot workspace against it with no downloads. It checks archive contents, locked external dependencies, repeatability, source/registry/configuration preservation, rejected index tampering and failures during native verification. GitHub Actions runs it on each CLI host. The checked-in EX-022 registry variation additionally exercises the captured CLI build, reports, delivered binary and failure-gated collection; passing the host probe alone does not prove that isolated scenario. The compiled-CLI Linux scenario suite additionally builds applications, libraries and local workspaces, executes delivered binaries, checks snapshot crate contents, measures application coverage, verifies repeatability and confirms failed tests/formatting block collection. The registry example adds a locked public dependency with no Oyzu configuration; its CI checks require retained dependency identity, versioned outputs, JUnit/coverage, unchanged inputs and rejection of a modified lock checksum. New registry and feature-gate scenarios must pass that suite before being described as verified captured behavior. Native host checks alone do not prove isolated build acceptance. Remaining work includes private/alternate Cargo registries, private Git sources and credentials, persistent acquisition reuse, full feature/profile/platform matrices, doctest coverage/individual-case reporting and broader test-framework support, custom task artifact production, release policy, publication, remote caching and complete authored-scenario acceptance. The build goal remains broader than this implementation increment. Native binary capture now identifies a planned binary by its target-relative Cargo manifest path and target name. This preserves ownership when a prepared target rooted at /workspace executes under /workspace/<target> in a mixed repository. Cargo package IDs remain opaque; Oyzu does not rewrite or parse them. The change fixes the nested-target failure observed by the live logging acceptance probe. The sole version-1 inventory records relative manifest paths; the superseded package-ID inventory reader has been removed.

Explicit artifact platforms select the local Linux cross-compilation image. The six supported selections are linux/amd64, linux/arm64, darwin/amd64, darwin/arm64, windows/amd64 and windows/arm64. The curated native baselines are musl for Linux, Apple Darwin with a macOS 13 deployment target, and LLVM MinGW for Windows. These baselines remain experimental until the real CLI flow has passed; they do not establish older operating-system compatibility. After building the standard reporting image above, provision the cross worker: docker build -f tooling/images/rust-cross.Dockerfile -t oyzu-toolchain/rust-cross:v1 . This is local environment setup. The build command uses that image automatically for explicit platforms; a missing image fails with a provisioning diagnostic. The image contains the native cross linkers and SDK prerequisites, while the project's locked compiler and target standard libraries are restored separately. The compiler must be declared in oyzu.toml and installed into oyzu.lock. oyzu install on Windows also provisions the local Linux compiler distribution when the project declares a Rust build. The worker uses the embedded mise library; no separate mise executable is invoked. Within one build, equivalent locked selections share compiler verification. The verified archive is extracted once per archive digest and worker image into a build-owned Linux volume, mounted read-only for preparation and execution. Each mount checks its archive digest; Cargo homes, outputs and workspaces remain private. Normal build completion or failure releases the volume; the persistent oyzu-tools-* volumes are reused by identity and superseded ones are pruned (see build logging). Execution runs without network access. The complete project entry point remains oyzu build, with platforms and builder options in build.yaml. Explicit cross-platform Rust actions currently reserve 8 GiB and allow up to two hours per action. The executor caps target concurrency using Docker's available memory, retaining 25% for engine/controller headroom; a Docker engine needs about 11 GiB to admit one such action. These are builder-declared execution resources recorded in the plan, not additional project flags. Locked compiler preparation reserves 4 GiB. The CLI project's native Cargo test profile retains line-level debug information instead of full type debug data, reducing linker pressure from the embedded mise dependency graph. Coverage instrumentation and required test/report gates remain enabled. An earlier cold self-build exceeded a one-hour test-action limit while linking and starting tests; that failed run is not a successful build. Tests and coverage execute on the Linux worker. Cross-compiled executables are checked for the requested binary format and architecture before collection; this is compilation evidence, not a claim that tests ran on each target OS. macOS and ARM runtime qualification remain separate. Rust uses a private Linux scratch filesystem for Cargo extraction and Git checkouts. It keeps a 2 GiB minimum size ceiling and grows to match larger action memory reservations; the reservation itself does not increase. Where cgroups are available, their limit covers process and tmpfs use together. Git acquisition copies back only the bare object databases, keeping registry extraction and upstream symlinks off Windows host mounts. This accommodates the CLI's measured 1.27 GiB of unpacked locked registry inputs without imposing a smaller fixed scratch ceiling. Captured build inputs and execution workspaces live under the repository's .oyzu state directory, on the same volume as the project, rather than filling the operating system's temporary volume. They remain private run state and are excluded from source snapshots and published bundles. Formatting uses the same read-only locked compiler mount as compilation, tests and lint; it never adds Cargo feature-selection arguments to cargo fmt. Shared compiler restoration is automatic and does not add build YAML options. Reuse is scoped to one invocation; it does not deduplicate target metadata, crate acquisition or complete preparation, and does not provide a persistent compiler cache.

Build manifests now include oyzu.dev/tool-requirements for selected Rust targets. The static detector reads literal package.rust-version and Rust toolchain channel constraints with source digests and field locations, in every toolchain-file form rustup accepts (details). It reports compiler components, platform standard libraries, and selected formatting, lint and test requirements. Fast builds omit unselected quality helpers; explicit toolchain components remain requirements. Inherited Cargo MSRV currently requires workspace metadata and fails with an explicit diagnostic rather than being ignored. These records are discovery evidence only. Automatic resolution/provisioning and oyzu pin are still being connected; a reported requirement is not proof that the tool is installed. Test helpers currently remain supplied by the provisioned worker.

oyzu run list discovers Rust install and fetch tasks without running Cargo. For a single Rust target, oyzu run install runs cargo install --path . --locked in that target's directory. With several targets, qualify the task, for example oyzu run cli:install. Explicit task overrides retain their existing precedence. This replaces the previous misleading install mapping to dependency fetching; use oyzu run fetch for cargo fetch --locked. oyzu run install -- --root /path/to/bootstrap --force oyzu run fetch -- --offline Trailing arguments are forwarded as argv to Cargo. Installation uses Cargo's release profile by default; Cargo chooses package binaries and reports native errors for packages without installable binaries or virtual workspace roots. Use --bin to select a binary, and --force explicitly when replacement is wanted. --root and CARGO_INSTALL_ROOT choose the installation root; otherwise Cargo's configured/default destination applies. Its bin directory must be on PATH. Cargo and native build prerequisites must already be usable under Oyzu's existing tool-installation policy. A lock selects dependencies but does not make Cargo offline: forward --offline when caches suffice. Native output and failures use the existing task output/JSON contracts. oyzu install still provisions development tools. oyzu build does not execute this installation task unless explicitly connected by authored task dependencies or hooks. This is not a substitute for required build/report gates or publication eligibility. The inferred Windows Oyzu self-install with an explicit root uses staged bootstrap replacement: the current binary remains available during compilation, and successful results replace it while preserving an adjacent backup. Generic Cargo installations keep native behavior.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/target-workspaces.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Native oyzu build prepares a separate source workspace per selected target before native dependency preparation.
