Target hooks and stages share that target workspace; ordering dependencies do not expose another target's generated files. Direct oyzu run tasks retain their intentional checkout behavior. This is workspace separation, not enforced filesystem or network sandboxing. Host processes retain ambient host access. This behavior does not establish production publication eligibility.
documents.s: Host target workspaces and artifact inputs

documents.t: Named builds require explicit source inputs only for their selected targets and required dependencies, including task prerequisites and hooks. A missing prepared input belonging to an unselected target does not block the build or its read-only preview. For example, oyzu build cli needs no prepared docs input; oyzu build docs and an all-target build still require it. Missing inputs of a selected target or dependency fail before native execution. Affected selection observes inputs across the workspace to determine which targets changed. Captured source retains available authored inputs for prerequisites discovered during native preparation, such as archive hooks; their inputs become required when that target joins the selection. Existing snapshot boundary and link restrictions still apply to those retained inputs. The target's source directory is captured with current edits and eligible untracked files using the existing snapshot exclusions (including .git, .oyzu, dist, target, node_modules and virtual environments). Native project ownership still belongs to discovery. Files outside the target directory require explicit source inputs when not already part of that native ownership unit: builds: api: uses: node/app path: api inputs: [../../shared/schemas] inputs is a list of literal file/directory paths relative to the declaring build.yaml, not the target's path. Paths must resolve within the enclosing Git repository. Without a Git repository, the selected build root is the boundary. Absolute paths and boundary escapes fail. On the captured execution path the captured source is the boundary: an input must stay under the directory holding build.yaml and name at least one captured file, and it joins the target's action-cache scope and stage contracts (declared inputs). Snapshot link/reparse restrictions remain in force. Captures preserve repository-relative layout; each target receives its own copies. Additional source contents participate in recorded source-projection identity. This does not enable host action-result caching. Generated outputs from another build must use artifact relationships, not source inputs. A snapshot detects changes while copying individual files; it is not an atomic repository-wide snapshot. Unsupported native inputs fail through their native tools; arbitrary script dependencies are not automatically inferred. Source capture caches directory ignore decisions within one invocation; explicit inputs and mandatory metadata/repository exclusions keep their existing rules. Host workspace refresh walks each target's known source/input roots directly, without a preliminary whole-repository inventory for that target. It still hashes every admitted source file on each build. Files whose size, modification time and read-only state match the retained private copy are not rewritten; other files are copied again, and stale generated files are removed. This reduces preparation work on repeated builds without depending on Git's tracked-file list. Refresh uses a nonfollowing source-file handle for live metadata, hashing and the post-read change check, avoiding a separate path-based file metadata open. For Oyzu's own checkout, keep the source revision current when testing this behavior: a successful self-build promotes that checkout's compiled executables back into .oyzu/bin, including artifacts restored from cache. Replacing only the launcher cannot keep a fix absent from the sources being built. See local executable promotion. Temporary source captures and complete admitted-source copies used by dependency preparation preserve modification times and do not flush each file to durable storage. Complete copies keep already-admitted inputs without reapplying ignores. Content hashing, change detection and independent copies remain required. Prepared dependency/output snapshots and final bundle/store publication retain their durability boundaries. Completed prepared trees are inspected directly when only their validated identity is needed; no discarded duplicate is created for that observation.

builds: server: uses: rust/app path: server consumer: uses: node/app path: consumer materialize: - from: server to: inputs/server - from: server into: inputs/original from selects a producer. Optional artifact selects its logical output name; omission requires an unambiguous primary artifact. Exactly one destination is required: to: exact destination for a file, or contents-under-destination for a directory. into: destination directory for a file, preserving its exported basename. When the producer fixes the file name only as it runs (a native wheel), the collected name is used, not the planned one; see file name discovery. Directory artifacts use to. Optional runtime names a provisioned local image that must accept native files (such as a Python wheel) for this input; see native wheels. It is valid only with usage: runtime, the image must match the consumer's platform, and it is never pulled. Destinations are relative to the consumer target. No implicit archive extraction, source overwrite, overlapping destination, or scraping of old output trees is allowed. Producer platform compatibility and artifact identity are validated. materialize establishes ordering automatically; do not repeat depends_on. Native metadata and dependency preparation still precede action execution. Inputs that generate a consumer manifest or are needed by npm ci during preparation are not supported by this slice; handoff occurs before the consumer's first action. Artifacts are collected once all required producer actions and report obligations succeed, before its consumers run. Each consumer receives an independent copy verified against the collected digest. The manifest records handoff receipts. A failed producer blocks dependents; successful independent artifacts can remain in a failed bundle, without making that bundle successful. The producer's pre_build, build and post_build actions share its private tree. Post-hook changes to declared output are included in the artifact handed to the consumer. A failure in any of those actions prevents producer artifact publication, even if the build already wrote output files. Native failure diagnostics remain in the failed bundle; fixing the hook or command and rebuilding starts with a fresh private source tree. This is not a guarantee that post-hooks run on cancellation. A host-built (native local) Python output is a wheel directory named primary, so use to for it. A python/package target built in a worker image (--image pip=<image>) exports file outputs named wheel and sdist; select one with artifact: wheel and into. Typed image bindings remain separate work. Host-coordinated image execution is described below.

The experimental host coordinator admits docker/image alongside supported native targets. It reuses the existing captured Docker metadata and rootless BuildKit executor; ordinary host targets still run as host processes. Docker is required only when an image target is selected. No build container receives the host Docker socket, and no nested Docker daemon is started. Provision the existing worker image explicitly from this repository: docker build -f tooling/images/docker-metadata.Dockerfile -t oyzu-toolchain/docker:buildkit0.25.0 . Image bases must already be available to the provisioned Docker daemon. Preparation captures their identities; worker actions remain offline. This does not install Docker or change host security settings. Existing docker.apparmorProfile configuration and executor enforcement still apply. Explicit tool pins must be satisfied by their supported executor contract; an image tag does not verify pins. An intended Linux producer/consumer flow is: builds: package: uses: python/package path: package image: uses: docker/image path: image materialize: - from: package to: payload oyzu build image --plan includes the producer, artifact edge and each target's executor without contacting Docker. oyzu build image runs that graph. The image's Dockerfile can use COPY payload/ /wheels/ without predicting a versioned wheel filename. This assembles a wheel payload; installing it into an application runtime is a separate Dockerfile responsibility. Native source selection and Dockerignore filtering apply to the image's context; materialized artifacts are explicitly added. Additional source files outside that context do not become Docker COPY inputs. Artifact compatibility is separate from producer execution provenance. Captured matrix expansion selects the declared producer variant matching each consumer platform; it does not select by filename or matrix enumeration order. Host Python wheel directories are inspected after collection: every wheel must report pure Python and none-any tags before the directory is admitted across platforms. Python tags remain in evidence; the image's package manager must check interpreter and other runtime requirements. A host-built wheel whose tags all name one Linux x86_64 or aarch64 platform (linux_*, manylinux*, musllinux_*) is recorded as native and is consumed only as described under native wheels. Any other native wheel tags (for example Windows or macOS) remain unqualified and fail runtime handoff, including on the same OS. Platform-independent sharing of native wheels through captured matrix expansion is not implemented. Plain native builds still select host producer outputs. For a native binary matrix feeding a foreign-platform image, use --all-platforms; the CLI does not automatically switch that producer to a cross-compilation executor. materialize.usage defaults to runtime. Explicit usage: data permits deliberate inclusion without claiming runtime compatibility. It still requires a unique logical output, successful producer, verified bytes and safe placement. Data edges do not propagate consumer platform requirements into producers; ambiguous matrix outputs still fail. to and into retain their existing placement semantics. Artifacts carry extensions.oyzu.dev/artifact-compatibility: target records the resolved artifact platform, pending requires builder inspection before use, independent retains native runtime tags, native binds package files to one platform plus the builder that verifies them against the consumer runtime, and unknown explains absent qualification. Bindings/receipts record oyzu.dev/artifact-consumer platform and usage. Pending or unknown artifacts cannot satisfy runtime consumption. This extends the existing version-1 contracts; it does not certify arbitrary binaries or runtime ABIs.

A native wheel is accepted only after the consumer runtime check. For generic linux_x86_64 and linux_aarch64 wheels, Oyzu inspects ELF .so dependencies in the wheel and probes the exact consumer image's Python process. A positively identified glibc/musl mismatch is refused before the consumer image build, naming the wheel, ELF member, linkage and consumer image. If linkage or consumer libc is inconclusive, the check reports NATIVE_WHEEL_LIBC_UNVERIFIED and continues to pip. This includes wheels with no identifiable libc dependency and wheels with other unidentified .so members. A missing Python runtime remains an error. UNVERIFIED means Oyzu has no libc conclusion. Separately, for generic Linux wheels with a recognized interpreter-specific *.cpython-<version>-<platform>.so member, Oyzu compares that filename suffix with importlib.machinery.EXTENSION_SUFFIXES from the exact consumer Python. When its CPython-specific suffix is absent, or the consumer cannot report those suffixes, Oyzu emits NATIVE_WHEEL_EXTENSION_SUFFIX_UNVERIFIED in human and JSON diagnostics, naming the wheel, member, observed suffix and consumer. Pip still decides wheel tags and ABI, and a warning does not block the build. A plain .so or .abi3.so does not trigger this specific comparison. The member may be a helper or data library, so this check does not claim that every .so is a required import module. A warning calls for checking the module import in the final image and, if it fails, building the wheel with that consumer's Python and native toolchain. For manylinux* and musllinux_* tags, pip retains its existing decision without the extra ELF or suffix checks. Pure *-none-any wheels keep their independent handoff. Before a native wheel enters the consumer workspace, Oyzu runs pip install --dry-run --no-index --no-deps for it in that image with networking disabled. Pip decides whether the interpreter version, ABI and wheel tag fit; the extra refusal handles only positively identified libc mismatches for generic Linux tags. The suffix comparison is diagnostic only. The runtime image is, in order: the input's explicit runtime: <image> (a provisioned local image; it overrides the captured base and must match the consumer platform), else the consumer's captured pip dependency base (a requirements.txt consumed from the pinned base image; see Docker images). materialize: - from: package to: inputs runtime: registry.example/python:3.12-slim # only needed without a pip base A consumer with neither (for example a plain COPY into scratch) cannot receive a native wheel; usage: data still includes it without a runtime claim. A rejection fails the consumer with the wheel name, the image reference and either the linkage mismatch or pip's message. The human summary shows it as an ERROR line (terminal controls escaped, line breaks kept); --json carries it in diagnostics, and the action log keeps the full text. Wheel classification covers Linux wheels whose tags all name x86_64 or aarch64 (linux_*, manylinux*, musllinux_*), including abi3 wheels. The proof shows version-specific tags (cp313-cp313-linux_x86_64) accepted only by the matching Python and an abi3 wheel accepted by both Python 3.12 and 3.13. Because pip is the authority, Python versions need no Oyzu list. Not covered: a Linux arm64 consumer (classification is unit-tested; no arm64 build or execution was available), broader libc version and transitive library checks, and Windows/macOS tags, which stay unknown and are refused. These and the Windows/macOS host qualification are tracked in implementation status. Qualification: python tooling/test-native-wheel-abi.py --cli <compiled-oyzu> (needs Docker, a host C compiler and oyzu-fixture/python-abi:<version> images; the script header describes them). The producer's CPython is pinned with .python-version; Oyzu provisions it. These host-built cases need a Linux host: a Windows or macOS host builds win_*/macosx_* wheels, which stay unknown and are refused by a Linux consumer.
documents.s: Native wheels and the consumer runtime

documents.t: A Linux native wheel can be produced from any host with Docker by building it in a worker image: oyzu build --image pip=<image>, where the image is a Python image with a C compiler (not a -slim image) and the Oyzu worker at /usr/local/libexec/oyzu/oyzu. The wheel's tag comes from that image's interpreter, for example cp313-cp313-linux_x86_64. Collection finds it (below), reads its tags from the wheel's own WHEEL metadata and records native compatibility for the image's platform, so the consumer check above applies unchanged. The case is tooling/test-native-wheel-abi.py --worker-image <image>; on Windows add --captured-only to skip the host-built cases.
documents.s: Wheels built in a worker image

documents.t: A planned file output has an exact name and collection requires that file. The one exception is a builder-declared discovery, used when the name cannot be known until the build has run: It is consulted only when no file exists at the planned path, so an output that exists under its planned name, such as a pure py3-none-any wheel, is collected exactly as before and never reinterpreted. Python implements it for the wheel output of python/package: the single regular file {name}-{version}-*.whl next to the planned file. No match keeps the original missing bundle path failure; more than one match fails and names them. sdist, applications and other builders have no discovery. The result is a file name in the planned directory, never a path; symlinks are ignored and the usual containment, regular-file, digest and size checks still apply. The bundle's artifact record carries the file actually collected, and compatibility is inspected from that file's metadata, not from its name. The frozen plan, --plan output and plan digest keep the planned name (py3-none-any), so the planned and collected names can differ for a native wheel. materialize with into writes the consumer's file under the collected name; the receipt records where it was written. to names an exact file and therefore cannot address a name that is only known after the build; use into for a discovered file. Collisions with the collected name are detected when the file is written, not at planning, and an existing file is never overwritten. Limits: the lookup also applies to a legacy setup.py wheel whose planned tag is absent, so a mismatched tag there is collected and classified from its metadata rather than failing. The Windows/macOS wheel tags are not classified (below). Named image platform lists must include the resolved worker platform for this path; use the existing --all-platforms captured path for matrix execution. Worker task replacements and pre/post hooks run through the shared task executor and retain report obligations. Hooks share the private target workspace. Docker context membership is frozen during preparation: hooks may modify admitted files, but newly generated undeclared files do not automatically enter the context. --isolated continues to select the captured build path for the whole graph. Fast builds assemble and verify the OCI image without selecting optional checks. --full adds the existing image assertions, lint and formatting stages, with reports collected through the shared owner. Image content and platform integrity are always verified before publication, including fast builds. The bundle records worker image identity, dependency evidence and per-action enforcement; this does not imply that host producer actions were sandboxed or establish production publication eligibility. Windows image-only fast/full flows have passed. The Windows Python-to-Linux runtime fixture installs/imports the wheel in Linux and verifies exact materialized bytes. Failed-producer blocking, unknown native-wheel rejection and explicit data-only inclusion also passed. See the three-platform Rust-to-image proof, which independently exports Linux amd64, Linux arm64 and Windows amd64 binaries and executes only the matching Linux amd64 binary in its consumer image, in the qualification record.

During an executing build, Windows Ctrl+C or Unix SIGINT/SIGTERM requests coordinated cancellation. Oyzu stops admitting actions, terminates owned native process groups/trees or removes active named workers, retains available logs and a failed bundle, blocks pending dependents, and returns exit code 130. Normal private workspace cleanup then runs. Windows console, Linux SIGINT and Windows-coordinated image-worker flows are verified. Post-hooks are not guaranteed to run. Forced termination (SIGKILL), deliberately detached descendants, every acquisition phase and macOS runtime behavior are not qualified. Inspect remaining processes and build-owned storage after an unhandled termination; do not assume cleanup. oyzu build --plan shows declared shared source inputs and artifact relationships without tool installation, copying source, or running a build. Physical artifact selection and source admission are verified during preparation. Private trees use .oyzu/host-workspaces under the existing build transaction lock. They persist between builds as exact source copies: each build refreshes them in place, rewriting only files whose bytes changed and removing anything outside the selection, and at the end of a build removes what the build generated inside them. On Windows this avoids re-creating every source file per build, which on-access scanning made the slowest preparation step (about 46 seconds for this repository's 2,600-file CLI projection). Interrupted builds leave state that the next build reconciles under that same lock. Native Rust compiler caches remain in the original target's .oyzu/native/rust store with existing budget controls. Copies preserve modification times and use stable paths for repeat builds. Tool stores and native download caches remain shared. This does not promise unchanged cache keys after target selection or source layout changes. Offline runs still require tools and native dependencies already available. Fix an invalid input path, artifact selector, collision or failed native command, then rebuild. No manual copying into a consumer is required. Private workspace cleanup does not remove finalized bundles, tools, or compiler caches.

tooling/test-host-workspaces.py --cli <compiled-oyzu> exercises real host producer/consumer builds, shared parent inputs, edits, verified handoff, clean checkout behavior, preview, hook continuity, pre/build/post failure blocking, diagnostic retention, recovery and cleanup. Qualification results are recorded in implementation status. Linux/macOS runtime qualification and enforced sandboxing are not implied by Windows checks.

An explicitly selected python/package output named wheel can bind one producer to multiple consumer platforms when the producer declares no platform matrix. Collection inspects the actual wheel before runtime consumption; pure Python platform-independent wheels can be shared. Explicit producer platforms remain authoritative. A Linux native wheel is native and is accepted only after pip accepts it in the consumer runtime (native wheels); unknown wheel compatibility (for example Windows or macOS tags) still fails closed. A wheel built in a worker image keeps its real file name through discovery. materialize.usage: build selects compatibility against the execution platform, while the default runtime uses the consumer artifact platform and data carries no executable compatibility claim. The current build-tool path requires an unambiguous producer; selection from a multi-variant generator matrix remains unfinished. Its end-to-end qualification passed on Linux amd64 (2026-10-07): an amd64 generator ran on the executor and a linux/arm64 consumer built from its output. Rust recipe lookup selects the smallest pinned recipe that contains the requested components and still fails with TOOL_LOCK_AMBIGUOUS for incomparable recipes; a cross target's request includes its target-platform standard library. Windows, macOS and other Docker versions are not qualified. See the qualification record for measured portable-wheel and worker-hook results and remaining limitations.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-commands.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Status: implemented for the tools Oyzu admits today; the design is the accepted OEP-0021 tool commands proposal (design accepted 2026-10-07; implementation experimental). Syntax, error codes and the choices listed under accepted choices may still change. Platforms: developed and verified on Linux x86-64 only; Windows and macOS are unverified (see verification). These commands change what a scope requires ([tools] in configuration) and what it has locked (oyzu.lock) together, and inspect the result. They use the existing providers: node, go, python, java, maven, gradle, helm, kubectl, k3d, liquibase, tailscale, npm, pnpm, rust, the Cargo helpers cargo-nextest and cargo-llvm-cov, and, experimentally, registry packages written aqua:<owner>/<repo> (see the aqua: backend) or github:<owner>/<repo> (see the github: backend). No account is needed. oyzu install go@1.26 # this project: declare, lock, install oyzu install -g node@22 # your user configuration, all projects oyzu install go # declared: ensure installed; undeclared: go@latest oyzu update go # newer version within the requirement; config untouched oyzu uninstall go # remove the project declaration and lock entry oyzu tools current # what is in effect here oyzu tools list # what is in the store, and what references it oyzu tools versions go # what could be installed oyzu tools info go # provider, verification, eligibility
documents.s: Tool commands: install, update, uninstall and inspection

documents.t: oyzu pin kubectl@1.34 helm@3.22.0 edits the project's [tools] requests and locks their exact archives for the configured platforms in one transaction. All archive providers use this path, including Python, Maven, Gradle, npm and pnpm. --dry-run previews the result without writing. Explicit specs cannot be combined with --refresh or --offline; bare oyzu pin retains discovery-driven pinning, refresh and offline behavior. Normal configuration precedence and policy still apply, and overridden requests fail without changing files. The result uses the shared declaration presentation: requested/selected versions, covered and unavailable platforms, configuration path and lock path. oyzu --json pin kubectl@1.34 helm@3.22.0 returns the same facts with status: "pinned". Pinning does not install payloads or prepare shims. Publisher metadata acquisition may verify archive bytes where its checksum format requires conversion; indexed pinning reads the index/catalog only (Rust also reads the approved manifest). Run oyzu install --frozen afterward to install. The defaults include linux/arm64/gnu; locks can carry it on any host. An unavailable provider/platform is omitted and reported. macOS amd64 and musl are not added to installation support. See implementation status for explicit-spec and ARM64 verification results.

Flag Configuration written Lock none, inside a project project oyzu.toml (created if absent) project oyzu.lock -g, --global the user configuration file (OYZU_USER_CONFIG or the native location) the oyzu.lock beside it --local oyzu.local.toml project oyzu.lock --profile NAME (global option) that profile's [profiles.NAME.tools] as above A project is --root, or the workspace root when it holds oyzu.toml, oyzu.local.toml, build.yaml or a Git marker. Outside a project, a command without -g fails with TOOL_NO_PROJECT and writes nothing; it never guesses. --global and --local conflict. A command acts on the selected scope only and prints a note when the same tool is declared elsewhere. -g ignores project files entirely, including when run inside a project.

install with no arguments installs everything declared in the effective configuration (--frozen, --offline, --update). oyzu install --global installs the global selection independently of the current project, using the user configuration and its sibling oyzu.lock. It accepts the same frozen, offline, update and store controls; it never edits project declarations or locks. For example, oyzu install --global --frozen --offline restores a previously locked global selection using locally available installation or acquisition data. Missing locks fail with TOOL_LOCK_MISSING; an offline installation still requires the needed cached data. With specs: A spec is [provider:]name[@version], split at the last @. go@1.26 is a prefix, go@1.26.8 is exact, go@latest is the newest eligible version, and go alone keeps a declared requirement (ensuring it is installed) or takes latest when undeclared. Several specs are applied together or not at all. Naming a tool twice is TOOL_SPEC_INVALID. Configuration stores what you typed ("1.26"); the lock stores the exact version. Core tools (node, go, python, java, maven, gradle, rust) are written under the name you typed; other tools (cargo-nextest) are written under their canonical ID ("cargo:cargo-nextest") so a later alias change cannot alter the file. An existing declaration keeps its spelling. Existing TOOL_ALIAS_UNSUPPORTED and TOOL_ALIAS_AMBIGUOUS behavior is preserved, and an ambiguous bare name fails listing the exact retry spellings. Order of operations: parse specs, evaluate tools.allowed, resolve every platform in the default set (Linux x64, macOS arm64, Windows x64 for archive tools; tools.platforms overrides), install only the host archive, then publish configuration and lock in one journaled transaction. Any failure leaves both files unchanged. Concurrent edits fail with PIN_EDIT_CONFLICT. Declared tools of the same lock that are not yet in the portable lock layer are resolved in the same run, keeping the exact version they already had, and are installed too, so the whole selection remains consistent. Replacing a requirement reports Replaced "1.25" (1.25.9) -> "1.26" (1.26.8) and reuses an installation already in the store. --dry-run resolves (reading publisher catalogs) and reports versions, files and platforms; it downloads no archive and writes nothing. Specs with --frozen, --offline or --update fail with TOOL_FLAGS_CONFLICT before any project, configuration or network access, as do --dry-run and --local without specs. Archive tools and Rust-family tools resolve through different contracts; one command cannot mix them (TOOL_FLAGS_CONFLICT: run two commands). Result (human, then the shape of --json: tools[] with tool, key, request, version, previous, status, platforms, otherScopes; plus configuration, lock, scope, store): ✓ Installed go 1.26.8 Declared "1.26" in ./oyzu.toml (project) Locked in ./oyzu.lock for 3 platforms (darwin/arm64/native, linux/amd64/gnu, windows/amd64/msvc)

install recipe:owner/name@version --artifact-set FILE [--artifact-set-digest sha256:D] supplies the tool from a resolved artifact set instead of a built-in provider, and tools info … --artifact-set shows the same eligibility without side effects. --dry-run reports eligibility only. Details, output and limits are in artifact sets; the flags are provisional, apply to the project scope only (-g/--local fail TOOL_FLAGS_CONFLICT) and the install downloads and verifies the artifact and writes the lock, but does not yet extract or activate a recipe tool. install --frozen replays locked recipe: tools from the lock alone.

update [TOOL...] re-resolves within the existing requirement, locks the result for all platforms, installs the host selection and never edits configuration. No arguments updates every tool of the selected scope. It takes names, not versions. install --update remains as a deprecated alias with its old behavior (all scopes). A tool still missing from the portable layer is migrated, keeping its version. Hand-edited removals are not pruned from the lock.

uninstall TOOL... removes the declaration (comments elsewhere in the file are kept) and every lock record for the tool at the selected scope, in one transaction. Shared payloads are never deleted: they remain in tools list as unreferenced. A tool not declared at that scope fails with TOOL_NOT_DECLARED and names the scope that does declare it. --dry-run writes nothing.

All inspection is read-only, performs no installation, never re-hashes installed payloads (installs are verified once, then trusted) and prints the store path. tools current [-g] [--all] [--details]: one row per effective tool with the requested and selected versions, scope and status. --global shows only global declarations; --all adds declarations a more specific scope overrides. Statuses: ok, not installed (locked but absent from the store), blocked (tools.allowed, naming the rule), stale lock (no lock, no matching entry, or no entry for this platform or provider), ambiguous (conflicting lock records or names), and deprecated (reserved; no provider reports it yet). tools list: installations in the store with size and what references each: global (the user lock), project (this project's lock) or unreferenced. Other projects are not indexed, so an installation reported unreferenced may be used elsewhere. tools versions TOOL: selectable versions, newest first, from the publisher's catalog, or from the tool index when one is configured and lists the package (which also works offline from its cached copy). Otherwise requires network (TOOL_OFFLINE with --offline). Pre-release, snapshot and nightly versions are not offered by the adapters, so excluded is always empty today; a tool blocked by tools.allowed reports why. Rust and Cargo helpers have no catalog (TOOL_VERSIONS_UNSUPPORTED). tools info TOOL: provider, accepted names, commands, platforms, verification, eligibility, declarations by scope and current state. tools check --catalog and tools migrate [--write]: check declarations against the tool index, and move mise.toml tools and aqua: ids to Oyzu names; see the tool index reference.

Code Meaning TOOL_SPEC_INVALID Unparseable spec, empty version, duplicate tool TOOL_NO_PROJECT Project scope outside a project; use --global TOOL_NOT_DECLARED uninstall/update of a tool the scope does not declare TOOL_FLAGS_CONFLICT Specs with --frozen/--offline/--update; spec-only flags without specs; mixed resolution contracts; a declaration overridden in this invocation CONFIG_OVERRIDE_DENIED tools.allowed excludes the tool; names the rule, nothing written TOOL_ALIAS_*, TOOL_LOCK_*, PIN_EDIT_CONFLICT Existing codes, unchanged An interrupted configuration/lock publication is recovered before reading configuration when retrying oyzu install, oyzu update or oyzu uninstall. Install recovery precedes configuration preflight and artifact-set replay, including plain, --frozen, --offline, spec and artifact-set forms. Offline configuration reads also use the offline session policy. oyzu pin also recovers it. Read-only commands report PIN_RECOVERY_REQUIRED with the affected directory and a recovery command. Unexpected external edits stop recovery with PIN_EDIT_CONFLICT; the journal remains for investigation. Configuration and lock readers capture one consistent pair under the shared edit lock, then release it before acquiring or launching tools. A concurrent first edit or a change while capturing additional targets reports CONFIG_EDIT_CONFLICT; retry the command. Recipe-staleness errors identify the actual tool, version and lock path. Use oyzu pin --refresh to refresh recipes while retaining selected versions, then oyzu install to materialize them. Tool-preparation failures identify the tool, requested or pinned version, store path and recovery command. Windows paths in these diagnostics use the plain C:\... or \\server\share\... form in both human and JSON output; the extended \\?\ prefix remains an internal filesystem detail. Unix diagnostic paths are unchanged.

Recorded in the proposal's decision record (accepted 2026-10-07): no provider prefix beyond canonical IDs; core tools stored as typed; no allow-list patterns; no prerelease flag; tools versions has no offline source; no project index; bare oyzu tools unchanged. A platform for which the provider publishes no artifact for the requested version is omitted from the lock and reported as unavailable (a warning in the human view, unavailablePlatforms in --json). The other platforms lock and the host installs normally; selecting the unavailable platform fails. Example: oyzu install node@14 locks Linux and Windows only, because Node 14 has no macOS arm64 build. This applies when a tool is first declared or re-declared with a new request, and only for the Node, Go and JDK catalogs; an update re-resolves only the platforms already locked, and a tool with no artifact on any platform fails. Any other resolution failure (for example a missing checksum file) still fails the command.

Linux only verified. Mixed archive and Rust-family specs need separate commands. Installing one tool also installs the other declared tools of its lock group. Config and lock publication is journaled, with recovery as described above. Managed (enrolled) mode is rejected as for the other tool commands.
tooling/test-tool-commands.py drives the compiled CLI against real Go and Node downloads; tests/integration/tool_commands.rs covers the no-download cases. See the qualification record.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-management-development.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Node, Go and Rust installation use Oyzu configuration, internal tool mechanics, version-1 locks and the shared installation store. The mise application and fork are not runtime dependencies. Adapted code retains its upstream notices. This remains development functionality, not a distribution-qualified release. All archive providers now share indexed pin/install governance, including npm and pnpm. Native host support includes Linux ARM64 GNU alongside Linux amd64 GNU, macOS arm64 and Windows amd64 MSVC. Node ARM64 archives use the vendor's linux-arm64 spelling. Historical proofs below do not establish native ARM64 qualification. See implementation status for current verification. See provider coverage, indexed Rust and pin declarations. Build with Rust 1.95 or newer using cargo build --locked --bins. A private Oyzu worker installs Rust from frozen inputs; Node and Go use internal metadata and archive mechanics through the acquisition broker. No separate mise executable is used. The provider contract now has an Oyzu-owned identity. Unreleased locks from the retired adapter must be regenerated with oyzu pin --refresh, followed by oyzu install. There is no legacy compatibility reader or receipt relabeling; existing payloads are retained. See provider identity.

Pin output separates managed tool requirements from executor prerequisites. Inventory JSON includes category (managed-tool, executor-prerequisite or constraint); category does not claim provider support or installed availability. Pinning records managed resolutions, not observed machine paths or SDK inventory. Installation remains limited to admitted tool providers and never installs OS components. Native project dependencies retain their native manifest/lock owner. See native build readiness and the design boundary. Native npm execution uses the selected Node installation's bundled npm/npx through Oyzu's verified execution environment. No aube installer or mise application is embedded. Native npm retains its own registry, authentication and cache semantics; Oyzu controls prerequisite selection, execution and evidence. Bundled commands need no separate tool declaration. Explicit npm/pnpm releases use their own providers; selecting npm overrides Node's bundled copy. Python similarly exposes its interpreter aliases and bundled pip through the selected Python, including Windows module-only layouts. Developer commands use the shared composed-PATH lookup, including host commands; controlled builds retain their separate admission rules. Mise's aube-dependent Node workspace task provider is omitted; Oyzu owns its own task discovery and execution.

The shared-store/portable-lock realignment is in progress. Resolution records now contain request facts and recipe roots without scope/profile labels. Rust lookup uses version, execution platform and required components and selects the smallest pinned recipe that contains them; incomparable matching recipes fail with TOOL_LOCK_AMBIGUOUS. A cross target's request includes its target-platform standard library. Configuration continues to own profile and directory precedence. Installation records are also keyed by effective requests, and store leases consume an exact selection digest rather than a directory or profile. Schema version remains 1. Earlier development records containing scope/profile or the obsolete requirements inventory are rejected by the strict decoder rather than silently reused. Regenerate these unreleased locks with the current CLI; retain existing payloads until reuse is verified. User-origin requirements use the lock beside the user configuration file; project-origin requirements use the project lock. An arbitrary invocation directory does not acquire a lock for user defaults. A project overriding one tool retains unrelated user defaults. Configuration chooses the owner before lock matching; owner labels and paths are not persisted in portable records. OYZU_USER_CONFIG can select an absolute user configuration file without changing machine policy locations; see the configuration reference.

oyzu tools list oyzu tools current oyzu tools current --details oyzu tools current --json oyzu which node tools list reads installation receipts in the selected store independently of project configuration. tools current resolves effective configuration and its locks, showing selected versions, missing installations, configuration provenance and component purposes. Both support --details for full locations, identities and cross-compilation targets, --store, and the global --json flag. Inspection does not install tools, update locks or acquire over the network. A nonexistent store remains nonexistent. Human output uses a concise aligned summary with configuration filenames; --details includes full paths. JSON always retains the complete structured records. These inventory commands report stored metadata, not freshly verified payload integrity. which and execution use verified installation selections and can therefore reject an installation whose receipt was visible in inventory. A missing lock is reported as stale lock; stale, ambiguous or incompatible locked selections fail rather than selecting an unrelated installed version. Install the declared selection explicitly to resolve missing payloads. Declaring, updating and removing tools and browsing versions are covered by tool commands, which also defines the current status words (ok, not installed, blocked, deprecated, stale lock, ambiguous); pruning remains separate follow-up work. Successful installation output reports installed or reused for each selected tool, its version and Rust components. Reuse still verifies the selected payload; these result labels do not change lock selection or acquisition. Errors retain their failure exit status and do not produce a successful installation summary. Native installer diagnostics use the shared invocation logger on stderr, including structured records under --json; stdout remains the command result. Use oyzu build --store <path> when building with a store selected by oyzu install --store <path>. Omitting the override always selects the shared user store, not a store remembered from an earlier command. See local builds.

Create oyzu.toml at the workspace root: [tools] node = "22.15.0" [env] APP_MODE = "development" Then run the Oyzu binary: oyzu install oyzu install --frozen oyzu install --frozen --offline oyzu which node oyzu env --json oyzu exec -- node --version oyzu exec -- node -e 'console.log(process.env.APP_MODE)' The shell quoting in the last example is suitable for Bash and PowerShell. -C DIRECTORY, explicit root and profile selection use the existing configuration resolver. Installation supports Node, Go and Rust selections at the workspace root. The Node selector is interpreted by the extracted metadata library against the actual Node catalog. Existing locks retain the exact version unless an update is explicitly requested. If a maintained adapter changes an installation layout (for example, adding the bundled npm entrypoint to Node), ordinary or frozen reuse reports TOOL_LAYOUT_STALE. Run oyzu install --update node to explicitly rebuild the selected layout from verified archive inputs. This uses the normal online update contract: version constraints still apply and metadata refresh requires access. Repinning alone does not replace an existing installation. The replacement is staged and verified before publication; the older installation and its receipt remain intact, including for existing leases. Subsequent selection prefers the currently admitted layout and still verifies its payload. Updating a different tool does not authorize changing Node's layout. Duplicate equally eligible receipts remain an ambiguity error. No schema migration or receipt relabeling is performed. Tool names are resolved locally from the admitted adapter definitions, with upstream alias provenance retained in the extracted registry. Name resolution does not start a backend worker, inspect an installation or access the network. Version/catalog resolution and acquisition still use their existing backend and verification contracts. For the currently admitted backends, node and "oyzu:node" identify the same tool, as do go and "oyzu:go", and rust and "oyzu:rust". Oyzu's own providers were named core:<name> before 2026-10-10; core:node is still accepted as an input alias for oyzu:node (in configuration, commands and route scopes), but the lock and every report use oyzu: ids. Registry packages follow the same rule; see tool ids. Quote canonical TOML keys containing a colon. Changing only between these names preserves the normalized request identity and existing lock; it does not require installation or relocking. Defining both names for one tool fails with TOOL_ALIAS_AMBIGUOUS, even if their versions agree. Unknown registry names fail with TOOL_ALIAS_UNSUPPORTED. This does not enable additional backends or make alias names executable commands: use node, go, cargo, rustc or rustdoc for exec. Selective updates accept the same registry names. Administrative tools.allowed values are compared through that same alias map; this setting remains admin-only. The real acceptance runner is python tooling/test-tool-aliases.py --cli PATH --workspace NODE_ACCEPTANCE_PATH; it reuses the two-version Node workspace above without changing its projects. Add --update for online canonical-name resolution. On a disposable root Linux host only, --disposable-linux-host temporarily creates an administrative policy to check both allowed-name spellings and denial; it refuses an existing policy and removes its own file afterwards. Linux offline replay with networking disabled and the separate online update passed on 2026-10-02. Native CI remains pending. After editing the Node requirement in TOML, run: oyzu install --update node oyzu exec -- node --version For a Node-only project, bare --update and --update oyzu:node select the same root. The command resolves through the Oyzu provider, prints the previous and proposed exact version, installs the result and then commits the lock using the existing compare-and-swap transaction. It never edits TOML. Ordinary install rejects changed requirements with TOOL_LOCK_STALE and an update remedy. --update conflicts with --frozen and --offline; unsupported tool names fail. A failed update leaves the previous lock intact. An unchanged resolution preserves lock bytes. A newly configured Node/Go project can reuse an exact installation even before it has its own installation lock. After backend version resolution, installation looks up the matching user-store receipt before downloading an archive to learn its size. It validates the layout and verifies the payload through the same publication/lease contract, then writes the project's portable lock. Version resolution can still require catalog metadata; this is distinct from downloading or extracting the tool again. Offline/frozen installation still requires pins. Updates operate on effective requests grouped by their configuration-owned lock. Replacing a request set preserves other request sets and platform distributions; conflicting acquisition facts for the same exact identity/platform fail rather than being overwritten. Other projects sharing the store keep their own locks and versions. Publication is atomic per lock owner, not across user and project locks together. Installation prepares the current host selection; it does not materialize every platform recorded in a portable lock. The default store is user-level: %LOCALAPPDATA%/Oyzu/tools on Windows, ~/Library/Application Support/Oyzu/tools on macOS, and ${XDG_DATA_HOME:-~/.local/share}/oyzu/tools on Linux (relative XDG values use the home fallback). On Windows, an absolute HOME different from the native profile selects <HOME>/AppData/Local/Oyzu/tools; unset HOME or use the normal profile to retain the native LocalAppData location. All default consumers resolve this location independently of the project directory. Explicit --store PATH overrides remain available for install, which, exec and environment commands; relative overrides resolve from the invocation directory. Use --store .oyzu/tools explicitly to inspect/reuse a previous project-local store. Existing contents are not automatically moved or deleted. Store routing is implemented; complete context-independent lock matching, automatic existing-content reuse and user-global selection remain under the active implementation brief. Installation requests metadata and the archive through Oyzu's existing HTTP host fetcher, using https://nodejs.org/dist/ unless an administrative connector route applies (see below). It checks the archive against Node's declared SHA-256, derives the layout from the extracted metadata library, stages and publishes the installation, then commits the lock through the existing lock-edit transaction. The lock explicitly records digest-only verification; it does not claim a verified publisher signature. An existing incompatible lock fails rather than being silently replaced. A failed installation does not publish a new lock. install --frozen requires an existing compatible lock and never resolves a new version. Both ordinary and frozen installs reuse an already installed selection after verifying its receipt and contents; this path needs no network and leaves the lock unchanged. If the installation is absent, Oyzu first verifies the cached archive against the locked digest and size, then restores the installed tree. Only a missing archive requires acquisition from the selected route; invalid cached content fails instead of silently downloading a replacement. install --offline forbids metadata and artifact networking. It requires an existing compatible lock and either a verified installation or its cached archive. Combine it with --frozen to explicitly prohibit lock edits. Missing locks or archives fail with an online-install remedy. Run ordinary install online to create the initial lock and acquire the required bytes. which node prints the selected receipt entrypoint. Trusted PATH overrides can choose another program during exec. Inspection shares read-only developer selection and verified installation lookup, makes no network request and does not install or launch anything. A missing installation fails instead of returning a system PATH executable. Without a compatible pin, inspection can reuse matching recorded installations; it never creates a lock. Developer exec composes configured tools with ordinary executable lookup on PATH. Missing configured tools install on invocation by default through Oyzu's existing acquisition, lock and receipt machinery. Compatible locked versions are retained; a new configured selection may publish oyzu.lock. This behavior is separate from controlled build admission: system PATH cannot satisfy a locked build requirement. See invocation controls. The selected installation leases remain held during native execution. Arguments, streams, cwd and native exit status pass through; no shell expression is inferred. exec also accepts an explicit absolute or relative executable path. It resolves relative paths against -C/the invocation directory and applies the same developer selection, configuration eligibility and environment. For example: oyzu exec -- ./bin/development-runner "argument with spaces" oyzu exec -- /usr/bin/python3 scripts/check.py On Windows, use a full executable path such as oyzu exec -- C:\Python313\python.exe scripts\check.py. Drive-relative paths such as C:python.exe are rejected as ambiguous. A program started this way can find the selected Node at the front of PATH; the explicit program itself is a requested development command, not a verified locked tool. This is ordinary development execution, not the hermetic build executor. Invoke an interpreter explicitly for scripts that need one. No implicit shell parsing is added. Bare commands use the composed PATH, including ordinary globally installed executables. Commands absent from PATH fail with COMMAND_NOT_FOUND. Explicit missing paths and directories fail lookup; invocation preparation may first install configured tools when automatic installation is enabled. which npm returns the bundled npm JavaScript entry point; exec npm and the npm shim launch it with the same verified Node interpreter. Managed execution and process-tree/signal supervision remain unfinished. Exercise the actual explicit-path flow against the retained two-project acceptance workspace with: python tooling/test-tool-exec.py --cli PATH_TO_FEATURE_ENABLED_OYZU --workspace PATH Linux amd64 passed this scenario with container networking disabled on 2026-10-02. Native Windows/macOS explicit-path execution acceptance remains pending in CI.

oyzu exec -- bash scripts/check.sh and oyzu exec -- sh scripts/check.sh use the same developer selection, composed PATH, tool environment and child-stream/exit contracts as other exec commands. Configured tools follow invocation install controls; Oyzu does not install the host shell or add implicit shell parsing. Linux/macOS resolve these shell names normally on PATH. Trusted project PATH prepends precede selected tool directories. On Windows, bare bash/sh select a native shell in this order: bash.exe/sh.exe on the composed PATH, excluding %SystemRoot%\System32 and %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\WindowsApps WSL launchers/aliases. Git for Windows' bin\bash.exe/bin\sh.exe, derived from git.exe found on PATH under cmd, bin, mingw64\bin, mingw32\bin or usr\bin. Git\bin under %ProgramFiles% or %ProgramFiles(x86)%, then %LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\Git\bin. If no native shell is found, the error describes the search and requires Git for Windows' shell. Make an existing Git installation discoverable or supply its explicit executable path. No WSL fallback occurs. Explicit paths still select exactly the requested executable. The host shell itself is not a locked tool. Git Bash/MSYS converts ordinary Windows PATH entries to its POSIX form on startup; Oyzu continues exporting ordinary drive paths, not verbatim \\?\ paths or a manually rewritten POSIX PATH. The same resolver serves host tasks, including shell-string tasks. tooling/test-tool-exec.py also checks bare bash/sh, argv tasks and shell-string tasks against the real pinned Node executable in its provisioned acceptance workspace. These additions still need desktop/CI execution on Windows, Linux and macOS; earlier explicit-path results do not establish this coverage.

A project can request both tools in the same TOML file: [tools] node = "22.15.0" go = "1.24.13" oyzu install oyzu which node oyzu which go oyzu exec -- node --version oyzu exec -- go version oyzu install --update node Installation resolves the configured roots, prepares missing installations and publishes one version-1 lock only after the complete selection is available. Existing content-addressed installations can be reused across single-tool and mixed projects. Failure leaves the previous lock intact; acquired cache entries may remain for reuse. --update node or --update oyzu:node resolves only Node and retains Go's exact record, version and artifact identity. The equivalent Go names preserve Node. Multiple update names select those roots; bare --update selects all configured roots. Adding a tool requires an update that includes it. Removing a tool from TOML requires bare --update. Changing an unselected request fails with TOOL_LOCK_STALE; include that tool in the update or restore its requirement. The command never edits TOML. Unchanged requests/records retain their existing text through the lock-edit contract. For portable pins, updates refresh the selected tool's recipes for every platform already recorded for that request. Unselected recipes retain their identities; the host installation is verified before the candidate portable lock is committed. Exact requests and Node/Go ranges use the same provider selection rules as pinning. The candidate passes the same native-constraint and component validation as frozen execution; updates do not bypass that contract. Adding a tool resolves its recipes using the same platform defaults and tools.platforms selection as oyzu pin. Ambiguous prior requests still require explicit pinning. Removing a configured tool changes the active selection; it does not delete shared installations or portable pins that another selection may use. Exec and shell activation acquire one verified lease for the complete selection. Both bin directories are prepended in deterministic configuration-key order, and each backend adds its environment. A Node process can therefore launch the selected Go, and vice versa. An incomplete or stale environment fails as a whole; execution does not silently use one valid tool while replacing another from ambient PATH. Shell selection identity includes every selected executable, so changing either locked tool causes the next hook to recompute the environment. env --json now includes tools (canonical IDs to executables) and executables (command names to executables). The existing tool and executable fields remain for single-tool projects; mixed projects use the maps. Sensitive environment values remain protected; ordinary configured values are visible. which accepts either selected command and still returns its path. The real runner installs both tools, changes only Node, verifies the complete Go record is unchanged, and runs Node with a Go child under the composed environment: python tooling/test-tool-mixed.py --cli PATH_TO_FEATURE_ENABLED_OYZU --workspace PATH Use --store PATH to reuse an existing shared store. Retain the workspace and repeat with --offline-check under externally disabled networking to verify frozen reuse and both tools without acquisition. Add --pin for portable pinning, multi-platform recipe refresh, exact/ranged Node updates and unchanged Go recipes. Add --add-tool with --pin to start with Node alone, add Go through a selected update, remove Go from configuration, and restore it using frozen offline reuse. Ambiguous scoped/profile selections still require explicit pinning. Add --shell bash, --shell zsh or --shell pwsh to exercise both commands through an activated shell. Linux frozen replay, Node-to-Go child execution, redacted inspection and mixed Bash activation passed with networking disabled on 2026-10-02. Windows mixed execution and Linux portable add/remove/update flows also passed during extraction on 2026-10-05; native macOS remains unverified.

Host target mapping currently covers Linux amd64 GNU, Windows amd64 MSVC and macOS arm64. On 2026-10-02, Linux amd64 under Rust 1.95 passed both versions, shared-store project switching, frozen/repeat installs, which/exec agreement, arguments, cwd, TOML environment, unchanged locks and exit status. The same projects then passed replay under Docker --network none. A separately mounted store also passed installation/publication. Removing the installed trees while retaining their real archives then passed install --frozen --offline restoration and execution for both versions with networking disabled; an empty cache failed as expected and locks remained byte-identical. The original install/exec scenario at revision 73bb33d passed on macOS arm64 and Windows amd64 in CI run 37045134221. Frozen/which/restoration then passed on macOS at 01e81be in run 37047681781 and Windows at 1acb16f in run 37048375166. Run the real user acceptance scenario with Python 3.11+ and public Node access: python tooling/test-tool-management.py --cli PATH_TO_FEATURE_ENABLED_OYZU The runner creates two projects selecting Node 22.15.0 and 22.14.0, installs into one store, checks frozen version selection, literal arguments, cwd, TOML environment and exit-code propagation, and revisits both projects. These are actual downloads and executions, not mocked backend or store behavior. Use --workspace PATH to retain these projects, then rerun with the same path and --offline-check in an environment with network access disabled. The replay checks frozen and ordinary install reuse, which/exec executable agreement, unchanged locks and both project versions. --offline-check itself does not disable networking; the surrounding environment must enforce that condition. Add --restore-cached to move the retained installed trees to WORKSPACE/installs-before-restore and restore them through install --frozen --offline, then verify actual execution and empty-cache errors. Use this restoration check once per retained workspace; the backup is preserved. With online access and a retained workspace, exercise explicit updates with: python tooling/test-tool-updates.py --cli PATH_TO_FEATURE_ENABLED_OYZU --workspace PATH The runner changes the first project's requirement from 22.15.0 to 22.14.0, checks stale-selection rejection, updates and executes the new version, then restores 22.15.0 through an explicit update. It checks that the second project is unchanged and a repeated update preserves lock bytes. On failure it retains the workspace at the failing step for diagnosis. This complete update scenario passed on Linux amd64 with Rust 1.95 on 2026-10-02 and Windows amd64 at 1acb16f in CI run 37048375166. Native macOS update acceptance passed at e335d70 in run 37051685318. The complete Linux mixed runner also passed from a fresh project on 2026-10-02: initial installation, Node-only update preserving the exact Go record, rejection of a changed unselected requirement, frozen reuse and cross-tool execution. This extends the offline replay evidence above; native mixed CI remains pending. Remaining functional work includes other tools, native constraints, scoped/profile/multi-platform updates, managed connector grants and selection, npm entrypoints, full shim/shell lifecycle qualification and build handoff. Managed configuration is explicitly rejected by this standalone proof. Child stdio currently carries internal metadata; authenticated worker IPC, full process tree cleanup and further hardening are deferred. Transitive notices/SBOM and distribution approval remain separate from the authorized development import. Native checkpoint: at 1c2bd16, CI run 37056475928 passed Windows PowerShell profile installation/removal and explicit-path exec on both Windows and macOS. Its Linux job passed Go installation, compilation, cached restore and shell execution. Windows Go and macOS profile failures were corrected subsequently; the corrected native results remain pending. See the consolidated review checkpoint for the remaining functional scope and evidence boundaries.

oyzu pin --dry-run and oyzu pin show one requirement row per kind, name and constraint across the selected matrix, with an affected-target count. Different constraints remain distinct. Rust components retain their formatting, linting and coverage purposes. Installation support describes the current host's capability, not proof that the tool is installed: pin does not check availability. Use oyzu tools current for that metadata observation. The JSON inventory includes consolidated requirements with targets and sources, while retaining the original per-target facts. Native and isolated build diagnostics use the same summary, emitting a request only once even during replanning. This presentation consolidation does not merge lock identities, platform recipes, constraints or execution requirements. Unsupported discovery remains explicit. External linker/SDK prerequisites remain separately provisioned. Human tables wrap long cells within columns at ordinary terminal widths; only very narrow terminals use labeled records. Pin platform coverage uses OS, architecture and ABI columns. A dry-run success does not mean tools were installed. Pin shows the requested version separately from the tool name. It uses the resolver-selected request before lock metadata resolution, including configured requests and builder defaults. Components marked With Rust share the selected Rust toolchain; they are not independently pinned. Multiple target requests remain visible. JSON retains these requests by tool and target in requested_versions.

Pinned Rust distribution inputs use 8 MiB HTTP range requests. Each request keeps the broker's 45-second deadline, source/redirect authorization and bounded retries; a progressing large download no longer has to fit into a single request deadline. The response ranges must be contiguous, match the requested offsets and lengths, and agree on the total size. The complete artifact must still match its locked SHA-256 before rustup can use it. The existing 256 MiB artifact and 1 GiB session byte limits include partial/failed transfer bytes as before. A server that ignores ranges may return a complete first response, still subject to the ordinary request timeout and byte limit. A full response after partial segments, inconsistent ranges or digest mismatch fails closed. No alternate source or unpinned download is used. Errors identify the pinned Rust input name without including upstream URLs or credentials. Other acquisition paths retain their existing request behavior.
Tool Go Installation. Tool Proxy Acquisition. Tool Shell Environment. Tool Rust Installation.

With Node configured in oyzu.toml, a fresh oyzu install records both Node and its bundled npm in the verified installation. oyzu exec -- npm ci and bare npm ci in an oyzu activate shell use that installation. Persistent native shims produced by activation can also run without an active shell session; they resolve the current project on each invocation. No global npm is selected. oyzu which npm reports the JavaScript entry point, not a standalone Windows executable; use exec npm rather than attempting to execute that path directly. npm's existing version is the one bundled with the selected Node release. There is no separate npm request or version pin for that bundled copy. An explicit npm selection can override it. Known bundled npx and Python/pip aliases are discovered inside an already leased installation, so accepted existing receipts and frozen locks do not need edits or reinstalling. This does not revive rejected legacy lock/receipt formats. which pip reports the backing Python interpreter; exec pip and the pip shim supply -m pip. Ordinary environment configuration is passed to npm through existing execution and shell contracts. The local broker experiment sets proxy and CA variables without storing upstream tokens in npm configuration. This is a laboratory integration, not automatic platform connector discovery or authorization. Without the experimental session setting below, explicit native command-line settings can still override environment routing. No machine-wide network enforcement or prevention of deliberate bypass is claimed. Publishing is supported only through oyzu publish. Developer sessions must use an upstream read-only identity and never receive a publish connector. The npm launcher is not itself a method filter or a security boundary against a user who owns the host. The publishing command's platform integration is outside this proof. The Node/npm layout covers Windows and Unix distributions; measured results and OS qualification belong in the linked qualification record, not inferred support.

For the isolated local-agent experiment, configure this once in user configuration: [npm] sessionEndpoint = "http://127.0.0.1:43100/session" This is an opt-in laboratory integration, not a working platform login workflow. The local agent must already be running and supply the experimental session contract. The compiled CLI has no developer login command; existing managed-mode enrollment safeguards remain unchanged. Remove the setting to return to standalone behavior. npm.sessionEndpoint is absent by default and follows normal configuration precedence/constraints. It accepts numeric-loopback HTTP only, with no credentials, query or fragment. No project-specific proxy settings are required. After installing the requested Node into a fresh store, use oyzu exec -- npm ci or activate the shell and run npm ci. Each invocation resolves its current project and contacts the endpoint; shell activation itself remains offline. User transport settings are intentionally excluded when Oyzu detects CI. This user-level setup therefore covers local developer sessions, including non-TTY shells, but does not configure CI jobs. CI needs an eligible job/administrative configuration source and its own authorized agent session; automatic CI bootstrap is not implemented by this experiment. An absent effective endpoint retains standalone behavior; it is not a managed fail-closed configuration. The experiment supports command-first install, i, ci, run, run-script, view and session-approved audit. Help/version skip the agent. Other command spellings, flags before the command, and native npm publish are unsupported in this mode. Publishing requires oyzu publish, whose integration is not part of this experiment. These restrictions do not certify that arbitrary npm scripts cannot bypass Oyzu; developers still control their machines. The child receives proxy, registry/scope, audit and public CA settings, never an upstream credential from this adapter. No .npmrc is generated. The installed npm resolves its effective configuration before execution; conflicting proxy, registry, bypass, audit or TLS overrides stop with NPM_ROUTING_CONFLICT. Remove the conflicting option/configuration and retry. Nonempty inherited NO_PROXY also conflicts. Approved environment values can legitimately supersede project settings through npm's normal precedence. Audit defaults to disabled because it submits dependency names; an unapproved explicit audit returns NPM_AUDIT_DENIED. NPM_SESSION_UNAVAILABLE means the agent is absent, denies access or cannot prepare it. Start/restore the agent and retry; there is no direct network fallback, even for cached dependency commands. NPM_SESSION_INVALID identifies an invalid response or missing public CA file. NPM_CONFIG_UNAVAILABLE means native effective config could not be inspected. npm execution retains native exit status after preparation. Native caches and installed packages persist normally; child settings do not modify the parent shell. Working directory association is unverified local context. Nested npm lifecycle commands re-enter the shim and request their own session; frontend recursion markers end at the verified native tool handoff. This proves neither hostile-host isolation nor production IPC authentication/TLS provisioning. Upstream ACLs must supply narrow read-only authority. The Linux merge regression covers managed installation, private retrieval and Bash with Node 22.15.0 using a loopback HTTP fixture. macOS, broader Linux transport coverage, other npm versions and real local-agent/account lifecycle need qualification. Measured outcomes and failed attempts are recorded in automatic-session qualification.

oyzu install uses the shared linear progress display: a checking status per tool followed by a ready or failed marker. Interactive terminals update the active status and show bounded installer output beneath it; redirected output retains a start and completion line without repeating intermediate verification messages. --json retains structured diagnostics on stderr and a machine-readable result on stdout. -q suppresses progress. Verification is still performed before a tool is marked ready.

Pin/build requirement resolution includes explicit tools from each selected target’s resolved configuration, even when that target’s builder does not request them. For example, repository tools.rust remains a resolvable configured requirement inside a nested Node project. Builder requirements retain their components and native constraints; configured entries do not fabricate build stages. Unsupported tool adapters still fail explicitly. This does not supply missing versions for other tools or add native multi-target execution support.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-shell-environment.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. See tool management for shared prerequisites, command conventions and qualification limits.

oyzu env and oyzu env --json inspect available selected installations and report selected executables and effective environment variables. Ordinary values are visible; credential-like fields and detected sensitive values are redacted. See project environments for provenance and PATH views. Missing tools are omitted without installation; invalid locks, corrupt receipts and enforced denials retain their errors. Explicit project pins and commands with no configured tools do not read unrelated remembered developer selections. Those snapshots are loaded and validated only when an unpinned requirement actually needs installed-selection fallback. An invalid remembered snapshot still fails that fallback; it is never accepted as a usable pin or silently deleted. The environment composition is shared with exec: literal TOML values plus the selected binary directory prepended to inherited PATH. An already leading selected directory is not prepended again. exec --json captures application output in stdout and stderr fields alongside exitCode; default execution passes the streams through. Place Oyzu flags before the child argument separator --. To explicitly print assignments with their actual values, select a shell: # Bash eval "$(oyzu env --shell bash)" node --version For Zsh use --shell zsh. For PowerShell 7 use: oyzu env --shell pwsh | Out-String | Invoke-Expression node --version --shell with --json returns the rendered code in a script field alongside the shell name. Without --json, code remains directly evaluable. See the CLI output contract. Environment patches use the extracted mise diff operations in the internal oyzu-shell library. Bash, Zsh and PowerShell rendering run directly through that library, without initializing a mise backend worker. Windows POSIX path normalization retains the pinned upstream utility. It performs no network or installation. Values remain literal, including quotes, dollar signs and shell metacharacters; they are not interpreted as config code. Shell activation (including env --shell), prompt hooks, shims and oyzu exec require project/local environment and PATH additions to pass folder trust: environment consumers can interpret literal values as executable instructions. Untrusted projects keep their selected tools and skip those additions without prompting. oyzu run, oyzu build, build planning and the build configuration digest always retain those settings. oyzu env shows configured values and provenance, marking project entries skipped until trusted when shell/exec use would withhold them. PowerShell literals escape ASCII apostrophes and all four Unicode single-quote delimiters, including values and frontend/profile/shim paths. Rendering requires UTF-8 environment values. Pass the same --store used for installation when using a shared store. This is a one-time application to the current shell. It does not install prompt hooks, automatically switch on directory changes or restore old values. Use the activation commands below when testing automatic transitions instead. The lookup/rendering lease ends when the command returns; this does not establish an active-shell retention lease. Those lifecycle capabilities remain unfinished.

From an installed project, start a session in Bash or Zsh: eval "$(oyzu activate bash)" # use zsh for Zsh node --version cd ../another-installed-project node --version oyzu deactivate For a shared store, pass --store /absolute/store to activate. Without that option each hook uses the default user-level store. Root/profile options from activation are retained for the session. The PowerShell equivalent is oyzu activate pwsh | Out-String | Invoke-Expression. The original PowerShell activation/switching/deactivation scenario passed on Windows at 83049fa in run 37050580618; native acceptance with the newly added shims remains pending. The internal oyzu-shell library renders Bash, Zsh and PowerShell prompt/directory hooks and deactivation using extracted mise mechanics. Oyzu adapts the generated namespace before inserting the real frontend path through the renderer's literal quoting. The hooks call this same Oyzu binary, never a separate mise executable. A missing command may install its configured provider on invocation, subject to the controls below. The shell retries with the refreshed environment. Prompt/directory hooks use read-only local selection, with no network, installation or project task execution. PowerShell missing-command acquisition requires the command name to appear as a token in the initialized PSReadLine session's latest typed line, matching Mise; noninteractive script lookups do not trigger that hook's installation path. Explicit exec/tasks and already invoked native shims retain their separate invocation controls. Changing directories applies the new project's locked Node and literal TOML environment. Unchanged selection emits no environment changes. Unchanged prompts compare the working directory, relevant environment inputs and source/lock metadata before resolving configuration or reading lock contents. Creation and deletion of sources also invalidate the cached selection, including changes to the user's trusted-project records. Installed executables, payloads and receipts are not watched or hashed: installation verifies them once, and subsequent use trusts the installation. The hook observes each prompt without a time-to-live delay or background service. Old records without freshness data refresh once. Unreadable inputs force resolution. Failed selection still clears the previous environment and reports unavailable. This is prompt freshness, not an integrity cache: metadata checks do not detect all hostile/backdated content edits. exec, shim dispatch, tasks and builds continue obtaining verified leases. oyzu env also retains verified inspection; it can take longer than config show. Neither consumes a prompt cache as execution authority. The embedded mise revision is part of backend identity; after changing it, refresh pins and install through oyzu pin --refresh and oyzu install, never by rewriting receipts. Oyzu records changed variable values and PATH under its native per-user state directory's shell-sessions folder; the environment carries a random token. Unix directories are private (0700), with ownership and ancestor protection checked; linked directories are rejected. Windows uses the user's LocalAppData state directory and rejects reparse points. Session files are atomically replaced. Deactivation removes the record after rendering cleanup; JSON deactivation is a preview and retains the record. Missing or unreadable records produce a warning and hook/marker cleanup, while shims fall back to ordinary configuration options. Values from a lost record cannot be reconstructed: open a new terminal for a clean environment, or activate again to begin a fresh session. On activation, records older than 30 days are reclaimed only when their shell is gone (or the activation was never consumed); records belonging to live shells are retained.
